Welcome to CALM 10

In this course you will practise decisions about careers, work, money and personal information. You will read realistic documents, follow an explained example, try a decision with help and apply the method to a new situation.

All the information needed for the course activities is supplied here. People, employers, budgets and incidents in the cases are fictional. Official reading records are labelled with their source and the date they were checked. You can open the original page for current information, but you do not need another account or a paid service to do the lesson.

Start with one lesson

  1. Open Find evidence about your strengths.
  2. Read Start here to see what you will make. Open How to complete this lesson for the steps.
  3. Meet the person and read the documents. Their facts are the evidence for your answers.
  4. Follow the explanation and example. Try the supported activity, check its feedback and revise.
  5. Complete the new independent case. Compare the model, review the four criteria and select Complete lesson.

You can pause at a section break. A lesson's fields save automatically when saving is available; check the status beside your work before closing. My Work lets you return to a draft, see completed lessons and download a backup.

What the symbols mean

  • Draft: you have started a final response.
  • Green check / Complete: you have filled the required final fields, reviewed the criteria and selected Complete lesson.
  • Practice feedback: explains a choice or calculation. You can try again.
  • Model response: one supported answer with reasoning. Other answers may work when the documents support them.
  • Optional reference: opens further reading. The in-course record supplies what this lesson needs.

A completion check records your review. It does not mean a computer has judged the quality of your writing. Editing the independent answer reopens that lesson for review and keeps your text.

If you get stuck

I do not understand a word. Open Core vocabulary beside the lesson guide. Return to the sentence where it appears and connect it to the case.

I do not know which document to use. Read the heading directly above the task. It names the person and record. A “new situation” has its own documents; do not carry numbers from the previous example.

I do not know how to begin. Open the first-step hint. Find one fact before writing the whole answer. The complete model remains available whenever you need it.

My calculation differs. Check the units, time period and rounding note. Compare one step at a time. A blank field is different from zero.

My answer is different from the model. Check whether every claim is supported, whether you respected the case constraints and whether you explained your choice. Use the self-checks to revise. The writing tasks can have more than one sound response.

A website or video will not open. Continue with the in-course reading record and written explanation. No required answer is hidden in a video or behind an external login.

Saving is unavailable. Keep this page open and download your work. The status will tell you when a browser save failed. A download is a backup file; it is not a submission.

Plan your pace

The course has 40 lessons in seven sections. The suggested schedule spreads approximately 75 hours across 15 weeks. Some lessons need more time for calculations or revision. Use a section break as a stopping point and return to your last work.

Name two possible study times and one place you will pause to review.

Optional practice. Use the supplied exercise rates.

One program page has no date. Another is current and lists a prerequisite the learner has not completed. Which note is sound?

An award message asks for a bank password today. What is the next action?

Find the base, change and result

For a 10% increase on $50, the base is $50 and the change is 0.10 × $50 = $5. The result is $55. For a decrease, subtract $5 to get $45. Interest also needs a time period and a stated method; use the method supplied in that lesson.

A new worker is asked to use an unlabelled cleaning chemical without training. Choose an immediate action and a follow-up.

Change an input to explore the scenario.

Optional experiment · separate from your lesson response

Investigate a sample pay stub

Now investigate a different fictional pay period: 20 regular hours at $16.50; 2 additional hours at $24.75; listed deductions total $31.40. Enter gross and net pay, then explain how it differs from Mika’s example.

Change an input to explore the scenario.

This is arithmetic practice using invented deductions. A real pay stub may show taxes, CPP, EI, other deductions, and year-to-date amounts.

Optional experiment · separate from your lesson response

Adapt a monthly budget

Adjust a fictional budget after an unexpected cost. Compare the remaining amount with the desired savings contribution.

Change an input to explore the scenario.

The output is a balance check. Explain the change you would make; a negative number is a decision prompt, not a grade.

Optional experiment · separate from your lesson response

Explore the life of a loan

Start with the fictional $1,000, 12-payment case in the document above. For Alex and Ren, choose the ordinary monthly-rate loan: annual rate divided by 12, with interest rounded to cents. The Canadian semi-annual option is available for an optional comparison. Existing saved experiments keep their selected convention.

Optional rate reset for a fictional loan

Leave both fields blank for a constant rate. At the start of the reset month, calculate a new payment over the remaining original months. Fees stay separate.

Change an input to explore the scenario.

Alex and Ren use the ordinary-loan option, which divides the nominal annual rate by 12. The optional Canadian mortgage model converts semi-annual compounding to a monthly rate. This classroom model displays rounded amounts; it does not predict a real offer.

Optional experiment · separate from your lesson response

Compare debt repayment priorities

Two fictional debts accrue monthly interest. Compare directing an extra monthly amount toward the higher-rate or lower-balance debt.

Change an input to explore the scenario.

The simulation uses fixed rates, no new charges, and monthly compounding. Real minimum-payment rules and fees vary by agreement.

Input bounds: starting balance and monthly deposits $0–$100,000; whole years 1–50; annual effective return −50% to 50%; annual fee 0–10%; inflation −10% to 20%.

Optional experiment · separate from your lesson response

Test a saving scenario

Change the initial amount, monthly contribution, time, illustrative return, annual fee, and inflation. Compare nominal and purchasing-power values.

Change an input to explore the scenario.

The result is a scenario, not a guaranteed investment outcome. It assumes regular monthly contributions and a constant rate.

Optional experiment · separate from your lesson response

Stress-test an integrated financial plan

A fictional learner plans monthly essentials, flexible spending, debt repayment, and saving. Add a surprise cost and choose an adjustment.

Change an input to explore the scenario.

Check required payments and essential needs before adjusting. Explain the trade-off and how the plan will recover.

Optional experiment · separate from your lesson response

Classify and respond to a scam

Three fictional messages use different tactics. Classify the first, then choose the safest way to verify it.

Change an input to explore the scenario.

Other categories include emergency, romance, purchase, and investment scams. A familiar logo or urgent language does not verify a sender.

Optional experiment · separate from your lesson response

Compare two phone agreements

Test a second fictional twelve-month offer. Unlike the document above, this version has six promotional months and six regular months; no device instalments are included in the calculator. Compare the listed costs before tax, then name the missing terms.

Change an input to explore the scenario.

Check device financing, coverage, taxes, cancellation, overage, and post-year pricing before recommending a real plan.

Core vocabulary
Something you want to explore or enjoy doing.
An ability demonstrated through an action, rather than only a claim.
Something that matters to you about how or where you work.
A specific observation or record that supports a claim.

Start here

What can an experience tell you about a possible career?

Jordan likes making things look clear. After seeing Jordan's school poster, a friend says, “You should become a graphic designer.” It is an idea worth exploring, but Jordan wants a better reason than a friend's opinion.

You will help Jordan turn experiences into useful evidence. Later you will prepare a strengths-and-goals card for Amina, using a different set of notes. You do not need paid work experience, a survey account or personal information to complete this lesson.

Work through Meet the situation, Learn the method, Follow a complete example, Practise with support, Check your understanding, Apply independently and Review and complete. Pause after the practice if you need a break; your entries save automatically. The time you need will depend on how much you revise. Practice is a place to try ideas. Amina's completed card is your final saved evidence.

Optional references and word help stay available beside this roadmap. Everything needed for the tasks is on this page.

Meet the situation and read the documents

Jordan's experience notebook

An experience note records what happened during a particular task. It is different from a reference letter or an interest survey: it supplies actions that a reader can examine. Jordan wrote the notes below after two school activities. All people and events in these notes are fictional.

Experience What needed doing What Jordan did What happened afterwards
School-event poster Two classmates could not find the time and location on the first draft. Jordan moved those details to a larger heading, reduced decorative text and asked the classmates to check the revision. Both classmates found the time and location without help.
Three-person science display Three parts of a display needed to be ready by Friday. Jordan asked each person what they could finish, made a shared checklist and arranged a Wednesday check-in. The group noticed a missing caption on Wednesday, finished it Thursday and had all three parts ready Friday.

Jordan's reflection note

“I enjoyed deciding which poster information people needed first. I liked changing the draft after feedback. On the display, I liked making the next step clear, but I found chasing missing work tiring. I would like work with a reasonably predictable schedule. I also want chances to improve an idea after feedback. My current career goal is to investigate work that combines visual problem solving and clear explanations. My life goal is to keep regular time for activities outside work.”

A career goal describes a direction for work or learning. A life goal describes something you want your wider life to support. They can influence each other without being identical.

Check the notebook. Which detail is observable evidence of Jordan's action?

Learn the method

Separate three kinds of clue

An interest is something that attracts your attention or that you enjoy doing. A skill is an ability used to carry out a task. A work value is something you want work to support, such as a predictable schedule, variety, helping people or time to improve your work. “I enjoy drawing” is an interest. “I rearranged information so two readers could find it” gives evidence of a skill. “I want regular hours” describes a value. None of these clues chooses an occupation on its own.

A person can enjoy an activity while needing practice. They can also perform a task well and dislike doing it repeatedly. Jordan's successful checklist suggests organization, while the reflection says repeated follow-up was tiring. Record both. Hiding a difficulty would make the career question less useful.

An interest or strengths inventory organizes a person's answers to a set of questions about themselves. Its results describe what the person reported; they do not independently prove a skill or assign a career. Imagine an inventory suggests “creative work” for Jordan. The poster notebook adds actual evidence, while the schedule preference adds a condition to investigate. If a suggested direction conflicts with experience, keep the conflict as a question rather than accepting the label. No inventory account or survey score is needed here.

Make the action visible

“Jordan is creative” is a claim: a statement you would like a reader to accept. Evidence is the information that supports it. Useful evidence names the setting, the person's action and an observable result. The result need not be an award. Two readers finding the information is a result because it shows what changed after the revision.

Be precise about whose action it was. Jordan arranged the check-in; the group finished its display. Writing “Jordan did every part” would give Jordan credit for actions the notebook does not report. You can explain a person's contribution to a team result without pretending they worked alone.

Build a cautious pathway idea

A transferable skill can be useful in more than one setting. Organizing information might matter in a poster, a set of instructions or a customer explanation. Transfer does not mean that someone already knows all the technical work in a new role. A school example provides a reason to investigate; it is not proof of professional expertise.

Use this sequence:

Recorded action → possible skill → limit of the evidence → question about work.

For example, “revised a poster after feedback” can support “some skill in making information clearer.” Its limit is one school task. A useful question is whether Jordan enjoys repeated revisions for other people's purposes. That question could change the plan; “Is design good?” is too broad to guide a comparison.

Connect the idea to a goal

A provisional goal is a goal you can revise as evidence develops. It might be “Compare two roles that use visual explanations” rather than “Choose my lifelong occupation today.” Keep a career goal and a life goal visible when deciding what to investigate. A role might use a skill but conflict with a strongly held work value.

Financial goals can shape the route too. Wanting to keep training costs within a stated budget is different from wanting the highest advertised wage. Later lessons will connect goals to complete cost records. Here you are learning to state the direction and values before assuming a particular occupation, income or training expense will fit.

Dated reference record — alis (Alberta’s career information site): The article Explore Your Occupational Options, read on September 28, 2026, encourages investigating several possibilities and asking about tasks, working conditions and preparation. In this lesson, that becomes a question you can answer from supplied notes; it is not a requirement to interview anyone or leave the course. Watch or read · FINLIT 101

Factors Affecting Your Values

You have read Jordan’s notebook. Watch or read how family, friends and other influences can shape what matters to a person. Listen for the difference between a preference and something a person can demonstrate.

Read the video transcript

Visuals: a presenter speaks to the camera against a plain blue background; the spoken examples carry the main point.

Your values are kind of like your inner cheerleader. They motivate you to do the things you care about. Your values represent what you think is most important in life. So let's take a closer look at that inner cheerleader. Now this is important. Why you ask? Because your values help shape all of your financial decisions. What material things are important to you? How much money will you need? And how will you earn that money? Your values affect these decisions. But what influences our values? Our family, teachers, and friends play a big role in determining our values. Movies, music, and culture can make an impact too. Your value set is made up of a number of factors. Let's picture a big value web. Everyone's will look different. This is a big web. These values influence your financial decisions. Do you want a budget for a gym membership? Own an electric bike or maybe a motorbike? Do you want a budget for basketball tickets? Or maybe you're a fan of the symphony?

Jordan wants a reasonably predictable work schedule. How should that note be used?

Read a worked example

See how Jordan’s poster note becomes an evidence card

Instructions: read the worked example

Read first; you do not need to write here. Use the school-event poster row in Jordan’s experience notebook. Read the completed evidence card below and look for these four parts.

  1. Find the action and result. What did Jordan change, and what could the classmates do afterward?
  2. Find the skill claim. How does the answer connect Jordan’s actions to a possible skill?
  3. Find the limit. What does this one school task leave unproven?
  4. Find the next question. How could the question help Jordan explore work that fits the stated goals?
Show more guidance

What you will do here: Read an answer that has already been completed, then follow the steps that explain how it was built. This is a worked example: it shows how to use the evidence before you try the method yourself.

An evidence card is a short written response that connects an action and its result to a possible skill, explains what the evidence cannot establish, and identifies a useful question about work. You will write your own response in the lesson’s fields.

For this example, use the school-event poster row in Jordan’s experience notebook. Read the four steps below, then find those parts in the completed paragraph.

Connect the video to this task. Use the video’s distinction as you read: Jordan’s poster action supports a skill claim; the predictable-schedule preference helps frame a question about work.

  1. Start with the recorded action and result. Two classmates could not find the time and location. Jordan moved those details into a larger heading, reduced decoration and asked for another check. Both classmates then found the details without help. This gives us something observable to use.
  2. Explain the possible skill. These actions suggest some skill in organizing visual information and responding to feedback. The claim explains what the action shows; it does more than call Jordan “brilliant.”
  3. Keep the claim within the evidence. The notebook describes one school task. It does not show that Jordan can manage a professional client’s project, use professional software or meet every workplace deadline. A useful skill claim can still have a limit.
  4. Connect a question to Jordan’s goals. Jordan wants visual problem solving and clear explanations, with regular time outside work. Asking about revisions and unpredictable deadlines could help Jordan test whether a possible role fits both goals.

The completed evidence card

“During a school poster task, Jordan enlarged the time and location and reduced decorative text after two classmates had trouble finding the details. Both readers could then locate the information without help. This suggests some skill in organizing visual information and responding to feedback. It is evidence from one school task, so it does not establish professional design expertise. Jordan could investigate visual communication work and ask how often the work involves revisions and unpredictable deadlines. This would test the career goal against Jordan's wish for regular time outside work.”

Check the example before moving on: Find the action and result, the possible skill, the limit and the question in the paragraph above. The question keeps a career possibility open for investigation; it does not promise that an occupation will fit Jordan.

Next, you will practise these same steps using Jordan’s science-display experience. You will choose a claim, write three short notes and compare them with a model.

Amina’s strengths-and-goals response
What you will produce: One strengths-and-goals card, written across the three fields below. Here, a “card” means a short written response that connects experiences, possible skills, goals and questions about work.
Meet the new person: Amina is considering practical problem-solving work. Her two experiences, goal note and possible work directions are supplied below. Use the method you practised with Jordan, with Amina’s own evidence.
Start by reading: Read both rows of Amina’s experience notes, then her goal note and the two role sketches. You have the information needed for this task here in the lesson. A role sketch is a brief description of work to investigate; it does not establish actual hours or entry requirements.



Amina's experience notes






Situation
Amina's action
Result and reflection





A bicycle brake rubbed during a community workshop.
With the workshop leader present, Amina compared the wheel movement before and after an adjustment and explained the observed difference to a neighbour.
The wheel turned without rubbing during the workshop check. Amina enjoyed finding the cause but needed help selecting the tool.




A younger cousin was learning a board game.
Amina replaced a long explanation with one demonstration turn, then asked the cousin to explain the next move.
The cousin completed the next turn without help. Amina liked making the instructions clearer.





Amina's goal note: “I want to explore practical work where I solve problems and explain useful information. I value movement during the day and a predictable time to finish. I would like to develop my technical knowledge before taking responsibility for unfamiliar repairs.”


Two fictional role sketches for inquiry: A repair-shop assistant helps identify problems and explain service information; this sketch supplies no actual employer schedule or qualification rule. A recreation activity assistant demonstrates activities and helps participants use equipment; this sketch supplies no actual balance between desk duties and active work. These are possibilities to investigate, not offers or complete occupation profiles.

What is an evidence card? A short written response that connects actions and results to possible skills, explains the limits of the evidence, and asks useful questions about work.
  1. Two examples and what they suggest: Use both the bicycle workshop and the board game. For each, describe Amina’s action, the result and a skill it could support. Identify a growth area: something Amina still needs to develop. Keep help received and limits of the evidence visible.
  2. Goals, values and two directions: Use Amina’s goal note to state her career direction and what she wants work to support in her life. Explain how each role sketch might connect to her experiences. Separate demonstrated skills from preferences such as movement or finishing at a predictable time.
  3. A question that could change each direction: Write one specific question about repair-shop assistance and one about recreation activity assistance. For each question, explain how its answer could make that direction a better or poorer fit for Amina.
Review your own reasoning: Try the three parts, then use Compare your response with a model to check how the example uses Amina’s evidence. You may open it whenever you need support. Different wording and different priorities can be reasonable; your claims must come from the supplied notes. Revise your fields, then use Review and complete to check the four statements and finish the lesson.


Use the idea in this new case. For Amina, use her own action records and goal note. Movement during the day and a predictable finish are preferences to investigate, not qualifications.

Core vocabulary
A summary of an occupation's duties, conditions and preparation for a stated place and time.
A task that is part of a role.
A feature of where, when or how the work happens.
Canada's National Occupational Classification, which groups occupations; its codes identify groups, not personal ability.
Start here
What does an occupation profile actually tell you?


Jordan's poster experience suggests an interest in making information clear. Jordan now wants to know what graphic designers do at work. A career website has much more information than Jordan needs for a first decision. Reading every number without a question could make the choice more confusing.


You will learn to separate duties, working conditions and preparation, then use a source without claiming more than it says. Your final product compares two occupations for Nia, a different fictional learner. All source information needed for that comparison is provided in dated records below. Opening a live website is optional.


The route is Meet the situation, Learn the method, Follow a complete example, Practise with support, Check your understanding, Apply independently, then Review and complete. Allow time to reread the records and revise; you can pause after any section. Practice saves separately from Nia's final comparison. A saved answer is not an automatic writing grade.


Meet the situation and read the documents


Jordan's research question


Jordan enjoyed rearranging a poster so readers could find the important information. Jordan wants work involving visual problem solving and prefers predictable finishing times. The question is: Could graphic design be worth exploring while keeping that schedule preference visible?


An occupation profile summarizes a kind of work across workplaces. It is not an advertisement for one vacancy. The source record below is a short original paraphrase of selected parts of an Alberta government profile. It keeps the source's scope and dates so you can distinguish it from the fictional learner's notes.


Graphic Designer profile — alis; Alberta






Field
Dated source record





Duties
Designers discuss project needs with clients, develop visual solutions and prepare work for approval.




Working conditions
Weekday work is usual, but deadlines can bring overtime or weekend work.




Preparation
Post-secondary design education is common; a strong portfolio is important.




Classification
2021 National Occupational Classification group 52120, Graphic designers and illustrators. The group includes more than one related occupation.




Dates
Duties, conditions and education sections show March 22, 2023. Retrieved September 28, 2026.





Optional: open Graphic Designer profile — alis (new tab) ↗. This record is sufficient for the lesson; it is not a current local job offer.


A different document: one employer's notice


A job posting advertises one opening. The following posting is invented for this lesson, not extracted from the alis (Alberta’s career information site) page.


Prairie Print Studio — Junior layout helper, fictional notice dated September 15


“Help check event flyers and prepare corrected drafts. Initial work is supervised. Usual hours are Monday to Friday, 9 a.m.–4 p.m. During the two weeks before our annual festival, one Saturday shift may be scheduled. Applicants provide three examples of layouts they have created. Previous paid studio work is helpful but is not required for this practice opening.”


Read the two documents. Which statement describes work a person would do?
Learn the method
Begin with the work, not a title


A job is a particular position with an employer. An occupation groups work with similar duties. A career is a longer path that may include different jobs, learning and other life roles. Jordan could hold a layout job while exploring the broader graphic-design occupation; neither would determine every later career choice.


A career cluster is a useful way to group related work for exploration, such as work involving visual communication. A classification system has a different purpose: it organizes occupations so sources can describe or compare them consistently. Canada's National Occupational Classification, or NOC, assigns codes to occupational groups. A code helps you check that two sources concern the same group. It is not a personal ranking or a guarantee that all jobs in the group have identical duties.


Sort what each sentence can establish


A duty answers, “What would I do?” A working condition answers questions such as, “When, where or under what demands?” Preparation concerns learning, experience or credentials used to enter the work. These categories answer different parts of Jordan's question. An appealing duty does not answer a concern about evening work.


Be attentive to words such as common, some, preferred and required. If some employers prefer experience, that is narrower than a rule that every applicant must have it. A broad profile's preparation summary is not a particular program's admission decision. A credential is a formal record of qualification; a portfolio is a selected collection of work showing what someone can do. They are different kinds of evidence.


Keep the source attached to the claim


Read a source in three passes: locate the relevant field; state the fact in your own words; explain what it supports and what it leaves open. Preserve the date and scope. An update date indicates when a section was revised. A retrieval date says when you accessed it. Accessing an older section today does not turn it into a newly updated section.


Use this comparison strip:






Question
Best starting evidence
What remains open





What tasks are typical?
Occupation-profile duties
The exact duties of one opening




Would the schedule fit Jordan?
Working conditions plus a posting
The employer's actual scheduling expectations




What preparation should be investigated?
Profile preparation section
Exact program admission and employer requirements





Disagreement can reveal a better question


A broad profile may mention deadline overtime while one posting mostly lists weekday hours. These statements can both be true. They concern different levels of detail. Do not average them or ignore the inconvenient one. Ask what the particular employer expects during busy periods. In this course, the supplied posting answers part of that question without requiring a real conversation.


Optional first-step hint: Highlight mentally the action words in a sentence. “Prepare drafts” is a duty. “On Saturday” changes the condition under which the duty occurs.


Follow a complete example
Test Jordan's first idea


I start with Jordan's interest in visual problem solving, then choose the duties field in the Graphic Designer profile. Preparing visual solutions gives a reason to explore the occupation. I have a match between an interest and a task category; I do not yet have evidence that Jordan can do every professional task.


Next I check the schedule concern. The Graphic Designer profile warns that deadlines can affect hours. The fictional posting makes that issue concrete: it includes a possible Saturday shift before the festival. A regular weekday pattern therefore does not establish that weekends are always free.


Completed research note: “Graphic design is worth investigating because its visual-solution work relates to Jordan's interest in arranging information. The Graphic Designer profile is an Alberta profile, with relevant sections updated March 22, 2023 and retrieved September 28, 2026. It also indicates that deadlines can affect hours. Prairie Print Studio's fictional posting includes a possible Saturday shift, so Jordan should not assume every job has a predictable weekday-only schedule. The next useful question is how often a particular opening changes its hours. Jordan also needs to investigate portfolio expectations before applying.”


The alternative “Jordan likes posters, so this job definitely fits” skips both the schedule and preparation. “No designer ever has regular hours” is also unsupported: the record describes possibilities, not every workplace. A careful conclusion keeps the promising connection and the remaining question together.


Next: Read the preparation evidence. Try “Classify the experience statement” before opening its comparison model.
Practise with support
Read the preparation evidence


Continue with Jordan and the same two documents. This time, focus on the posting's request for three layout examples and its statement about previous paid work.


Choose how to classify “Previous paid studio work is helpful but is not required”: universal legal requirement / preference in this opening / guaranteed admission to a program. Use Check the category. The correct category is preference in this opening. The notice does not establish a law or a program's admission policy.


Write in Evidence and source, What Jordan can conclude and One unresolved preparation question. Use two or three sentences in total. Your response should explain why Jordan can investigate this opening without pretending that three examples establish professional expertise.


Show a first-step hint
Optional hint: Keep “three layout examples” separate from “previous paid work.” One is requested evidence; the other is a stated preference.

“The Graphic Designer profile describes visual-solution work, which connects with Nia's interest in arranging images and text. Career planning and future readiness · Lesson 3

    
Compare routes into a career

    

      
Learning goal
Compare two ways toward a stated role using entry requirements, time, full listed costs and uncertainty.

      
What you will produce
A primary and backup route recommendation for Owen, supported by calculations and the facts in his new case.

    

  

  
About 35–45 minutes. Work through the supplied records, practice and final response. Your entries save automatically in this browser.

  

    How to complete this lessonOpen the six steps
    
    
      
  1. Meet Leah and find the role she wants. Read the employer notice before comparing training.
    2. 
      
  2. Read her two route notices. Check entry, length, one-time costs and monthly travel. Answer the document check.
    3. 
      
  3. Learn the decision steps. Watch the FINLIT clip or read its transcript, then follow the complete Route A example.
    4.

FINLIT referenceVideo transcript and original question

    
The FINLIT career-planning clip supplies the decision sequence used below. The original Decision Making — Key Steps Assignment 2.6, page 1, questions 1–2 asks learners to apply decision steps to training and career choices. This lesson gives you complete fictional records so the method can be practised without an outside account.

    
Read the original FINLIT questions (PDF) ↗. The PDF’s answer boxes are an image of an assignment; enter your work in this lesson instead.

  

  
Current Alberta referenceOptional real pathway research
Leah’s and Owen’s records supply every fact needed for this lesson. For a real route, check current entry, recognition, timing and costs with the provider. Open alis (Alberta’s career information site) Explore School and Program Options ↗.

  
Core vocabularyRoute, prerequisite, credential, trade-off

    
Route: the learning and work steps toward a possible role. Prerequisite: preparation needed before the next step. Credential: a record of a qualification. Trade-off: what you gain and give up with a choice.

  


  

    
Start with a decision
What is Leah trying to decide?

    
Leah likes organizing equipment and explaining how to use it. She wants to explore the Event Support Assistant role at community events. Two training routes might lead to an application. She has one year to enter the field and $1,400 for the fees, supplies and travel listed here.

    
Her decision is which route to investigate first and what to keep as a backup. A route’s name or shorter price line cannot answer that alone. Leah must see the work, read each entry condition and count every listed cost.

    
All people, employers, programs, dates and prices in this case are fictional. They provide the facts for this lesson; they are not real admission rules or employment offers.

  


  

    
Meet the situation · Read the documents
First find the destination

    
A role notice describes work the employer wants someone to do. Read this one first: its final sentence explains why Leah can compare the two routes for this particular role.

    
Harbour Events · Fictional role notice
Event Support Assistant
Practice recruitment information · not a live posting

      
Work in this role
Assist a supervisor with equipment inventories, room diagrams and visitor instructions. Follow approved venue setup procedures. This assistant role does not include electrical installation or independent repair.

      
Routes considered
For this practice recruitment, Harbour Events will consider either its four-month trainee route or Bay College’s ten-month Event Support certificate. Completion of either route does not guarantee selection.

      
What matters in an application
Clear communication, accurate checking and willingness to learn supervised procedures.

    

    
Learner record · Supplied for this case
Leah’s preparation and limits
Leah completed the fictional school courses Communication 1 and Practical Mathematics 1. She organized equipment lists for a club and wants more practice explaining unfamiliar instructions. She can live at home during either route. She has $1,400 for listed training and travel costs and wants to enter the field within one year. Living costs are unchanged between routes and are outside this comparison.

    
Now read the two route notices
Look for four things on each notice: what Leah must have before entry, how long it runs, the listed cost lines and what remains uncertain.

    

      
Route A · Harbour Events
Employer trainee route
Next selection round: March 15 · four months after selection

        
Entry
Communication 1 and Practical Mathematics 1; employer selection required.

        
Learning
Supervised venue procedures, inventory and visitor instructions.

        
Completion
Employer training record.

        
Fees and supplies
$300 fees once; $200 required supplies once.

        
Travel
$120 each month for four months.

        
Unresolved
Selection and place availability; any pay amount is not supplied.

      

      
Route B · Bay College
Event Support certificate
Apply by April 30 · ten-month program starts in September

        
Entry
Communication 1 and Practical Mathematics 2. Mathematics 1 comes before Mathematics 2.

        
Learning
Venue planning, equipment records, visitor instructions and group projects.

        
Completion
Provider’s Event Support certificate.

        
Tuition and supplies
$1,600 tuition/fees once; $250 required supplies once.

        
Travel
$80 each month for ten months.

        
Unresolved
Admission, a way to cover the cost gap and whether Mathematics 2 is offered in time.

      

    

    
Why may Leah compare these routes for the assistant role?
      
      
      
      

    

  


  

    
Learn the method
Use the decision steps to read the records

    
FINLIT gives an order for a choice, not an answer about Leah. Watch or read for the sequence below. Then use Leah’s documents to fill the steps with evidence.

    
    
Read the video transcript
Visuals: two presenters speak against a blue background. The route notices on this page contain the actual comparison facts.
Number two, make good choices. Follow our super handy decision making guide. This will help you with any decision, but will also help you make the best career choice for you. Start by defining the decision you have to make. In this case, what career to plan for, then establish your criteria. That's what's important to you in a job. Next, identify the options of most interest to you, and then evaluate those options based on your criteria. Finally, make a decision. You can always reassess and change course as you go. But following these steps will help put your priorities in focus and make the best decision you can. Career tip number three, get out and volunteer.

    
  1. Define the decision. Which route should Leah investigate first for the stated assistant role?
  2. Choose criteria. Can she meet entry now? Does it fit one year? What is the complete listed cost against $1,400? What learning matches her growth area?
  3. Compare options. Use the two notices, multiplying monthly travel by the number of months.
  4. Decide provisionally. Name a first route and a researched backup. Give a reason and a trade-off.
  5. Reassess. State what new information or changed condition would make Leah revisit the decision.

    
A credential name does not make two programs equal. Harbour Events explicitly connects both routes to this one assistant role. It does not claim that either qualifies someone for every technical job, electrical work or guaranteed paid employment.

  
What does a route’s name tell you?
A credential is a record of a qualification, such as a certificate, diploma or degree. An employer training record describes learning recognized by that employer. Similar subject matter does not make them interchangeable. A short course about equipment does not automatically authorize work requiring a different qualification. The link between a route and a destination must be stated or verified.
In this case, the employer has supplied that link for one assistant role. It has not said the routes are identical or that either leads to every technical occupation. Leah should compare the routes for the stated purpose and keep their different learning and completion records visible.
Recognize different kinds of learning routes
The names below help you interpret a provider's offer. They describe different learning arrangements; a longer list of credentials does not automatically make one route the best fit.




Term
What it means for a route comparison





Certificate
A post-secondary credential commonly used for focused preparation for an occupation. Check the particular program: some certificates are for beginning learners, while others require an earlier diploma or degree.




Diploma
A post-secondary credential preparing learners for a field or group of occupations. Its admission requirements, learning and completion requirements belong to the specific program.




Degree
A credential from a degree program. A bachelor's degree includes theoretical or academic learning; advanced degrees build on earlier study. The word alone does not identify a particular occupation's entry requirements.




Apprenticeship
A formal education route combining on-the-job learning with technical classroom training and required examinations. Check the specific trade's requirements and the qualification earned. Ordinary employer training is not automatically an apprenticeship.




Microcredential
Recognition of a specific skill or competency after a brief learning program and assessment. There is no single fixed duration or assessment format. Check what is assessed and whether the intended employer or next program recognizes it.




Dual credit
High-school programming connected with post-secondary or industry pathways. Offerings vary by school. Alberta distinguishes single-enrolled courses, which provide high-school credits, from dual-enrolled courses, whose credits appear on both high-school and post-secondary transcripts. Check the actual pathway and credit recognition; the name does not mean a whole diploma or degree has been completed.



Dated source record — checked September 28, 2026: Alberta's credential guide distinguishes program outcomes and admission requirements. ALIS explains that microcredentials assess focused skills and usually add to other learning. Alberta's dual-credit guidance distinguishes the two course arrangements above. These are category descriptions, not admission offers. Optional credential guide, optional microcredential explanation and optional dual-credit guidance.
For Leah, Route A is the employer training record described in the fictional document, not a registered apprenticeship. Route B is the fictional certificate described there. Neither record promises transfer credit, a microcredential or dual credit. Their stated connection to the assistant role is what makes this particular comparison possible.
Trace entry conditions back to today
A prerequisite must be completed before the next course or step. Route B's Mathematics 2 is not a label to copy onto a plan; Leah needs time to complete it after Mathematics 1. Her current strengths help explain why the direction interests her. Her growth area—explaining unfamiliar instructions—helps her inspect what each route teaches.
Think in a chain:
Current experience and courses → missing preparation → entry decision → route → possible work.
A career cluster can suggest related directions, but a cluster does not choose the school course for Leah. The actual route record supplies the requirement. This is why high-school planning belongs in a career comparison.


  

    
Follow a complete example
Investigate Route A first

    
Watch how each sentence comes from a line in Leah’s records. The calculation is only one part of the decision.

    
    
      
  1. Destination: Harbour Events considers its trainee route for Event Support Assistant. This says the route is relevant; it does not guarantee a place.
    2. 
      
  2. Entry and time: Leah has both named courses. Four months fits her one-year aim, if selected.
    3. 
      
  3. Listed cost: $300 fees + $200 supplies + ($120 × 4 travel months) = $980. Against $1,400 for these categories, $420 remains.
    4. 
      
  4. Fit and next check: Supervised visitor-instruction practice addresses something Leah wants to improve. She must check the March 15 selection round and place availability.
    5. 
    

    
“I would investigate Route A first. Leah has its stated school prerequisites, it runs four months and its listed direct costs total $980. Its supervised visitor-instruction practice fits her growth area. She still needs selection, so I would check the March 15 round and keep Route B as a researched alternative.”

    
Why this answer is careful: It does not claim Route A guarantees a paid job. The documents give no pay figure, and the employer has not selected Leah.

    
Optional: watch another route comparison
This course-made video uses Riley and different figures. It can help you see another example of entry, time, cost and uncertainty. Return to Leah’s notices for her answer.
Read the written equivalent
Compare two career routes by looking at the steps, not just the destination. Imagine Riley wants to explore electrical work. A career title does not tell Riley how to enter the field, what training is required, or how much time and money each route needs.
Riley draws two possible routes. One begins by investigating an apprenticeship and asking what a sponsoring employer would require. The other begins with a named training program. Both routes need current entry requirements, a credential or training outcome, and a person or source who can confirm the next step.
Here is a fictional first-pass comparison. Route A might need nine hundred dollars for tools and travel, with a possibility of wages while learning. Route B might need three thousand two hundred dollars for fees and materials and eighteen hundred dollars for travel. These are classroom figures, not actual Alberta fees. Route A depends on a suitable placement. Route B depends on admission and on whether the program counts toward later training.
Now make a decision that can change. A student who needs income soon may investigate Route A first, but should not assume a placement exists. A student who can travel may investigate Route B, but should confirm recognition and total cost. Keep a source and access date beside every requirement. Leave an honest question mark beside what is still unverified. A good career plan is a testable next step, not a promise about the future.

  
Next: Complete Route B, then compare. Try “Route B travel for ten months ($)” before opening its comparison model.


  

    
Practise with support
Complete Route B, then compare

    
Leah has Practical Mathematics 1, not Mathematics 2. Start by counting all ten travel months. Then compare Route B with the same $1,400 limit used for Route A.

    

    

    

    
Compare with a model after you try
Entry: Leah has Mathematics 1 but needs Mathematics 2 before the September start. She must check whether it is offered in time and whether Bay College admits her.
Costs: $80 × 10 = $800 travel. $1,600 + $250 + $800 = $2,650, which is $1,250 above her $1,400 limit. Route B offers a certificate and broader projects, but takes ten months and needs another course and funding. It is a real backup only if those conditions can be met.
Your wording can differ. Check that every claim points to a notice and that you have not invented funding or admission.

  
Next: Try a choice, then read why. Choose an answer and check it. Use the hint to revise; a repeated unchanged check is not another attempt.

Apply independently · New situation
Make Owen’s route recommendation

    
Owen is a different learner. Do not reuse Leah’s budget, courses or dates. Owen wants to explain places and activities to visitors. He has practised giving directions but wants to get better at checking unfamiliar information before answering. He completed fictional Communication 1 and Local Studies 1. He has $1,700 for listed training and travel, can live at home, and prefers a route of eight months or less.

Core vocabulary
The relationship between people seeking work and organizations seeking workers in a place and period.
An estimate about a future pattern, not a guaranteed outcome.
A position an employer is seeking to fill.
The occupation group, place, period and measure that a statement actually covers.
Start here
A forecast and a job search answer different questions


Noor is exploring database work. An Alberta occupation profile shows a favourable forecast label, while a search near home finds only two advertised openings. Noor wonders whether one source must be wrong.


You will identify what each record measures before using it in a decision. Your final product is an annotated comparison of two official source records and a fictional local search for Ellis, a different learner. The required sources are reproduced as short dated records in the course; no live job search, account or outside contact is needed.


Use Meet the situation, Learn the method, Follow a complete example, Practise with support, Check your understanding, Apply independently and Review and complete. Pause after annotating the first record if useful. Read slowly enough to keep occupation, place and date together. Your practice notes and final conclusion save automatically in their separate places.


Meet the situation and read the documents


Noor's decision note


Noor enjoys finding patterns in information and wants to explore database-related work. Noor can currently travel within 20 kilometres of the fictional community of Meadowcross. Moving is not included in the current plan. Noor has not yet researched training requirements. The immediate decision is whether the evidence supports further investigation, not whether to accept a job.


A labour market concerns work and workers: occupations, employment, vacancies and conditions affecting them. A forecast is an estimate about a specified period. A vacancy is an unfilled position; an advertisement is one way it may be publicized. An employment count is the number reported as employed in a defined group, not the number of openings.


The two records below answer different questions. The Database Analyst record summarizes dated information from the Alberta career website alis. Noor's Meadowcross search log describes a fictional search near home. Use these names when referring to the evidence.
Database Analyst — dated alis profile record


ALIS Database Analyst, Employment & Advancement / 3-Year Job Market Forecast
NOC means National Occupational Classification. Its number identifies an occupational group used in Canadian statistics. A group can contain several related jobs. Keep the group name beside its number so you know which workers a figure describes.






Item

Forecast label

Optional: Open Database Analyst on alis (new tab) ↗. The displayed section update, forecast period and retrieval date are different pieces of metadata. The record reports what was displayed; it does not claim every number was collected in 2022 or that the forecast starts in 2026.


Noor's fictional Meadowcross search log


A search log records how a search was done, including its limits. This log is invented for interpretation practice, not real Meadowcross employment evidence.


Search date: September 24, 2026. Area: within 20 kilometres of Meadowcross. Search words: database analyst and data administrator. Places checked: two fictional employer boards. Results: two different advertisements, both still open on that date. One requested prior database work; the other advertised a temporary data-assistant role. The log does not include unadvertised positions, all employers or future hiring.


Reading check: What does “2,470 employed in Alberta” represent in the Database Analyst record?
Learn the method
Attach a label to every number


A number without its measure can mislead. “2,470” might mean employed people, advertised vacancies or dollars; those would answer very different questions. Before using a number, identify what, which occupation/group, where and when. Also identify who published it and what the source says it does not cover.


Use a source label such as: “reported employment count; NOC 21223; Alberta; forecast source 2024–2026; ALIS page retrieved September 28, 2026.” That label is longer than a headline because it preserves the facts needed to interpret the figure.


Keep three clocks separate


The source period is the span of time described by the data or forecast. The update date records a revision to a page or section. The retrieval date is when you read it. A forecast labelled 2024–2026 does not become a forecast for 2026–2028 when someone opens it in 2026.


Different dates on a page are a reason to label information carefully. Do not silently choose the newest date and attach it to every item. For a future real decision, the original source would need checking again. For this lesson, analyze the dated record as supplied.


Compare questions before comparing answers






Record
Question it can help answer
Question it cannot settle





Provincial forecast
What pattern was projected for this occupational group and period?
Will one person be hired in a particular town?




Employment count
How many people are reported as employed in the group?
How many vacancies are open today?




Local advertisement search
What advertisements did this search capture on its date?
What is every employer planning or hiring privately?





Both a favourable forecast and a small local search can be accurate. They cover different geography, time and measures. A low advertisement count can reflect a small local market, search terms, sources checked or the search date. These are possible explanations to investigate, not facts the log has already established.


Include the cost of living when interpreting wages


Cost of living means the expense of meeting everyday needs in a place and household situation: for example, housing, food, utilities and transportation. Childcare or other needs may also matter. A higher advertised wage does not automatically leave a person with more money after those costs. Hours, the length of a job and payroll deductions also affect the income available.


Dated source record — checked September 28, 2026: ALIS advises interpreting salary information alongside location and whether work is temporary. Its moving guide identifies housing availability and costs, transportation and childcare as questions to investigate. Optional salary-context source and optional community-planning source.


For Noor, a provincial opportunity label does not answer whether work within the stated travel area would be affordable. The supplied records contain no wage offer or household expense quotes, so they cannot establish a cost-of-living comparison. A later real comparison would need dated local costs and income on the same time basis. There is no extra calculation or outside search in this lesson.


Turn uncertainty into a next step


A conditional conclusion says what the evidence supports now and which condition might change it. “Investigate further within the travel limit” is different from “there will definitely be a job.” It is also different from dismissing the occupation after one search.


Labour evidence is only part of a career decision. Noor's preparation, interest, transport and costs still matter. A source may suggest an opportunity while leaving those personal constraints unanswered. The goal is to organize evidence so a plan can be revised when new information arrives.


Optional first-step hint: Ask whether a number describes people already working or positions being advertised. If you cannot answer, reread the field heading before calculating anything.


Watch a worked decision
What does a wage headline mean?
This illustrated video uses Sam and a wage headline as a separate example. Follow how date, region and the meaning of a wage figure change a conclusion. Use the Noor and Ellis records in this lesson for your written responses.
Read the lesson’s written equivalent
A headline is a clue, not a job offer. Start with the question you are actually trying to answer. Sam wants an entry-level job within travelling distance of home.
Document A reports a provincial median of twenty-eight dollars an hour. Median means the middle observation in an ordered set. It does not mean every worker earns that amount. The data include different experience levels, so Sam cannot treat the median as a starting wage.
Document B lists a local assistant job at nineteen dollars an hour. That is useful for this particular opening, but it does not describe the entire occupation. It may also be a different role from the occupation in Document A.
Now compare the dates. The report was published in 2026, but its wage observations are from 2024. A recent publication date does not automatically make every number current.
A careful conclusion is: I have evidence worth investigating, but not a guaranteed job or starting salary. Sam's next step is to check the role, entry requirements and travel, then compare another relevant source.
Original CALM 10 classroom demonstration. Figures and people in this example are fictional; check current sources before real decisions.
Follow a complete example
Explain Noor's apparently conflicting records


I first identify the Database Analyst record as Alberta group information. Its Hot label belongs to the stated three-year forecast period. The 2,470 figure is an employment count. Neither tells me how many entry opportunities are inside Noor's travel area.


Noor's Meadowcross search log answers a narrower question: what two employer boards displayed using two search terms on September 24. It found two advertisements. I can preserve that fact without claiming it is the entire local market.


Completed interpretation: “Noor's records do not necessarily conflict. The Database Analyst record is an Alberta forecast/group record for 2024–2026; it is not a count of Meadowcross vacancies or a prediction that Noor will be hired. Noor's Meadowcross search log found two advertisements within the stated search limits on September 24. That small snapshot matters because Noor currently has a 20-kilometre travel limit, but it cannot establish every employer's future plans. I would continue investigating related entry roles and preparation using the supplied record limits. A later, broader search could change the picture. I would not recommend moving or committing to training from these two records alone.”


“There are 2,470 jobs waiting for Noor” changes employment into vacancies. “Two advertisements prove the occupation has no future” generalizes a small snapshot to every place and year. Both fail because their conclusions exceed their records.

Use Check the claim. The second statement preserves the observation. The first expands to an occupation-wide claim. The third invents a reason for the change.


In Observation with scope/date, record what changed. In What the two searches cannot establish, explain the limit. In A useful next comparison, describe another piece of evidence that would help Noor's travel-limited plan. You are drafting a research step, not carrying it out outside the course.

Start here

Tariq wants to keep two post-school directions possible: visual communication and information services. Listing interesting courses is a start, but a useful plan must put prerequisites before later courses, meet application dates and fit the time available.


You will build and revise a targeted Grade 10–12 pathway plan using complete fictional school and provider records. These invented course names and requirements are not actual Alberta admission or graduation rules. No counsellor appointment or teacher feedback is needed: the notices and feedback required for the activity are already here. Your final plan belongs to a new fictional learner, Nessa.

The rest of Tariq's fictional core program is already arranged. This exercise plans the pathway-relevant courses, not a complete real graduation audit. Reading check: Which item is required for Program A, rather than merely recommended? Select 
Learn the method
Work backwards, then check forwards


Working backwards starts with the destination. Program A needs portfolio pieces by April 15, so Tariq must have time to make them before then. Working forwards starts with what is already completed. Digital Media 1 allows Digital Media 2, which allows Portfolio Lab. A workable plan makes the backward deadline and forward prerequisite chain meet.


Draw the chain before assigning dates:


Digital Media 1 → Digital Media 2 → Portfolio Lab → two pieces before April 15.


The communication chain is separate: Foundations → Applications → Capstone. A course can support both routes. Recognizing shared preparation avoids treating the two directions as entirely separate sets of work.


Separate a requirement from a useful way to prepare


Required means the provider's record makes it a condition. Recommended means it may help but is not stated as compulsory. Tariq could theoretically prepare two portfolio pieces another way, but this case supplies a complete school route with known time and materials. Using that route is sensible without rewriting it as a universal requirement.


A course appearing on a program page does not prove the school offers it in the needed term. The provider controls its entry conditions; the school record controls the local sequence in this exercise. In a real plan, both sets of information would need current confirmation. Here their fictional dates and offerings are fully supplied.


Fit the route into a life, not just a table


The plan must respect Tariq's one-elective slot and three-hour weekly limit. Putting Digital Records and Portfolio Lab together would use two slots and five additional hours. The courses could be valuable but the arrangement would contradict the supplied capacity.


Financial and career goals also connect. The three elective material charges total $95. That fits the $100 limit for those categories, but it says nothing about future tuition. Record what a calculation covers. A plan that assumes unnamed funding or unlimited study time is not made workable by choosing an attractive program.


Use checkpoints and supplied feedback


A checkpoint is a planned moment to review evidence and make a decision. A trigger is something that makes a revision necessary, such as a cancelled course or changed application requirement. Record the old assumption, the new fact and what will change. Revision is how a plan stays useful.


Support can take the form of clear information, a different course format, an accessible planning tool or a knowledgeable service. For this lesson the support is in the school/provider notices and the model feedback. You can practise drafting a precise question without sending it. “Will Portfolio Lab finish before April 15?” is more answerable than “What should I do with my life?”

The prerequisite order works and the pieces will be ready well before the Grade 12 application date. Digital Records can then occupy Grade 12 fall, leaving winter as a buffer rather than filling every available slot.

Work-related experiences · Lesson 1
Show what you can do at work
Learning goal
Use a job advertisement and an applicant’s past experiences to write a truthful example of a skill.
What you will produce
A short application response for Rowan: one job duty and one or two sentences showing a matching experience.



How to complete this lessonRead, follow an example, practise, then write
  1. Meet Rowan. Read the situation so you know whose application you are preparing.
  2. Read the two documents. Learn what a job posting tells you, then read Rowan’s experience notes. Answer the short question about the posting.
  3. Learn how to show a skill. Read the claim-and-action comparison. Watch or read the FINLIT skills excerpt and try its short check. Then follow Rowan’s complete application example.
  4. Try the same method. In guided practice, check your evidence match, plan and write a response, then compare and revise.
  5. Check your understanding. Answer the six practice questions and read their explanations.
  6. Use a new case. In the festival application, use the new posting and notes to write your own response as Rowan.
At a check, try an answer, read the hint and revise. A different incorrect answer brings method support and an option to show the worked reasoning. Written responses use the comparison and self-checks; they are not automatically graded.


Skills for SuccessOptional reference · Government of Canada
If you want another explanation of communication or collaboration, open the official skill descriptions and choose that heading. These descriptions name skills; Rowan’s actions will supply the evidence. Everything needed for this lesson is on this page.
Read the skill descriptions ↗


Core vocabulary
A notice describing a role, its duties and what an applicant is asked to provide.
Notes about what someone actually did in a particular situation.
Something a person did that can be described specifically.
What happened after the action, limited to what the record supports.


Start with the situation
Rowan is applying for a first job
Prairie Library Hub runs Saturday activities for families. It needs someone at the welcome desk to greet visitors, explain how to sign in and help keep its records accurate. Rowan would like this job but has never been paid to work in a library.
An application is a request to be considered for a job. In this lesson, the employer asks applicants for a short written example of relevant experience.
Rowan has helped at school and community events. Those experiences may show skills the library needs. The challenge is to choose a useful example and explain it honestly, instead of simply writing “I would be good at this job.”
Your role: help Rowan prepare a short application response. You will read the employer’s advertisement, find a matching experience in Rowan’s notes and write as Rowan using “I.” You do not need to supply your own work history.
First, find out what the employer needs. Then look at what Rowan has already done.


Read the employer’s advertisement
What is a job posting?
A job posting is an advertisement an employer uses to find someone for a job. It usually tells you the job title, the work involved, qualifications or skills, practical details such as hours, and how to apply. Its duties are the tasks the successful applicant would do.
At this hub, signing in means recording that you have arrived. Reservation records list the people who have booked a place in an activity.
Read this practice notice in two passes. First, use the title and hours to understand the role. Then read “What you will do.” Those duties tell Rowan which experiences would be useful in an application.


Prairie Library Hub · Community programs
We’re hiring a Welcome Desk Helper
Help families get a clear, friendly start to our Saturday activities.
When
Four-hour Saturday events
Where
Community program welcome desk
Getting started
Training provided
About the role
You will be one of the first people visitors meet. You will help them understand the sign-in process and ask a supervisor when a request is unfamiliar.
What you will do
  • Welcome visitors and explain the sign-in process.
  • Keep reservation records accurate.
  • Ask for help with unfamiliar requests.
  • Protect visitor information.
What we are looking for
Clear communication, careful organization, sound judgement and respect for privacy.
Tell us about your experience
Give a short example of something you have done that matches one of these duties. Your example may come from school, volunteering or a community activity.
Practice job notice created for this lesson. This is a fictional opening.


Find the work Rowan would do
Which detail tells Rowan what the helper would actually do?


The posting tells us what the library needs. It does not tell us whether Rowan can do it. For that, we need an example from Rowan’s past experience.


Read the applicant’s preparation notes
What has Rowan already done?
Before applying, Rowan made notes about three school and community activities. These are experience notes: a way to remember what happened and choose examples for an application. They are not an employer’s form or a list of job requirements.
For each activity, notice the situation, what Rowan did and what happened afterwards. You will use these details to support a claim about a skill. A paid job is not the only place someone can practise a skill.


Rowan’s application notebook
Experiences I can use in an application
School welcome evening
What needed doing?
Visitors needed to sign in. Two student helpers needed to know their roles at the table.
What did I do?
I created a three-step sign-in order and explained each role to the two helpers.
What happened?
The helpers followed the order and the table opened on time.
Club attendance list
What needed doing?
The club attendance list needed to match the permission forms.
What did I do?
I checked the names against the forms, found two missing forms and asked the staff adviser before changing the list.
What happened?
The adviser obtained the missing forms. I then updated the list with verified names.
Community event
What needed doing?
Families arriving at the event needed to find their activity rooms.
What did I do?
I greeted families, gave directions and checked that each person knew where to go.
What happened?
The families could identify where their activities were taking place.
Rowan has not worked at a library or managed confidential library records. Do not add either claim.


You now have both sides of the application: the employer’s duties and Rowan’s experiences. Next, learn how to connect them in a sentence the employer can understand.


Learn how to choose evidence
Show the action behind a skill
A skill is an ability someone uses to do a task. For example, explaining instructions is a communication skill. An employer cannot tell how Rowan communicates from the sentence “I am a good communicator.” That sentence makes a claim but gives no example.
A claim on its own
“I am organized.”
This names a quality. It does not explain what Rowan did or why an employer should believe the claim.
A claim supported by an action
“I created a three-step sign-in order and explained the roles to two helpers.”
The employer can picture the action and ask Rowan how it worked.
That specific example is evidence: information supporting a claim. It must also fit the duty. Explaining sign-in roles is relevant to explaining the library’s sign-in process. Checking an attendance list is more relevant to keeping reservation records accurate.
Use three parts to make the example clear
ContextExplain where you were and what needed doing. The employer was not there, so give enough background.
ActionSay what you personally did. Use verbs such as checked, explained, organized or asked.
ResultExplain what happened afterwards. Use an outcome supplied in the notes; do not invent a success.
A result does not have to be a number or an award. “The table opened on time” is a useful result because it tells the employer the preparation was completed when needed.
Describe the original setting accurately. A school example can show a skill that could be used at work, but it does not become library experience. If an example involves other people’s information, describe the task without including their names or private records.
The demonstration below uses the welcome-evening notes. Watch how the writer chooses one duty, selects the matching action and turns it into a short application response.
Watch or read · FINLIT 101
Employment Income: skills you can show
You have met Rowan and read the experience notes. Watch or read how communication, teamwork and initiative can be used at work. For each skill label, look back at an action in Rowan’s notebook that could support it.
Read the video transcript
So let's talk about the skills you need to get and keep a job. If you want to impress your boss, you'll need three types of skills. First, you'll need some kind of talent. La la la la la la. You develop your talent or skills through education, training, and experience. Then there are employability skills. These include communication, problem solving, positive attitude, adaptability, the ability to work with others. These are key to getting and keeping a job you love. Can you multitask, plan large projects, work well with others? You know you can. Finally, there's enterprise and skills. These are not only important to entrepreneurs. Everyone can benefit from having enterprise and skills. The ability to be creative, take initiative, try new things, lead a team, learn from mistakes, and find new solutions. With your talent and skills, you'll enter the job market. Here, you'll also need to understand the forces of supply and demand.
FINLIT 101 · Employment Income: skills you can show · selected excerpt, used with permission.

Follow the writer’s decisions
Write Rowan’s first application example
Connect the video to this task. Notice how the example turns a skill label from the FINLIT clip into context, action and result. The reader can see what Rowan actually did.
We will answer the job notice’s request: “Give a short example of something you have done that matches one of these duties.” We are writing as Rowan, so the finished response uses “I.”


1. Choose one duty to answer
“Welcome visitors and explain the sign-in process.”
From the Prairie Library Hub notice
The useful action here is explain. The library needs someone who can make a process clear to other people. We need an example of Rowan explaining steps, not just an example of Rowan being at an event.


2. Find a matching action in the notes
“I created a three-step sign-in order and explained each role to the two helpers.”
From Rowan’s school welcome evening notes
This is a close match: both the job duty and Rowan’s action involve explaining a sign-in process. We also know the result—the helpers followed the order and the table opened on time. We can use those facts without guessing.


3. Build the response from the supplied facts
Context
At a school welcome evening…
Action
…I created a three-step sign-in order and explained each role to two helpers…
Result
…which helped the table open on time.
Finished application response
Duty: Explain the sign-in process.
“At a school welcome evening, I created a three-step sign-in order and explained each role to two helpers, which helped the table open on time.”
The context tells the employer where this happened. The action shows what Rowan contributed. The result explains why that contribution mattered. Together, the three parts give more useful information than “I am organized.”


4. Check that the claim stays truthful
Compare the finished response with “I am an expert at managing confidential library records.” The notes do not show expert status, a library job or responsibility for confidential records. That version adds facts Rowan cannot support.
The finished response names the school welcome evening and describes only the action and outcome recorded in Rowan’s notes. The employer can decide how that experience relates to the job.
You have seen one duty matched to one experience. Now use the same method for a different duty in the same library notice. The relevant details will be beside the task so you do not have to remember them.
