Practise with support
Help Rowan show careful record keeping
Connect the video to this task. For careful record keeping, return to the club attendance entry. Choose the checking action and its verified result; a communication label alone will not answer this duty.
This time, you will support “Keep reservation records accurate.” Accurate means correct: the names on a list should agree with the information used to check them. You will choose an experience, plan the three parts and write one or two sentences as Rowan.
1. Choose the experience that fits
Which past action most clearly shows Rowan checking information before updating it? Read the choices, select one, then check your match.


2. Plan with the club attendance notes
The club attendance example is the strongest match because Rowan checked information before changing a record. Use the excerpt below to plan your response. Short notes are enough in these three fields.
Duty from the notice
Keep reservation records accurate.
Facts from Rowan’s notes
Rowan checked the club list against permission forms, found two forms missing and asked the adviser before changing the list. The adviser obtained the forms; Rowan then updated the list with verified names.


3. Write as Rowan
Turn your notes into one or two sentences. Use “I” for Rowan’s actions. Include enough context for an employer who has never heard about the club. Do not claim that the club task was a library job.


4. Compare, then revise
Open the model whenever you need help. Your wording can be different. Compare the facts and explanation rather than trying to copy every word. Your writing is not automatically graded.
Compare my response with the club attendance model
Your response
Your writing will appear here when you enter it above.
One supported response
“For a club attendance list, I checked names against permission forms and asked the adviser about two missing forms. After the forms were obtained, I updated the list with verified names.”
Context“For a club attendance list” identifies the original task. It does not claim library experience.
ActionChecking names and asking the adviser show care with records. The writer states what Rowan did, rather than only saying “I am careful.”
ResultThe list was updated with verified names after the forms were obtained. Asking the adviser is an action; the updated list is the outcome.
Use these questions to revise
  • Can a reader tell which list Rowan was checking?
  • Have I explained the check and the decision to ask before changing the list?
  • Have I included the verified update as the result?
  • Have I removed claims about paid library work or expertise?
Make any changes in your application response above. A different sentence is acceptable when it uses the same supplied facts and shows their connection to accurate records.

Open Three Rights of Workers — CCOHS ↗
Core vocabulary
Instructions and information for a particular period of work.
Authority to carry out a specified action.
Something that could cause harm.
Information that should be accessed or shared only for an authorized purpose.
Start here
Helpful work includes knowing when to pause


Rowan has been given a first-shift sheet at Prairie Library Hub, a fictional community activity space. Some tasks can begin immediately; others require a demonstration or permission. Rowan wants to help without guessing about records, equipment or people's information.


You will use the sheet and floor plan to make a decision, explain its basis and write a precise message. At the end, you will complete two decision rows for a changed situation. This is an online simulation: you make decisions from the supplied documents, not by doing actual workplace tasks.


How to complete this lesson: Read Rowan's first-shift folder before answering the document check. Learn Read permission and responsibility together, then follow the reservation example. Try Three moments at the desk and revise with feedback. Answer six understanding questions and complete The spray and the information request. Review your two rows, check the criteria and choose Complete lesson. You can pause after the guided decisions; all work saves.


Meet the situation and read the documents


Rowan's first-shift folder


Rowan is a new helper. Morgan is the shift lead: the person assigned to explain tasks and approve work in this case. Rowan's shift is Monday, 9 a.m.–1 p.m. The first stop is the welcome desk. A shift brief is a short set of instructions for that working period; it is not evidence that the new worker already knows every task.


Prairie Library Hub — first-shift sheet


Start now: welcome visitors, prepare blank activity cards and restock public brochures.


Wait for Morgan: do not open or change reservation records until Morgan provides an approved individual login and demonstrates the process. Never use another person's login.


Spill or blocked route: stay on a safe, dry route; keep people away from the hazard, place the available cone only if this can be done without entering the hazard, and notify Morgan immediately. Do not attempt cleanup with an unfamiliar product or leave people walking into the hazard. The front-desk extension reaches Morgan without Rowan leaving the desk. The cone is within reach on the dry side of the welcome desk.


Private information: keep participant details face down in the secure desk tray when not being used. Do not share another participant's details. Ask Morgan to handle requests through the approved process.


Equipment: the supply cart may be moved along the clear route if stable and safe to move. One closed cleaning spray is labelled “Training required before use.” Rowan has not received that training. Permission to move the cart is not permission to use its contents.


Read the floor plan


The public entrance leads to the welcome desk. The brochure shelf is beyond the desk. Morgan is in the activity room. A spill blocks the shorter route across the open area. The marked clear route goes around the spill to the activity-room entrance. The cleaning cart is beside the blocked route. The extension and secure tray are at the welcome desk.


[Place the approved library floor-plan image here, followed by the same text description above.]


Check the brief: Which task can Rowan begin without a new permission or demonstration?
Learn the method
Read permission and responsibility together


A responsibility is something the role is expected to do. Authorization is permission to perform a particular action. Training is instruction and practice needed to carry it out appropriately. The three are related but not interchangeable. Rowan is responsible for helping at the desk; that does not authorize every action available on its computer.


A boundary tells you what must remain protected while you act. The reservation boundary protects accurate records and controlled access. The information boundary protects participant details. The hazard boundary protects people from entering a dangerous area. A useful response identifies the relevant boundary rather than simply saying “be careful.”


Pause the uncertain task and choose useful permitted work


Pausing one action does not mean abandoning the whole shift. If record access is not ready, Rowan can prepare blank cards or welcome visitors within the brief. If a spill is present, protecting people and contacting Morgan takes priority over routine preparation. The safest immediate step depends on the situation; “do another task” would not be enough if people were still walking into a spill.


The floor plan helps with this choice. It identifies a clear route and a way to contact Morgan without crossing the spill. A diagram is useful when its locations affect action. Here, choosing the short route would contradict the hazard information even if it saved time.


Make the message actionable


A good short message contains the location or task, the specific uncertainty or risk, what you have done within permission and what you need confirmed. Compare “I need help” with “The reservation login is not ready; I have left the record unchanged. Can you show me the approved process?” The second message allows Morgan to respond to a concrete need.


Decision sequence: notice the situation → identify the boundary → take a safe permitted step → give a specific message → wait for the needed instruction before the restricted task. Do not turn a plausible guess into permission.


CCOHS reference record — retrieved September 28, 2026; fact sheet confirmed current June 30, 2025: the right to know includes receiving hazard information and necessary instruction before work. In Rowan's case, the training label is a reason to ask before using the spray. The shift sheet supplies the actual case procedure. Optional “Three Rights of Workers,” Right to Know.


Show a first-step hint
Hint: Find the sentence in the sheet that directly governs the action. Write that sentence's meaning beside your proposed step before composing the message.


Follow a complete example
Reservation access is not ready


At 9:10, a visitor asks Rowan to change a reservation. Morgan has not provided an individual login or a demonstration. A co-worker offers a logged-in computer. No immediate hazard is present in this particular moment.


I locate the relevant rule: reservation records must wait for approved access and a demonstration, and another person's login is prohibited. The co-worker's offer does not change those instructions. Rowan can acknowledge the visitor without promising an unauthorized change.


Completed decision row


    

  • Boundary: record access and accuracy; no approved login or demonstration yet.
    • 

  • Immediate action: leave the reservation unchanged, explain that Morgan must assist, and contact Morgan using the extension.
    • 

  • Supporting fact: the shift sheet says to wait for Morgan and not use another person's login.
    • 

  • Message: “A visitor needs a reservation change. I do not have my approved login or a demonstration, so I have left the record unchanged. Can you help the visitor and show me the authorized process?”
    • 



After the request is safely handed to Morgan, Rowan can prepare blank cards while waiting. “Use the co-worker's login, then tell Morgan later” reverses the required order and removes accountability for the change. Being helpful includes respecting the limit and keeping the visitor informed.


Next: Three moments at the desk. Try “9:20 brochures” before opening its comparison model.
Practise with support
Three moments at the desk


Use the same shift sheet. These are separate moments; do not assume an action in one has solved the next.


    

  1. At 9:20, the brochure shelf is low; the marked clear route is open. Choose restock along the clear route / cross the spill to save time / edit a reservation first.
    2. 

  2. At 9:25, a new visitor approaches the spill; Rowan is on the dry side of the desk and can reach the cone safely. Choose direct the visitor away, place the cone from the safe side and call Morgan / walk through the spill / leave the desk to find a mop while the visitor continues.
    3. 

  3. At 9:35, a participant list lies face up. No visitor has asked to see it. Choose place it face down in the secure tray / photograph it for later / read it aloud to check it.
    4. 



Use Check my choice. Feedback: in moment 1, restocking is permitted and the clear route avoids the hazard; crossing ignores it and record editing is unrelated and restricted. In moment 2, the first option protects the visitor and obtains help; walking through exposes Rowan and leaving fails to protect the approaching visitor. In moment 3, the first option follows the supplied privacy instruction; a photograph creates an unnecessary copy and reading aloud discloses details.


Now write My spill message to Morgan, 2–3 sentences containing location, immediate protection and the help needed. Use Compare your response with a model, then revise.


Show a first-step hint
Hint: Name what a visitor could encounter. Do not guess which substance spilled or which chemical would clean it.

Open How to Succeed at a Job Interview ↗
Core vocabulary
An interview question asking for an example of how someone acted.
The task or part of the work a person was expected to handle.
Practising an answer so you can check its clarity and accuracy.
Building professional connections to exchange information and learn about opportunities.
Start here
Let the interviewer hear what you actually did


An interview is a conversation used to explore whether a person's experience and a role's needs fit. A general claim such as “I work well under pressure” gives the listener little to examine. A short, accurate example gives them actions, results and something useful to ask about.


You will prepare answers for Rowan using supplied fictional experience notes. Your final product is a 4–6 sentence answer about a disagreement, followed by a role-research question and a sensible way to investigate it. You may rehearse aloud or read silently; no recording, live partner or real interview is required.


How to complete this lesson: Read The role and Rowan's event notes. Learn Build an answer a listener can follow. Follow the cancellation example, then practise with the activity-card mix-up. Check six ideas and complete Answer a question about disagreement. Compare your answer with the annotated model, revise and sign off. Pause after rehearsal if useful; the written fields save.


Meet the situation and read the documents


The role and Rowan's event notes


Rowan is preparing for a fictional welcome-helper interview. The role involves explaining sign-in steps, keeping attendance information accurate, sharing tasks and asking the shift lead when an exception needs approval. Training is provided for the local system. The notice does not state which career qualification could lead to a later program-coordinator role.


An experience record is a description of an event already completed. It is evidence for an answer, not a script Rowan must pretend happened in a paid job. These events took place at school or in a volunteer setting. Use that context truthfully.


Record A — cancelled helper, school welcome evening


Ten minutes before doors opened, one of three helpers could not attend. Rowan was responsible for organizing the sign-in table. Rowan asked the remaining helper to check the attendance list, took the greeting position and explained the revised two-person arrangement to the event lead. The lead approved it. Arrivals moved through without a long line, and every arrival was recorded. After the event Rowan wrote, “Next time I would prepare a backup task plan before opening.”


Record B — mixed activity cards, community open house


Two stacks of activity cards had been placed under the wrong headings. Rowan noticed the mismatch before visitors used them, checked the approved activity list with the lead and relabelled the stacks with the lead's confirmation. A second helper distributed them. Visitors received the intended card for their activity. Rowan has used this local list once; the record does not establish expertise with every registration system.


Check the record: Which wording correctly identifies Rowan's role in Record A?
Learn the method
Build an answer a listener can follow


A behavioural question asks for an example of how someone acted, such as “Tell me about a time a plan changed.” Start by identifying the skill the question is exploring. A question about change needs an event involving change; an unrelated achievement may be impressive but fail to answer it.


Give enough situation and task for the listener to understand the problem and your responsibility. Then spend most of the answer on action: what you personally did and why. Finish with the result, limited to what the record actually reports. You can add learning or a next step when it helps. This structure is a guide for meaning, not a requirement to say the words “situation, task, action, result” aloud.


Answer path: what happened → what I was responsible for → what I did → what changed → what I learned or would improve. In a short answer, one sentence can contain more than one part. A precise action often communicates more than several adjectives.


Own your action and share the result


Teamwork creates a common wording trap. “We kept the line moving” credits the group but does not identify Rowan's contribution. “I did all the work” supplies a contribution by inventing one. Combine them: “I took greeting and arranged the task split; together we kept arrivals moving and recorded everyone.” The result can be shared while the action remains specific.


A limit marks what an example cannot prove. One local event does not establish years of professional management, and following an approved procedure does not establish qualification to design a new system. Naming a sensible limit strengthens the evidence instead of weakening it.


Practise the delivery and prepare a useful question


Rehearsal helps you notice long openings, missing verbs and unexplained results. Read your answer once as if a listener knows nothing about the event. If speaking is useful to you, say it aloud without recording. If you prefer silent rehearsal, underline the action and identify the result in the text. Both routes check the same content; accent, eye contact and performance style are not scored here.


Networking means building professional connections to exchange information and learn about opportunities. It need not begin with asking for a job. A career event, a workplace information session or a short informational conversation can help a person understand a role. A focused question respects the other person's time: “What training lets a welcome helper take on program coordination?” is more useful than “Tell me everything about your career.” In this course, you draft the question and choose an appropriate route; you do not contact anyone.


A mentor is someone who shares experience and feedback to support another person's development. Mentoring is a relationship, not a credential or a guarantee of an opportunity. An internship is an organized period of work-related learning; its actual duties, supervision, training, pay and entry conditions must be checked in its own agreement. A mock interview rehearses interview questions before a real selection process. This lesson provides that rehearsal in writing. Preparing a question for a mentor or employer is different from claiming that a conversation or internship has already happened.


alis (Alberta’s career information site) reference record — retrieved September 28, 2026: its interview-preparation guidance recommends researching the role, preparing concrete examples and developing questions for the employer. This lesson supplies a role brief and examples so the practice can be completed here. Optional: open How do I prepare for a job interview? — alis (new tab) ↗.


Show a first-step hint
Hint: Replace “I am good at…” with “When…, I…”. Check each verb against the experience record before adding a result.


Watch or read · FINLIT 101
Tips for Your Résumé
This excerpt discusses written applications: a résumé summarizes facts, while a cover letter explains relevance. You will transfer that idea to an interview answer. Listen for why specific accomplishments matter, then look back at Rowan’s school and community records.
Read the video transcript
Visuals: drawings show a learner at a laptop, a résumé beside a cover letter, and a spelling-and-grammar checklist. These are prompts to inspect the quality of an application.
why you'd be a good person to hire. When it comes to resumes, there is no one standard formatter template to use, though there are many templates available online if you need help starting out. Most resumes do, however, contain certain standard sections and information. It's always good to include a cover letter along with your resume. If you think of a resume as a summary of information and facts about yourself, a cover letter is an opportunity to expand on that information, as well as create a personalized message about why you want the job, why you're interested in the company, and most importantly, why you would be the best person to hire. As a rule of thumb, try to keep your resume to two pages or less in your cover letter to no longer than one page. Here are a few general tips for preparing a resume and cover letter. Think spelling and grammar carefully. With so much competition for jobs, spelling and grammatical errors are an easy way for those hiring to eliminate applicants since it shows a lack of attention to detail. Your objective with your resume should be to sell yourself. Use it to show your strengths, skills, accomplishments, and abilities. You want your resume to make you stand out from others.
FINLIT 101 · Tips for Your Résumé · selected excerpt, used with permission.
Which idea from the résumé excerpt also helps Rowan answer an interview question?

Follow a complete example
“Tell me about a time a plan changed.”
Connect the video to this task. The FINLIT excerpt concerns written applications. This example shows the transfer to speaking: choose a relevant accomplishment and explain it in a truthful event sequence.


Record A directly answers this question: a helper cancelled shortly before opening. I need only one sentence of background. Rowan's response is the important part, so I name the task split and approval. The recorded result is a moving line and complete attendance, not a numerical increase in efficiency that nobody measured.


Complete answer: “At a school welcome evening, a helper cancelled ten minutes before opening while I was organizing sign-in. I asked the remaining helper to check the attendance list and took the greeting position myself. I explained the revised arrangement to the event lead and received approval. Together we kept arrivals moving without a long line and recorded everyone. Next time I would prepare a backup task plan before opening.”


How the answer works: sentence 1 provides situation and responsibility; sentences 2–3 identify Rowan's actions and authority; sentence 4 credits the team result; sentence 5 uses the recorded improvement. It does not imply that Rowan supervised paid staff or handled an unknown computer system.


“I'm always calm and can solve any problem” sounds confident but supplies neither an event nor a limit. The complete answer lets a listener judge the evidence. The next example gives you a different event to organize, rather than asking you to copy this one.


Next: Answer from the card mix-up. Try “Relevant action in Record B” before opening its comparison model.

Answer from the card mix-up

Question: “Describe a time you noticed a detail that needed correcting.” Use Record B only. First choose the most relevant action: relabelled after checking the approved list with the lead / ran every registration system / cancelled the open house. Use Check my evidence.


Feedback: The first action is recorded and relevant. The second invents expertise; the third did not happen. The cancellation from Record A does not belong in this answer.


Fill Situation and responsibility, My action and the shared result, and A truthful limit or next improvement. Turn those notes into My practice answer, 4–6 sentences. Read it aloud or silently, then open Compare your response with a model.

Answer a question about disagreement


New question: “Tell me about a disagreement in a team and how you responded.” Use this new record, not the cancellation or card mix-up.


Record C — late arrivals at a community workshop


Two helpers wanted late arrivals to skip sign-in to shorten the line. Rowan was responsible for keeping attendance accurate under the lead's procedure. Rowan restated the shared aim of welcoming visitors while recording everyone, proposed one helper greeting and one helper staying with the list, and asked the lead to confirm the arrangement. The lead approved it. The team kept the line moving, every visitor signed in and no participant details were shared. The record does not say Rowan acted without support or that the disagreement never recurred.


The welcome-helper role still values accurate information and approved processes. A later program-coordinator role interests Rowan, but its training pathway is not supplied.

Work through a changing shift
How to complete this lesson
  1. Start here

Open Skills for Success — Government of Canada ↗
Core vocabulary
A problem that prevents the next required step from proceeding.
A task or condition that must be completed before another step can start.
Done one task after another.
Done during the same period by people or resources that can work independently.
Start here
A changed plan needs a new order of actions


During a busy shift, an equipment problem can affect a deadline while visitors still need help. Working faster on the original list may not solve the new problem. You will practise deciding what must stop, what can continue and what the shift lead needs to know.


Your final product is a timed decision log for a room change. It will name a first action, protect private information, use an approved alternative and explain one improvement from earlier feedback. All events are supplied simulations; no physical setup, supervised placement or contact with a real workplace is required.


How to complete this lesson: Read The printer incident and the shift rules, then check who can approve an alternative. Learn Replan without guessing, follow the revised printer response, and practise The outdoor change. After six questions, complete A room becomes unavailable. Compare the model and times, revise and sign off. Pause after the outdoor practice if needed; your work saves.


Meet the situation and read the documents


The printer incident and the shift rules


Rowan helps at fictional Prairie Library Hub. Morgan leads the shift. A blocker is a condition that prevents a task from progressing as planned. An alternative is a different way to reach the purpose; it still needs to meet the rules.


Desk rules for these cases


    

  • Report an equipment blocker when it is first noticed. State what it affects and the deadline.
    • 

  • Do not dismantle, force or repair equipment. A normal restart is allowed only if it is safe and does not delay reporting.
    • 

  • Morgan approves changes to activity method or location. A trained staff member must check a new activity area before setup. Rowan can observe and report a concern but cannot sign off that check.
    • 

  • Keep participant names and contact details in the secure tray. Public notices may include activity, time and approved location, not participant details.
    • 

  • Blank cards and public brochures may be prepared while waiting, if no immediate hazard needs attention.
    • 

  • Morgan can be contacted using the desk extension. If unavailable, leave a clear message and wait for required approval before the restricted action.
    • 



Completed incident record — Monday, September 14


At 10:05 the printer stopped. Cards were needed for an 11:00 activity. Rowan spent fifteen minutes trying to get printing working and notified Morgan at 10:20. At 10:25 Morgan approved blank cards with handwritten activity headings; preparing them took twenty minutes, and the cards were ready at 10:45. No private information was needed on the cards. The activity began on time.


Morgan's noon feedback: “The cards were accurate and ready, but I needed to know about the printer at 10:05. An early message would have given us more time to choose a backup. Please report a blocker when you first notice it.”


Check the authority: Who can approve replacing the printed cards with handwritten headings?
Learn the method
Replan without guessing


A priority is something that needs attention before another task. Priority depends on consequence and sequence, not just on which request is loudest. Immediate safety and privacy boundaries continue to apply when a deadline changes. After protecting those boundaries, identify the task whose delay would block other work.


A dependency is a step that must happen before another can begin. Location approval and an area check are dependencies for setting up in a new room. Writing a draft public notice can happen while waiting, but posting an unapproved location would skip a dependency. This difference lets a person stay useful without pretending approval has arrived.


Communicate the problem before it becomes a surprise


A concise update gives a time, blocker, consequence and request. “Printer stopped at 10:05; cards are needed by 11. May I use blank cards with the activity headings?” gives Morgan information for a decision. An early message does not require Rowan to know the cause of the failure. Reporting a problem and offering an option are compatible with taking initiative.


The original incident ended on time, but the feedback still identifies a process worth changing. A successful result does not prove every step was effective. Conversely, one late report does not prove Rowan is generally unreliable. Keep the improvement specific: report blockers when noticed and name the affected deadline.


Use time as evidence


Work backwards from the deadline. If a task takes ten minutes and must finish at 10:45, it must start by 10:35. If approval cannot arrive until 10:25, check whether the remaining sequence still fits. Activities that can occur at the same time must be assigned to different available people; one person cannot independently perform two ten-minute tasks simultaneously.


Replanning map: protect people and information → report the change → identify permissions and dependencies → assign feasible tasks and times → check the deadline → record the next improvement.


Optional training reference, read September 28, 2026: CCOHS explains that workers need information and instruction about hazards before the work. In this lesson, that supports waiting for an authorized area check; the fictional desk rules determine who is authorized. “Right to Know”.


Show a first-step hint
Hint: Draw arrows between steps that cannot change order. Put approval before posting a new location, and the area check before moving in equipment.


Follow a complete example
Improve the printer response


We are looking back at September 14, not rewriting what actually happened. The incident record says Rowan reported at 10:20. The model below proposes what Rowan could do at 10:05 in a similar future situation.


First, stop repeated repair attempts. The rules allow a normal safe restart, not dismantling or a fifteen-minute delay before reporting. The deadline is 11:00, and the purpose is readable activity headings, not printing for its own sake. Blank cards might meet that purpose, but Morgan must approve the change.


Improved decision log


    

  • 10:05, first action: leave the stopped printer safe and notify Morgan by extension.
    • 

  • Update: “The printer stopped at 10:05 and the activity needs cards by 11:00. I have stopped repeated attempts. May I prepare blank cards with handwritten headings as the backup?”
    • 

  • While waiting: gather blank cards and keep participant information in the secure tray; do not copy names onto public cards.
    • 

  • After approval: prepare the approved headings and check them against the activity list. The recorded backup took twenty minutes; use that duration to plan the work.
    • 

  • Improvement: report the blocker when noticed instead of waiting until a backup becomes urgent.
    • 



This is a complete response even though Rowan does not diagnose the printer. “Fix the mechanism quickly” requires skills and permission not supplied. “The activity started on time, so no change is needed” ignores the feedback about avoidable pressure.


Next: The outdoor change. Try “Workable outdoor sequence” before opening its comparison model.
Practise with support
The outdoor change


A separate shift takes place Monday, September 21. At 10:20, Morgan sends a message proposing that the 11:00 activity move outdoors. Cards are ready. A public notice must be posted by 10:45. Morgan is available by extension at 10:25 to confirm the final location and assign work. Trained staff member Lee can check the outdoor area in ten minutes beginning 10:25 if Morgan assigns it. Rowan needs ten minutes to finish and post the public notice after location approval. Equipment setup takes ten minutes and may begin only after the area is checked. Rowan and Lee are both available for setup after their first tasks. Participant records remain at the desk, secured before Rowan leaves.


Choose the workable sequence: set up outside immediately / draft a notice now, seek confirmation at 10:25, then split notice and area-check tasks / wait until 10:45 to report the change. Use Check the sequence.


Feedback: The second choice uses waiting time without skipping approval. Immediate setup skips the trained check. Waiting until 10:45 consumes the notice deadline before work begins.


Fill First action at 10:20, My 10:25 update and task split, and Times for notice, check and setup. Then open Compare your response with a model.


Show a first-step hint
Hint: Rowan can prepare wording now but should not publish an unapproved destination. At 10:25 Rowan and Lee can do different ten-minute tasks concurrently.


Your work saves automatically in this browser. Check the saving status before closing.
Compare your response with a model
Your current response
Model: “At 10:20 I secure the participant records and draft a notice with a space for the approved location. At 10:25 I ask Morgan: ‘Cards are ready; the notice is due at 10:45. Please confirm the outdoor location and assign Lee's trained area check while I finish the public notice.’ With approval, Rowan completes and posts the notice 10:25–10:35 while Lee checks the area 10:25–10:35. If Lee confirms it is ready, equipment setup takes 10:35–10:45. The notice meets its deadline and setup finishes before 11:00. If the check finds a problem, keep setup paused and ask Morgan for an approved alternative.”


Revise a plan that assigns Rowan both the area check and notice, begins setup before the check or omits what happens if the check fails. The model is a conditional plan, not a claim that an unperformed check succeeded.

A room becomes unavailable


New shift: Friday, September 25. At 12:10, the door to Activity Room A jams. The 12:45 activity cannot use that entrance. Rowan has not been trained or authorized to force or repair the door. People can wait safely in the clear welcome area; Rowan must direct them away from the jammed entrance.


Morgan can respond by extension at 12:15. Room B is available and Morgan has already completed its area check that morning. Moving the activity there still needs Morgan's approval. Updating and posting the public notice takes ten minutes after approval. Moving the prepared card box by the clear route takes five minutes after approval. Rowan is the only helper available for those two tasks, so perform them sequentially. The notice must be posted by 12:35. The participant contact list is face up at the desk and must be secured before Rowan leaves. No other task or equipment move is required in this case.


Write My changed-room decision log, using times and short paragraphs. Include the immediate action at 12:10, privacy step, exact message for Morgan, a feasible post-approval sequence and one improvement linked to the earlier printer feedback. Also enter Notice posted by and Card move finished by as times.

Your current response
Complete model: “At 12:10 Rowan directs visitors to wait in the clear welcome area and away from the jammed door, avoids repair attempts, secures the contact list face down in the tray and leaves Morgan a clear extension message. At 12:15: ‘Room A's entrance is jammed and I am keeping visitors clear. The activity starts at 12:45; may we use the already checked Room B? I need ten minutes for the notice and five to move the cards.’ If Morgan approves at 12:15, Rowan posts the notice from 12:15–12:25, then moves the card box from 12:25–12:30. The notice meets 12:35 and the cards arrive before 12:45. Reporting immediately applies the earlier feedback instead of spending time trying an unauthorized repair.”
The reverse task order also fits if the box moves 12:15–12:20 and the notice is posted 12:20–12:30. Both need approval first, secured records and visitors protected. If approval does not arrive, the plan must remain conditional; do not report a completed relocation as fact.

Employee rights and responsibilities · Lesson 1
Check the rules before a first shift
How to complete this lesson
  1. Start here
  2. Meet the situation and read the documents
  3. Learn the method
  4. Follow a complete example
  5. Practise with support

At a check, try an answer, read the hint and revise. A different incorrect answer brings method support and an option to show the worked reasoning. Written responses use the comparison and self-checks; they are not automatically graded.
Optional reference · Alberta youth employment laws
All facts needed for the activities are supplied in the lesson. Use the named original for further reading or to check current details.
Open Alberta youth employment laws ↗
Core vocabulary
A minimum legal requirement applying to an employment arrangement within its stated scope.
Permission given by the person whose permission is required.
Oversight by an appropriate person under the applicable rule or procedure.
The authority and scope under which a law or rule applies.
Start here
A shift offer can sound simple: “Can you close on Thursday?” To check it, a young worker needs more than the finish time. Age, workplace, school hours, tasks, permission and supervision can change which rules apply.


You will help Ellis check a proposed retail shift, practise checking a corrected offer, and then write a shift-review note for a different restaurant worker. Your final note will connect particular facts to particular rules and propose a workable next step. You are practising source-based investigation, not issuing a legal decision about a real employer.


Work through Meet the situation and read the documents → Learn the method → Follow a complete example → Practise with support → Check your understanding → Apply independently → Review and complete. Pause after the example or guided practice if useful. Your answers save automatically. Guided work and six questions are practice; the independent review note is your saved lesson evidence.


Useful terms. An employee works for an employer; the youth rules below concern employees. A permit is official permission for specified employment, not the same as a parent's consent. Retail sells goods, including food, directly to customers. Supervision means an adult is actually supervising the work; being able to telephone someone elsewhere is not the supervision supplied in our examples. A school day is a day on which this learner is scheduled to attend school.


Optional reference disclosure: Official pages for a current situation. The dated record below contains everything needed here. For an actual job, check the current Alberta youth employment page and use Employment Standards' question service if the situation differs. You do not need to open a website, contact anyone or enter personal employment details to finish this lesson.


Meet the situation and read the documents


Ellis is starting an ordinary employee job at fictional North Path Books, an Alberta retail bookstore. Ellis wants to answer a shift offer before it becomes the final schedule. Read the worker record, offer and rule record together: none is enough by itself.


Document A — Worker and school record






Item
Supplied fact





Age on the proposed shift
15




Job
Retail employee: cashier and shelving books




Arrangement
Ordinary provincial employment; not an approved off-campus education program, work-integrated learning placement, farm or ranch job




School on Thursday, October 8, 2026
8:45 a.m.–3:15 p.m.




School on Friday, October 9
8:45 a.m.–3:15 p.m.




Parent's consent
Parent has agreed to evening work ending by 11:00 p.m.; no consent to a later finish




Transport
Parent can collect Ellis at 11:00 p.m.





Document B — Draft shift offer, received October 5




Thursday, October 8: 9:30 p.m.–12:30 a.m. the next morning. Duties: cashier and shelving. Adult supervisor Mara, age 32, is on site and supervising until 10:00 p.m. Jordan, age 17, then supervises the closing team. Mara can be called after leaving. Please confirm whether this draft works before we publish it.




Jordan is experienced, but is not an adult. Ellis has not accepted or worked this proposed shift.


Document C — In-course Alberta youth employment record


Government of Alberta, “Employment standards rules – Youth employment laws”; relevant sections “Basic rules,” “Employees 13 to 14 years of age,” and “Employees 15 to 17 years of age.” Checked September 28, 2026. Limited paraphrase for this lesson:






Group
Rules relevant to the supplied cases





Age 15–17
Permits are not required. Parent/guardian consent is required for work during restricted hours. A 15-year-old cannot work during regular school hours except in an off-campus education program.




Age 15–17, retail/hospitality
Work from 9:00 p.m. to midnight requires adult supervision. Work from 12:01 a.m. to 6:00 a.m. is prohibited.




Age 13–14
Parent/guardian consent is required. Specified jobs may be done without a permit; other jobs require one. No work during regular school hours except in an off-campus education program. Maximum two hours outside school on a school day, eight on a non-school day. No work between 9:00 p.m. and 6:00 a.m.




Age 13–14, restaurants
Listed permit-free tasks include hosting, cashier work and bussing/cleaning tables. Food-service work requires continuous adult supervision.





This selected record does not list every permitted occupation or every employment rule. Permission does not erase an hours restriction. Meeting these selected rules does not establish that all employment and safety requirements have been met.


Read the documents


Which fact is missing from the original offer's claim of adult supervision after 10:00 p.m.?
Learn the method
Identify the rule before judging the offer


Start with the details that select a rule: age → employment arrangement → workplace/task → time. “Teen worker” is too broad. Ellis is 15, so the 13–14 school-day two-hour limit is not the rule to apply to Ellis. North Path Books is retail, so the retail evening rule is relevant. An exception for another kind of workplace cannot simply be moved to this one.


An official page is evidence about the rules; a shift offer is evidence about the proposed facts. The task is to connect them. Write “Ellis is scheduled after midnight in retail, which conflicts with the recorded overnight restriction,” rather than “the website says it is bad.” The first sentence lets another reader check your reasoning.


Divide the shift where a condition changes


Midnight crosses into the next calendar day. Adult coverage can change before the shift ends. A whole-shift label such as “night work” hides these differences. Break the offered shift into pieces:






Portion of Ellis's offer
What changes?
Question to ask





9:30–10:00 p.m. Thursday
Mara is supervising
Are the evening consent and supervision conditions supplied?




10:00 p.m.–midnight
Mara leaves; Jordan is 17
Is an adult supervising? Does parental consent cover the planned finish?




12:01–12:30 a.m. Friday
Overnight restricted period
Can adult supervision or consent remove this retail prohibition?





The answer to the last question is no under the supplied record. Do not spend time negotiating an adult supervisor for a portion that cannot be scheduled under that rule. Revise the hours themselves.


Separate a mismatch from an unanswered question


A mismatch exists when supplied facts conflict with the selected rule: a retail shift continuing to 12:30 a.m. is one here. An unknown exists when the documents do not tell you a relevant fact. Write a question for an unknown instead of assuming its answer. In Ellis's documents, the ages and coverage are supplied, so “maybe Jordan is an adult” is not an unknown.


A check can have several results. The shift is outside the recorded school hours, but that does not cancel the supervision and overnight problems. Conversely, finding one problem does not mean every detail is wrong. State which conditions your evidence answers.


Ask for a specific correction


A useful review ends with an action the recipient can understand: a revised start and finish, named adult coverage and confirmation that permission covers those hours. “Fix it” leaves the next decision unclear. You can be direct without accusing someone of deliberate wrongdoing: this is a draft offer and its reason is unknown.


A personal arrangement, such as a ride home, also affects whether the worker can accept. Label it accurately. The parent's 11:00 p.m. pickup is a case constraint, not a province-wide closing rule.


Show a first-step hint
Optional hint — Where do I begin? Open this hint to see: “The starting facts are Ellis's age, the retail setting, midnight and the supervisor change at 10:00 p.m. The matching row in Document C explains why each matters.”


Follow a complete example
I first select the age 15–17 retail rules. Ellis is 15 and the arrangement is ordinary employment. The shift begins after Thursday's school hours. That answers the school-hours question; it does not approve the rest of the shift.


Next I follow the time line. Mara supplies adult supervision only until 10:00 p.m. Jordan is 17, so the offer does not supply the required adult coverage from 10:00 p.m. to midnight. The parent has only consented to an 11:00 p.m. finish, so the offer also exceeds that permission. Finally, the offered 12:30 a.m. finish includes the prohibited 12:01–6:00 a.m. retail period. Neither permission nor adult coverage can make that portion fit the record.


Here is a complete draft review:




Ellis is a 15-year-old employee in an Alberta retail bookstore. The proposed October 8 shift is outside the supplied school hours, but it needs revision. Alberta's youth employment record, checked September 28, requires adult supervision for retail work from 9:00 p.m. to midnight. Mara leaves at 10:00 p.m., and Jordan is 17. The 12:30 a.m. finish also includes a prohibited overnight period. Parental consent currently ends at 11:00 p.m. Please offer a shift ending by 11:00 p.m. with an adult supervising the entire evening portion and confirm the corrected schedule before Ellis accepts. The parent's pickup is available at 11:00 p.m. This checks the listed youth conditions; it is not a complete workplace safety review.




“Ellis can work until 12:30 because the parent could give permission” is an unsupported alternative. It treats consent as an override of a prohibition. “Ellis cannot work more than two hours because school is tomorrow” selects the wrong age group's rule and does not use Ellis's actual school-day facts.


Next: Practise with support. Try “Which recorded facts select the rules?” before opening its comparison model.
Practise with support

Thursday, October 8: 9:00–11:00 p.m. Mara, age 32, will remain on site and supervise for the whole shift. Cashier and shelving duties are unchanged. The parent confirms consent to these exact hours and the 11:00 p.m. pickup. This is the only proposed shift that day.




Create a short verification note in three saved fields.


    

  1. Which recorded facts select the rules? Name the age, work arrangement and sector. Use one sentence.
    2. 

  2. Check the corrected time and supervision. Explain school hours, overnight boundary, adult coverage and consent in two or three sentences.
    3. 

  3. What can Ellis conclude, and what is the next action? State the limited conclusion and the schedule-confirmation action. Do not claim all employment or safety law has been checked.
    4. 



Show a first-step hint
 “Read the corrected offer as a new document. Do not carry forward Jordan's coverage or the 12:30 finish.”

If it still says Jordan closes alone, revise the old fact. If it says everything is legal, narrow the conclusion to the selected youth conditions.” No text is automatically marked right or wrong.

A case does not state a proposed supervisor's age. What is the strongest review note?

Apply independently
A new worker and a new age group


Rina is 14 and has been offered a school-day shift at fictional Willow Bowl Café in Alberta. Write a shift-review note to the scheduler, using the in-course source record. This is a saved simulation; do not send a message.


Document D — Rina's record. Rina is an ordinary employee, not in an off-campus education program or other special arrangement. On Tuesday, October 13, 2026, school runs from 8:40 a.m. to 3:20 p.m. Rina has no other work that day. A parent has consented to hosting and bussing/cleaning tables after school until 8:00 p.m. An adult supervisor, Anika, age 29, will provide continuous supervision during any shift between 4:00 and 8:00 p.m. Rina is available within that window. Rina has not accepted the draft.


Document E — Draft offer. October 13, 4:30–7:30 p.m., with no break scheduled: greet and seat guests, bus and clean tables. No cooking or other duties. Employer proposes no permit because the tasks are hosting and bussing/cleaning tables. The café asks Rina to confirm whether the hours work.


Make one coherent note using these fields:


    

  • Case facts and applicable conditions — identify age, sector/tasks, school-day status, consent and adult coverage. Two or three sentences.
    • 

  • Hours check and proposed revision — calculate the offered work duration, compare it to the correct school-day limit, then propose exact revised start/finish times inside the supplied availability. Explain the calculation. Two or three sentences; state hours, not just numbers.
    • 

  • Review note and next step — assemble a respectful note naming the dated rule record, the condition that needs changing and what the scheduler should confirm. About one short paragraph; use fictional facts only.
    • 



Success means selecting Rina's age group, checking the actual tasks and conditions, correcting the school-day duration, and requesting a specific schedule. There are several defensible revised schedules; show how yours fits all supplied constraints. You do not need to make the original draft acceptable.

Please confirm those corrected hours and the listed duties before Rina accepts. This review uses Alberta's youth employment record checked September 28, 2026, and addresses the selected conditions rather than every employment requirement.




A 5:00–7:00 p.m. shift is also defensible with the same checks. Keeping 4:30–7:30 and saying “the parent agrees” does not solve the duration conflict. Removing all supervision discussion would leave a separate restaurant condition unchecked.

Employee rights and responsibilities · Lesson 2
Stop, identify and control a hazard
How to complete this lesson
  1. Start here
  2. Meet the situation and read the documents
  3. Learn the method
  4. Follow the video example or its written explanation
  5. Follow a complete example
  6. Practise with support
  7. Check your understanding
  8. Apply independently
  9. Review and complete
At a check, try an answer, read the hint and revise. A different incorrect answer brings method support and an option to show the worked reasoning. Written responses use the comparison and self-checks; they are not automatically graded.
Optional reference · Three Rights of Workers
All facts needed for the activities are supplied in the lesson. Use the named original for further reading or to check current details.
Open Three Rights of Workers ↗
Core vocabulary
Something that could cause harm.
The possibility and seriousness of harm in the circumstances.
A measure used to remove a hazard or reduce exposure to it.
Instruction and practice needed to perform a task safely and appropriately.
Start here
On a first shift, you may want to show that you can handle a task without slowing anyone down. But a request does not supply the information, equipment or training needed to do it safely. Knowing when to pause is a useful workplace skill.


You will help Devin respond to an unidentified cleaning liquid, practise a follow-up when a coworker offers reassurance, and then create a response plan for a different equipment hazard. Your final product explains the observation, immediate action, report and conditions needed before work resumes.


Your route is Meet the situation and read the documents → Learn the method → Follow a complete example → Practise with support → Check your understanding → Apply independently → Review and complete. Read at your own pace; a useful pause is after the example. Responses save automatically. The guided activity and six questions are practice. Only your independent response plan and review sign-offs complete this lesson.


Vocabulary. A hazard is a source or condition that could cause harm. Risk concerns how harm could occur and how serious or likely it might be. A control is a measure that removes or reduces exposure to a hazard. A procedure is an agreed way to do a task safely. A concern report states what was observed and what action is needed. Reporting does not require proving a chemical's identity or a legal violation.


Optional disclosure: Current official sources. The dated Alberta records below are enough for the lesson. Links allow current verification for a real worksite. No external training, contact or login is required here.


Meet the situation and read the documents


Devin is a new employee at fictional Brookside Community Supplies in Alberta. At 4:10 p.m. on October 6, 2026, supervisor Jo asks Devin to clean a work surface beside a storage area. Devin has not started. The site is provincially regulated.


Document A — Observation and training record






What the record establishes
What it does not establish





Jo pointed to a container of liquid with no readable label.
Its identity, concentration or hazard classification.




The room feels stuffy; Devin does not know whether the ventilation is operating adequately for this product.
A measured exposure level or proof that the air is toxic.




Devin has not received the product information, chemical-use training or procedure for this cleaning task.
Which gloves, ventilation or other controls would be suitable.




Jo is helping another worker in the front area. Devin can reach Jo from the clear doorway without handling the container.
Permission to improvise while Jo is busy.




Devin has not opened, carried, mixed, smelled deliberately or used the liquid. No injury or visible spill is reported in this written case.
Any reason to perform spill cleanup.





Document B — Supplied worksite instructions




If an assigned task lacks safety information or training, pause it and tell supervisor Jo. Stay out of the affected area when its safety is uncertain. From a safe place, warn another person who may enter; do not take an untrained action to block, move or clean a hazard. Jo will arrange a competent person's assessment and controls. If immediate serious danger develops, move to safety and follow the site's emergency procedure. Devin's orientation identifies the clear front exit and the outside assembly point. This case involves no current injury or emergency alarm.




These are fictional site instructions for the scenario. They do not provide a method for handling any real chemical.


Document C — In-course rights and responsibilities record


Government of Alberta, “Young worker rights and responsibilities,” sections “Workplace safety,” “Job training,” and “Emergency training and equipment”; “Employer responsibilities,” “Overview” and “Employing youth.” Checked September 28, 2026.


Workers have rights to hazard information, participation in safety and refusal of dangerous work. Workers should report unsafe conditions, follow safe procedures and ask for training they lack. Employers must provide the skills, information, competent supervision and safety arrangements needed for the work. Learners still developing the necessary skills require direct supervision by someone who has them. Chemical work requires special training; equipment alone does not replace instruction.


Government of Alberta, “Refuse dangerous work,” “How it works” and “Worker obligations.” Checked September 28, 2026.


At provincially regulated worksites, the refusal right concerns a reasonable belief in an undue hazard: a serious, immediate threat actually observed or experienced. A worker should stop the dangerous work and promptly report what they refuse and why. The employer investigates and addresses it. Unless fixed immediately, an investigation report is provided. Safe alternative work the person can reasonably do may be assigned. Unresolved danger can be taken to Occupational Health and Safety (OHS). Exercising the legal right is protected from reprisal.


This record explains a process; it does not decide that every uncertainty automatically meets the legal threshold. A worker can ask for missing information and training before reaching a legal conclusion.


Read the documents


Which sentence states Devin's evidence accurately? Choose, 
Learn the method
Describe what you know without testing the hazard


Observation is useful when it makes the concern concrete: a label cannot be read, training has not occurred, or insulation is visibly damaged. You do not need to get closer, touch an object or deliberately smell a substance to make your report more convincing. Information gathering must not create the exposure you are trying to avoid.


Separate the observation from the possible harm. “The product is unidentified” is established. “Using an unidentified product without instructions could expose someone to harm” explains the concern. “This is definitely a poisonous gas” makes a claim the documents cannot support. Cautious wording can be specific and urgent without exaggeration.


Use rights as practical actions


The right to know connects to requesting the identity, hazard information, training and procedure. The right to participate connects to reporting the condition and contributing information during its assessment. The right to refuse dangerous work has an Alberta process and threshold, described in Document C. It is more than walking away silently: the employer needs to know which work is being refused and why.


Worker and employer responsibilities fit together. Devin must report and avoid unsafe improvisation. Jo and the employer must arrange appropriate information, assessment, supervision and controls. Devin does not become the chemical expert merely because Devin noticed a problem.


Choose the immediate action before the final fix


An immediate action keeps exposure from increasing while a competent person works out the fix. For Devin, that means not handling the liquid, staying clear and reaching Jo from the doorway. The final control depends on information Devin does not have. It might involve a verified product, a different task or another trained worker; this lesson cannot select gloves or chemical procedures for an unknown substance.


Use the four-step image as a reminder, with this complete text equivalent:


    

  1. Identify the potential hazard: name the observable condition and the information gap.
    2. 

  2. Pause and avoid guessing: do not handle or test the hazard; stay clear when needed.
    3. 

  3. Ask the responsible person: report promptly and request information, training and controls.
    4. 

  4. Reassess the remaining risk: verify the responsible assessment and safe procedure; report unresolved danger and use the applicable refusal process where warranted.
    5. 



“Reassess” does not mean giving yourself permission because the room looks normal. Work can resume only when the hazard has been addressed and the worker has the competence and controls required for the assigned work. Replacing Devin with another equally untrained person merely transfers the concern.


Close the loop


A useful handoff identifies who will act, what must be checked and how the worker will learn the result. “Someone will sort it out” does not tell the next shift what is unresolved. In a formal refusal, read the employer's investigation report and raise remaining concerns through the process. OHS is the external safety route; Employment Standards deals with matters such as wages and employment hours.


Optional first-step hint: “Write one observed fact, one thing still unknown and one action Devin can take from the clear doorway. Avoid naming the chemical.”


Optional supplied video — A first-shift hazard. Use the player if a narrated example helps. You may also read the written equivalent beside it. The video shows the same information gap; it is not a chemical-handling demonstration. Its pause instruction can be answered in the optional field My video pause response: observation, missing information and next safe action. Watching or using that field is not required. The Alberta process in Document C supplies the specific refusal threshold.


Watch a worked decision
Stop, identify, and control a hazard
Follow Devin’s first-shift decision: identify the hazard, pause, ask for instructions and training, then reassess. Compare those steps with the exact hazards and controls in the lesson record before writing your response.
Pause and decide: Before Devin acts: name the hazard, the missing information, and the safest next step.
Read the lesson’s written equivalent
Slide 1: The first shift
A request is not the same as safe information. UNLABELLED LIQUID; POOR VENTILATION; SUPERVISOR BUSY. What is unknown?
A first shift is a time to ask, not guess. Devin is asked to use a cleaning liquid beside a storage area with poor ventilation. There is no readable label, and the supervisor is helping another worker. A coworker says, “It is probably the usual cleaner.” That description is not enough to identify the substance or its safe use. Pause the task. We will separate what Devin observed from what still needs confirmation.
Slide 2: Name the hazard and the gap
Describe evidence before deciding what the substance is. OBSERVED: container has no readable label; CONDITION: air feels stale; ventilation uncertain; UNKNOWN: contents, exposure risk, required controls. Observed fact ≠ confirmed identity
A hazard is a source or condition that could cause harm. Here, the unlabeled container creates uncertainty; the ventilation condition may affect exposure. Devin should not infer the chemical from its colour, smell, or a coworker’s guess. The missing information includes the product identity, its instructions, possible exposure routes, and the site procedure. This is a case about a missing safety control, not about diagnosing a chemical or deciding whether a law was broken.
Slide 3: Use the three worker rights
Know • Participate • Refuse dangerous work KNOW: ask for hazard information and training; PARTICIPATE: report the concern and suggest a control; REFUSE: follow the applicable process if danger remains. Rights guide a safe process
Canadian workplace safety guidance describes three worker rights: to know about hazards, to participate in health and safety decisions, and to refuse work that may endanger someone. Devin can request the product label, the relevant safety information, instruction, and supervision. Devin can report the concern and take part in choosing a safer method. If the hazard remains, the worker follows the applicable refusal process; it is not a dare or an invitation to confront someone alone. Details belong to the current Alberta process and workplace.
Slide 4: Choose an immediate control
Reduce exposure before collecting more detail. 1  STOP the task; 2  KEEP CLEAR if safe; 3  TELL the supervisor; 4  WAIT for trained direction. Never smell • mix • pour • test
The safe immediate move is to stop before handling the container. If it is safe, Devin should keep other people away from the area and alert the supervisor or designated trained person. Devin should not smell the liquid, mix it with another cleaner, pour it down a drain, or carry it to find a label. Those actions can create exposure or a reaction. If there is immediate serious danger, move to safety and follow the site emergency procedure.
Slide 5: Pause: make the decision
Name the hazard, missing evidence, and next safe action. What is observed?; What must be confirmed?; What should Devin do now?. Pause the video and write a 1–2 sentence response.
Before Devin acts: name the hazard, the missing information, and the safest next step. Pause here and decide.
Slide 6: Worked response and follow-up
State facts, ask for controls, and close the loop. DO NOT handle the unknown liquid; Ask for identity, information, training, and procedure; Record the concern through the site process. A good response is specific—not dramatic.
A strong response says: the container has no readable label, ventilation is uncertain, and Devin has not received the safe procedure. Devin pauses, keeps clear if safe, alerts the supervisor, and asks for the identity, hazard information, training, and approved control before using it. The misconception is that a familiar-looking product or coworker’s confidence makes handling safe. It does not. After the hazard is addressed, Devin records the outcome and follows up. For an actual workplace, check current Alberta guidance and site instructions; this example does not decide a legal case. Before closing, Devin checks who will identify the liquid and what training is needed before anyone resumes the task. If no trained person is available, the area remains controlled and the concern is escalated through the site process. The follow-up is not “clean it up later”; it is to confirm that a responsible person has identified the product, selected controls, and explained how to work safely. This makes the handoff concrete and prevents the unknown hazard from becoming the next shift’s problem.
Original CALM 10 classroom demonstration. Figures and people in this example are fictional; check current sources before real decisions.
Follow a complete example
I begin with Devin's actual position: the work has not started, and Jo is reachable from a clear doorway. That makes it possible to pause and report without handling the container. I do not invent a spill because a general safety illustration happens to show one.


My observation is the unreadable label and missing training. My information request follows from those gaps: product identity, hazard information, approved procedure and appropriate instruction. “Give me any gloves” would jump to equipment before anyone has identified what the equipment needs to protect against.


Here is Devin's complete report and follow-up plan:




Jo, at 4:10 p.m. I found that the cleaning container beside the storage area has no readable label. I have not been given the product information or training for this task, and I cannot confirm that the ventilation is suitable. I have not handled the liquid. I am pausing the cleaning and staying at the clear doorway. Please arrange a competent person's assessment and explain the identified product, safe procedure, controls and training before assigning this task. I can warn someone approaching from this safe position and do another safe task that I am trained to do. I will record who takes responsibility and ask for the assessment outcome. If serious danger remains, I will promptly state the dangerous work I am refusing and follow the Alberta process, including OHS help if unresolved.




This uses the right to know and participate immediately. It also identifies the refusal route without pretending a classroom paragraph has already made a legal finding. “Use a small amount to see whether it works” is an unsafe alternative because the proposed test itself could cause exposure.


Next: Practise with support. Try “My video pause response: observation, missing information and next safe action” before opening its comparison model.
Practise with support
The observation, location and training record stay the same. At 4:12 p.m., coworker Cam says, “I used that container yesterday. It is probably the usual cleaner.” Jo has not yet assessed the product. No label, training or procedure has been supplied.


Construct a brief follow-up in these saved fields:


    

  1. What does Cam's comment establish, and what remains unknown? Write one or two sentences distinguishing the comment from verified identity and controls.
    2. 

  2. What will Devin say and do now? Draft two or three sentences to Jo from the safe doorway, including the paused task and a specific request.
    3. 

  3. What must be confirmed before Devin performs the task? Name the information, competence and control conditions, plus the follow-up route if danger remains.
    4. 



Show a first-step hint
 “A report that someone used a container yesterday is evidence of what they said. It does not establish today's contents or Devin's training.”

If you wrote 'safe because Cam used it,' replace that conclusion with the remaining uncertainties. If you assigned Devin to carry the container for inspection, revise the action so assessment is arranged without Devin handling it.”
Complete matching model:
    

  1. “Cam says they used this container yesterday. That does not verify its current contents, ventilation needs or safe procedure, and Devin still has no task training.”
    2. 

  2. “Jo, I am still pausing the cleaning because the container has no readable label and I have not received the product information or training. Cam's comment has not resolved those gaps. Please arrange assessment; I will stay clear and take a safe task I can do.”
    3. 

  3. “Before Devin does the work, the product and hazards need to be identified, the procedure and controls established, and the required training/supervision provided. Devin should receive the outcome and report remaining concerns; serious immediate danger is addressed through the Alberta refusal process and OHS if unresolved.”
    4. 

Select Return to my response to return to the fields. Your task is a report and a decision boundary, not a cleanup plan.

Check your understanding
Which action improves the evidence without exposing Devin to the unknown liquid?
Which request most directly uses the right to know?
What does the Alberta source mean by an undue hazard for the refusal right?
What is missing from “I am leaving this task because it is unsafe” as a complete handoff?
Jo offers another task while the concern is assessed. Which response fits the record?
Which follow-up best closes the loop?
Next: A new hazard: the damaged vacuum cord. Read the new situation and its supplied records before filling your independent response. Use the method you practised with the evidence in this new case.
Apply independently
A new hazard: the damaged vacuum cord


Imani is a new employee in fictional Alder Display Shop, an Alberta provincially regulated workplace. Create a safe-response handoff using the following complete records. Do not perform a real inspection, repair or test.


Document D — Observation, October 9, 2026, 5:20 p.m. Imani is asked to vacuum a dry sales-floor area. The vacuum is switched off and already unplugged. Before touching it, Imani sees a split in the cord insulation with metal visible. No one has been shocked; there is no fire, smoke, water or immediate injury. Imani stands in a clear area and has not moved, plugged in or tested the machine. Supervisor Ren is at the nearby service desk and can be reached safely.


Document E — Training and instructions. Imani has ordinary vacuum-use instruction, but no electrical repair training or authority to repair equipment. The shop's written procedure says: “Do not use damaged electrical equipment. Report the equipment and location to Ren; Ren arranges removal from service and assessment by a competent person. Workers must not improvise repairs. A replacement may be used only after its condition and safe use are confirmed.” A coworker says, “Wrap it in tape and finish quickly.” No replacement has yet been supplied.


Write the handoff in four fields:


    

  • Observed condition and possible harm — state the specific condition and explain why energizing or using the device could expose someone to harm. Keep observations separate from predictions.
    • 

  • Immediate action and report — draft what Imani should say to Ren, identifying time, place, task and what has been paused. Include an action that avoids exposure.
    • 

  • Information, control and competence before resuming — explain who arranges the response and what must be confirmed. Address the tape suggestion.
    • 

  • Unresolved-danger follow-up — connect the concern to at least two worker rights and name the Alberta safety route if serious danger remains. One short paragraph is enough.
    • 



Success means a specific report, no testing or improvised repair, appropriate responsibility for controls, and a follow-up that does not silently pass damaged equipment to another worker. You may describe a safe replacement or another safe task; do not assume either has already been supplied.


Your work saves automatically in this browser. Check the saving status before closing.
Compare your response with a model
Your current response
Compare your response with a model




At 5:20 p.m. on October 9, Imani observed split insulation with metal visible on the unplugged vacuum cord in the sales-floor area. Using or energizing damaged electrical equipment could cause harm; no shock or fire has occurred in this case. “Ren, I have paused the vacuuming and have not touched, plugged in or tested the machine. The cord is visibly damaged. Please arrange its removal from service and competent assessment under the shop procedure.” Imani stays clear and can warn someone approaching from a safe position. Taping is not an authorized repair, and Imani has no repair training. Ren must arrange assessment; before Imani resumes vacuuming, suitable safe equipment and the instructions/competence for it must be confirmed. Imani can ask for that information through the right to know and report the concern through participation. If directed to do work reasonably believed to pose an undue hazard, Imani should promptly explain the refusal and follow Alberta's process, including OHS help if unresolved. Safe alternative work may be considered. Nothing in this report requires Imani to diagnose the electrical fault.
