Core vocabulary
A protection or entitlement provided by the applicable rules.
An obligation attached to a role or situation.
A clear record of relevant facts, dates and actions.
A specific issue to raise with supporting facts and an appropriate requested action.
Start here
A concern becomes easier to act on when another person can understand what happened, locate the evidence and see what response is needed. “Work was unfair” may describe a feeling accurately, but a report also needs the event, date, records and requested action.


You will follow a report about a missing machine guard, practise recording a response without declaring the issue resolved too soon, then investigate a different worker's pay-record discrepancy. Your final product will be a factual review request with a calculation and a suitable follow-up route.


Follow Meet the situation and read the documents → Learn the method → Follow a complete example → Practise with support → Check your understanding → Apply independently → Review and complete. You can pause after the example or before the new case. Everything needed is supplied. Writing saves automatically; practice answers and model comparisons do not grade you. The independent report and review sign-offs become your lesson evidence.


Vocabulary. An observation records what someone saw, heard or did. An inference is an interpretation drawn from information. A discrepancy is a difference between records that should agree. A pay period is the date range covered by a pay statement. Gross regular wages are earnings for regular hours before deductions; net pay is what remains after deductions. A follow-up records what happened after the first report. Advocacy means expressing a need or right and requesting action supported by evidence.


Optional disclosure: Official sources for real questions. The dated source records are available within the lesson. Current links are optional; this activity does not submit an actual complaint or require contact with a workplace.


Meet the situation and read the documents


Owen is an employee at fictional Birch Sign Workshop in Alberta, a provincially regulated workplace. Owen has been trained to use Cutter 2 only with its fitted safety guard in place. Owen has not been trained to repair or alter the equipment.


Document A — Owen's observation note, October 7, 2026




4:05 p.m., cutting bench, Cutter 2. Before starting the assigned cutting task, I saw that the fitted guard was not attached. The machine was switched off; I did not turn it on or touch its controls. I do not know why the guard was absent. No injury occurred. I stayed clear of the machine. Supervisor Tessa was at the packing desk and could be reached safely.




Document B — Training card and report log


Training card: “Before use, verify the fitted guard is present. If it is absent or damaged, do not operate Cutter 2. Report to Tessa. Only an authorized competent person may inspect, repair and clear the machine for use. Do not perform a test cut to check an unguarded machine.”


Report log, October 7:






Time
Recorded event





4:08 p.m.
Owen told Tessa that Cutter 2's guard was missing and the task had not started.




4:10 p.m.
Tessa said, “Keep it out of use. I will arrange a competent inspection. Work at the packing table, which you are trained to use.”




4:15 p.m.
Owen began the safe packing task. No inspection result had yet been provided.





These facts establish an observation, a report and an interim response. They do not establish who removed the guard or that the machine has been cleared for use.


Document C — In-course responsibilities and source map


Government of Alberta records, checked September 28, 2026:






Topic and source
Limited paraphrase relevant here





Young worker rights and responsibilities — “Workplace safety,” “Job training”
Workers report unsafe conditions, follow safe procedures and ask for needed training. Employers ensure workers have the training and skills to do their work safely.




Employer responsibilities — “Overview”
Employers arrange competent supervision, hazard information, safe practices and required safety training/equipment. A worker's report does not transfer the employer's responsibility to provide controls to that worker.




Refuse dangerous work — “Worker obligations,” “Employer obligations”
Dangerous-work refusals require prompt notice and employer investigation. Unless resolved immediately, the worker receives the investigation report. Safe alternative work may be assigned. Unresolved danger belongs with Occupational Health and Safety (OHS).




Payment of earnings — “Pay statements”
Statements identify the pay period, work hours and rates, separate earnings items and deductions with their reasons. This makes comparison with an employee's records possible.




Make an employment standards complaint — “What a complaint can be about,” “Other workplace issues not covered”
Provincial Employment Standards handles matters such as wages and hours. Safety concerns go to OHS; protected-ground discrimination concerns go to the Alberta Human Rights Commission. Eligibility and procedures differ.





The selected source depends on the question. You may need more than one route if a situation contains different issues. None of these services is an all-purpose “workplace complaint department.”


Read the documents


At 4:15 p.m., which status is supported? Choose, 
Learn the method
Make the concern traceable


A report needs enough detail for someone who was not present. Include who, when, where, what was observed, what was done, and what response is requested. Use a date as well as a clock time; “yesterday” becomes unclear when the note is read next week. Name the machine or pay period so the recipient does not check the wrong record.


Record the source of information. “I saw the guard was absent” differs from “a coworker said the guard had been repaired.” The first is Owen's observation; the second would be another person's statement. Both could be relevant, but they are different forms of evidence. Quote only words supplied as exact words. If you remember the meaning rather than the wording in a real situation, label it as a summary.


Explain the responsibility without guessing intent


Owen's responsibilities are to avoid the prohibited use, report the condition and follow safe arrangements. The employer's responsibilities include ensuring safe practices, competent assessment and training. Owen can name those responsibilities without saying “Tessa deliberately endangered me.” A report about the condition is useful even when the reason for it is unknown.


Use a clear request: “Please confirm the inspection outcome and the conditions for resuming use.” This is more actionable than “make the workplace better.” An initial response can be useful without being the final resolution: moving Owen to packing reduces immediate exposure but does not repair or clear Cutter 2.


Read records on the same basis


For a wages question, first compare the same dates and kind of amount. A four-hour personal work record cannot be compared directly with a whole month's net deposit. Find the matching pay period and the regular-hours line. Then compare hours × rate with gross regular wages. Deductions affect net pay; they do not explain why a statement's regular-hours line differs from the work record.


For example, a clearly labelled fictional illustration of two regular hours at $20 per hour produces $40 of regular wages before deductions. A $37 net deposit could reflect deductions and does not by itself prove three dollars of unpaid regular wages. You would need the earnings and deduction lines. In the independent case, the necessary lines and timing are supplied; do not invent tax rates.


Select the route that can address the issue






Evidence you are investigating
Suitable first organizational recipient
Relevant outside information route





Missing guard or unresolved danger
Supervisor/employer or designated safety contact
Alberta OHS




Hours or regular-wage discrepancy
Payroll/employer with the dated records
Alberta Employment Standards




Negative treatment possibly connected to a protected ground
Appropriate support/HR contact when safe and useful
Alberta Human Rights Commission





An internal request and a formal complaint are different actions. The Employment Standards source explains starting with the employer and, for ordinary pay issues, waiting one pay period before a formal complaint to see whether the next statement resolves it. Urgent matters can differ. Its question service can help explain the applicable process; asking a question is not filing a complaint. A record should not promise an agency will accept a complaint or decide in the worker's favour.


Recognize other employment-standards questions


Pay concerns can involve more than the regular hours shown on a statement. Dated source record — checked September 28, 2026: Alberta's Employment Standards rules cover the categories below. Recognizing the category helps identify the right records and official explanation before deciding what is owed.






Category
What it concerns and what to verify in a real case





Vacation time and vacation pay
Time away from work and the pay connected with vacation are related but distinct. Check length of employment, applicable eligibility, time taken and vacation pay already recorded or paid. A vacation-pay entry alone does not describe when time off was taken.




General holidays
Rules for recognized holidays and associated pay or time off. Check the holiday, eligibility, whether it was a regular workday and whether the employee worked. Do not assume every holiday or worker has the same arrangement.




Overtime
Work hours that meet applicable overtime rules, and the resulting compensation or a valid arrangement for paid time off. Check daily and weekly time records, applicable occupation or industry exceptions and any written agreement. A long shift by itself does not settle the calculation.




Ending employment
Questions about notice, possible termination pay and final earnings when an employment relationship ends. Check who ended it, length of employment, the circumstances and applicable exceptions. A temporary lay-off and a permanent end of employment are different situations.





The optional official rules directory links to each category. This overview gives no new legal rates or entitlement calculation. The later regular-wage case supplies the information needed for its stated comparison; do not add hypothetical holiday, overtime, vacation or termination amounts to it. Safety hazards still belong with the OHS route, and possible discrimination with the human-rights route.


Preserve the evidence and the outcome


Keep a copy of the relevant original record and the dated response. Do not alter an original time entry just to make it match payroll. If you find your own error, write a dated correction that preserves what changed. Record resolution with specifics: what was corrected, by whom and how you know. “Closed” with no evidence prevents later checking.


Optional first-step hint: “Turn 'the machine is dangerous' into an observation with a date, machine name and missing part. Then add the action already taken and the response still needed.”


Follow a complete example
I start the report at 4:05, before the later conversation, so the sequence is clear. The missing guard is the observed condition. The training card explains why it matters: Owen must not use Cutter 2 without it. I can state that connection without claiming an injury or knowing who removed the guard.


Next I record both sides of the response. Owen reported at 4:08 and Tessa acted at 4:10. Omitting Tessa's actual response would make the record misleading. Finally I say what remains open: a competent inspection and clearance. Safe packing work does not establish that Cutter 2 is safe.


Complete report, prepared at 4:20 p.m. on October 7:




At 4:05 p.m. on October 7, 2026, I observed that Cutter 2 at the cutting bench had no fitted guard. The machine was off and I did not operate it. My training card says not to use it without the guard and to report the condition. I do not know why it was absent, and no injury occurred. I told Tessa at 4:08. At 4:10 she told me to keep it out of use and said she would arrange a competent inspection. I began my trained packing task at 4:15. Please confirm who is responsible for the inspection and provide the result and conditions for resuming use. Until then I will follow the instruction to keep it out of use. I will keep this log and the response together; unresolved safety concerns belong with the employer's safety process and Alberta OHS.




“Tessa did nothing and the machine was fine by 4:15” contradicts the documents twice. It ignores the interim instruction and invents a final outcome. Reliable advocacy depends on describing both the concern and any action already taken.

At 3:55, Owen asks Tessa for an update. Tessa replies, “The inspection is booked for 4:30 today. Continue the packing task; Cutter 2 remains out of use.” No injury has occurred.

The October 5–11 work record shows 4:00–8:00 p.m. on October 8: four hours, with no unpaid break. The statement shows 3.50 hours, a difference of 0.50 hour. At the agreed $18.00 per hour, the work record gives $72.00 of regular wages. The statement's $63.00 is consistent with its own 3.50-hour entry, but is $9.00 below the work-record calculation. October 16, 2026 — Morgan, please review my October 5–11 regular-hours entry. My signed record shows work from 4:00–8:00 p.m. on October 8 with no unpaid break, while the statement lists 3.50 hours and $63.00 at $18.00/hour. I can provide copies of the agreement, signed time record and statement.


Nadia should retain the originals and a dated copy of the request and reply. Employment Standards is the external information route for this ordinary wage issue. Its current complaint instructions distinguish an employer review, waiting one pay period for ordinary pay corrections, and a formal complaint; Nadia can ask about the process if the issue remains unresolved. Core vocabulary
Earnings before deductions for the stated pay period.

Start here
Did the payment match the work?


Mika has received a pay stub: the employer's written breakdown of a payment for work. The amount deposited is smaller than hours multiplied by the hourly wage. That difference might be an explained deduction, an error, or a detail that needs checking. Looking only at the deposit cannot tell you which.


You will learn to follow the payment from hours to earnings to deductions to the amount received. Your final product is a short pay-check note for a different worker, including calculations and a question about a mismatch. All records are fictional. You will not enter your own employment or tax information.

Meet the situation and read the documents


Read Mika's records


Mika is an adult working at the fictional Pine Street Print Shop. A time record lists hours worked. A pay stub explains how an employer calculated a payment. A bank deposit is evidence of money received, but does not show the whole calculation. Read the two documents together.


Pine Street Print Shop — statement of earnings

Mika's time record: September 3, 4.00 hours; September 7, 4.50 hours; September 12, 4.00 hours. Mika confirms these are the hours actually worked. All deduction amounts are fictional supplied figures for reading practice, not rates or eligibility rules to use for a real worker.


Check your reading: Which two items should you compare first to check the hours on this payment?
Learn the method
Follow the money


Gross pay is earnings before deductions. For the single regular-pay line in this case, multiply hours by the hourly rate. The unit check helps: hours × dollars per hour produces dollars. The decimal 12.50 means twelve and a half hours; it does not mean twelve hours and fifty minutes.


A deduction is an amount removed from gross pay. Some payroll deductions contribute to public programs or tax withholding; others can relate to benefits or an agreed arrangement. The label tells you what is being withheld. It does not by itself prove the amount is correct or that it applies to every worker. In this lesson the amounts are supplied, so add them. Do not try to calculate current tax or contribution rates from memory.


Net pay is what remains after the listed deductions. It is the amount this statement says should be paid. Subtract deductions once: they are already removed from the displayed net amount. If you begin a spending plan with net pay and subtract them again, you make the available payment too small.


One-payment map: time entries → hours × rate → gross earnings → subtract current deductions → net payment. A second check compares that net figure with the actual deposit. A matching deposit can still come from incorrect hours, which is why checking only the last box is insufficient.


Choose the right column and date


A different stub may include several earnings lines. Overtime is pay recorded for hours treated as overtime under the applicable arrangement; an additional earning might be a separately listed bonus. Read each line's supplied hours, rate and amount before adding gross pay. Do not assume that every worker's overtime threshold or rate is the same.


A second format to read: a fictional adult worker's statement lists regular earnings, 10 hours at $20 = $200; approved overtime earnings, 2 hours at the expressly supplied $30 rate = $60; and a $15 bonus. Gross is $200 + $60 + $15 = $275. These are the statement's supplied terms, not a lesson about legal overtime eligibility. A separately labelled expense reimbursement is money repaid for an expense; inspect its treatment on the actual statement instead of automatically calling every deposit amount wages.


Current means this pay period. Year to date combines payments within the current calendar year. The figures serve different questions. Use current amounts to check this deposit; use the cumulative column to examine totals over the year. Never subtract cumulative deductions from one period's gross.


The pay period and payment date also answer different questions. The period tells you which work is included. The payment date tells you when the money is paid. A shift after September 14 would not automatically belong on this stub simply because payment arrived September 18.


Describe a mismatch without inventing its cause


If the time record and stub disagree, identify the two records, period and difference. An omitted shift is a possible explanation, but the documents may not tell you whether the cause was entry, approval or processing. A useful question requests a check of a specific line. “You stole my pay” is an unsupported conclusion from a mismatch alone.


CRA reading note — retrieved September 28, 2026: the CRA's pay-stub lesson distinguishes the pay period, current amounts and year-to-date totals. Use those labels to keep your calculation within one payment. Optional CRA explanation.


Show a first-step hint
Hint — First calculation: Add the three time entries before multiplying. Keep cents to two decimal places when recording money.


Watch or read · FINLIT 101
Paycheque Deductions
Keep Mika’s September statement in view. Watch or read the distinction between gross pay and net pay. Find those two lines on the statement, then identify the deductions that explain the difference.
Read the video transcript
Visuals: a drawn pay slip separates gross pay and deductions and highlights income tax. The on-screen document is illustrative; use the fully labelled HTML pay statement below for the lesson arithmetic.
Often there can be a bit of shock when you look at your paycheck and see the gross pay amount, the amount before deductions, compared to the net pay amount, the amount of money you actually get. What is all that money that is being subtracted? Let's dig into paycheck deductions a little more so we can get a better understanding of what those amounts that are being deducted actually are. First, we have income tax. By law, an employer must deduct the amount of federal and provincial income tax you're likely to over the year and submit it to the government on your behalf. Taxes go towards things like roads, schools, parks and hospitals. You may also see Canada Pension Plan or Canada Pension Plan (CPP).
FINLIT 101 · Paycheque Deductions · selected excerpt, used with permission.
Which amount represents Mika’s current payment after the listed deductions?
This short practice check saves with your lesson work. You can change your answer after reading the feedback.
Watch a worked decision
Read Mika’s fictional pay stub
This demonstration uses Mika’s May 1–14 statement. The current lesson uses September 1–14. Both examples deliberately use $225.00 gross, $30.40 deductions and $194.60 net. Follow the calculation here; use the September dates and time record in the lesson task.
Pause and decide: Calculate gross pay and total deductions. What does a match establish—and what does it not prove?
Read the narrated and visual transcript
Slide 1: A smaller deposit
Start by finding the period—not by guessing at an error. Pay period  •  May 1–14; 12.5 regular hours × $18.00/hour; Gross earnings  $225.00. What is the statement actually measuring?
Mika expected the weekend deposit to equal hours multiplied by the hourly rate, but the deposit is smaller. The first move is not to accuse anyone or assume every line is correct. Find the pay-period dates and the hours covered. This classroom pay stub is fictional; its dates, hours, dollar values, and deductions are invented. We are learning how to read and reconcile a statement, not estimating a real student’s tax or benefits.
Slide 2: Calculate the gross amount
Gross pay is before listed deductions. Regular hours     12.5; Hourly rate        $18.00; 12.5 × $18.00 = $225.00. Gross earnings = $225.00
Gross earnings are the starting amount before deductions. For this fictional hourly example, multiply 12.5 hours by $18 per hour. The units cancel: hours times dollars per hour gives dollars. Twelve times eighteen is 216, and half an hour at eighteen dollars is nine, so gross pay is $225. Compare that result with the printed gross line. It matches here, but the match cannot establish that the recorded 12.5 hours are the hours Mika actually worked.
Slide 3: Classify the listed lines
Add only the deductions shown as deductions. Income-tax withholding     $16.00; CPP line                   $10.80; Employment Insurance (EI) line                     $3.60. $16.00 + $10.80 + $3.60 = $30.40
Now read the labels and determine which lines are deducted from this fictional cheque. Add the three listed amounts: sixteen dollars plus ten dollars and eighty cents plus three dollars and sixty cents. The total is thirty dollars and forty cents. In real payroll, eligibility, amounts, employer arrangements, and current rules depend on the situation. These invented figures are not current contribution rates, tax guidance, or evidence that a real deduction should apply.
Slide 4: Reconcile net pay
Subtract the deduction total once. Gross     $225.00; Deductions − $30.40; Net        $194.60. $225.00 − $30.40 = $194.60
Net pay is gross pay minus the deductions taken from this payment. Subtract the total once: 225 dollars minus 30 dollars and 40 cents equals 194 dollars and 60 cents. The printed net amount matches. Do not subtract each deduction from the previous line and accidentally omit one. Also check whether the document has a different payment method, an adjustment, or an informational employer-paid amount before assuming that the net line equals the bank deposit.
Slide 5: Pause: try the calculation
Use the document, then explain the limit. Gross?; Total deductions?; Net? What is still unknown?. Pause and write your calculation before continuing.
Calculate gross pay and total deductions. What does a match establish—and what does it not prove? Pause to work it out.
Slide 6: Worked answer and next check
Arithmetic can reconcile while a record still needs checking. 12.5 × $18.00 = $225.00 gross; $16.00 + $10.80 + $3.60 = $30.40; $225.00 − $30.40 = $194.60 net. Next check: same dates, actual hours, and applicable records.
The result is 225 dollars gross, 30 dollars and 40 cents in listed deductions, and 194 dollars and 60 cents net. A common misconception is that the deposit amount is gross pay; it is net in this example. Another is that matching arithmetic proves a pay statement is correct. It proves only that these lines add up. For a real discrepancy, compare the same pay dates with time records and the agreement, then ask payroll or check current official guidance. Never use this classroom example as a real deduction rate. Suppose the time record showed 11.5 hours instead of 12.5. At the fictional rate, gross would be 11.5 times 18 dollars, or 207 dollars, which is 18 dollars less than the printed 225. That difference is a question to check against the same dates and actual work record, not proof of intent. A clear follow-up would identify the exact pay period and ask payroll to review the hour entry. The invented deduction lines should not be scaled to estimate a real cheque.
Original CALM 10 classroom demonstration. Figures and people in this example are fictional; check current sources before real decisions.
Follow a complete example
Check Mika's payment
Connect the video to this task. Use FINLIT’s gross-to-net distinction, then take the additional step in this example: check the paid hours against Mika’s time record.


I start with the dates: all three time entries fall inside September 1–14. Their hours total 4.00 + 4.50 + 4.00 = 12.50 hours. That matches the regular-work line. I multiply 12.50 × $18.00 = $225.00 gross.


Next I add only the current deductions: $16.00 + $10.80 + $3.60 = $30.40. Subtracting gives $225.00 − $30.40 = $194.60 net. The payment summary reports that amount. I can therefore say the supplied arithmetic and time entries agree; I have not independently verified real payroll rules.


Completed pay-check note: “For September 1–14, Mika recorded 12.50 hours. At $18.00 per hour, gross pay is $225.00. Current deductions total $30.40, leaving $194.60. These figures match the supplied statement. The record supports this calculation; it does not establish that the fictional deductions would apply to another worker.”


An answer of $73.00 comes from $225.00 − $152.00. It uses the year-to-date deduction total. The subtraction is arithmetically possible, but its two numbers describe different spans of time. Choosing the appropriate figures is part of doing the calculation correctly.

Economic and financial decisions · Lesson 2
What shapes a money decision?
How to complete this lesson
  1. Start here
  2. Meet the situation and read the documents
  3. Learn the method
  4. Watch or read Factors Influencing Money Decisions; try the short case check
  5. Follow a complete example
  6. Practise with support
  7. Check your understanding
  8. Apply independently
  9. Review and complete
At a check, try an answer, read the hint and revise. A different incorrect answer brings method support and an option to show the worked reasoning. Written responses use the comparison and self-checks; they are not automatically graded.
Optional reference · Making a Budget — Financial Consumer Agency of Canada (FCAC)
All facts needed for the activities are supplied in the lesson. Use the named original for further reading or to check current details.
Open Making a Budget — FCAC ↗
Core vocabulary
A limit or condition that a decision must respect.
Something that shapes how a person sees or chooses an option.
Something required to meet a stated purpose or obligation in the case.
An option someone likes, which still needs to be weighed against the case's limits.
Start here
A purchase can fit the price tag and still squeeze the plan


Ari wants the hoodie friends are ordering. There is enough money to pay its price today, but some of that money already has a job. You will work out what is available, then consider why the choice feels urgent.


Your final product is a decision note for Ren: explain a purchase choice using the supplied budget, a personal priority and an influence worth questioning. You are not expected to disclose your family's finances or agree with someone else's spending values.


How to complete this lesson: Read Ari's next two weeks and check the money already committed. Work through Separate the amount from the pressure and its complete decision example. Try Change one fact, answer six understanding questions, then write Ren's backpack decision. Compare, revise and sign off. Pause after the practice if useful; entries save automatically. Practice checks support revision; the Ren note is final evidence.


Meet the situation and read the documents


Ari's next two weeks


Ari is a fictional student with $60 available now. No more money arrives during the next fourteen days. Necessary meals and housing are provided separately and do not come out of this $60. Ari has two commitments before the next payment: $42 for transit to school and $12 to repair the zipper on the bag used daily. There is no usable spare bag. Both commitments must be paid within the fourteen days.


The group order notice


“Club hoodie: $48, including all charges. Orders close tonight. The club's regular activities are open to members with or without a hoodie. No returns after a personalized order is placed.”


Three messages Ari sees


    

  • Friend: “Most of us are getting one. It'll look good in the group photo.”
    • 

  • Family member: “I like having the travel money set aside first. It makes the week less stressful.”
    • 

  • Shop banner: “One night only! Don't miss your chance.”
    • 



Ari likes belonging to the club and likes colourful clothing. Ari also wants reliable travel to school. Those are real priorities in the case; neither needs to be mocked to examine the purchase.


Check the money: How much remains after the two stated commitments?
Learn the method
Separate the amount from the pressure


A commitment is money already needed for a planned obligation. Available for this choice means what remains after those commitments, not the whole amount in an account. Ari can physically pay $48 now, but doing so would leave $12 for $54 of commitments. The consequence is a shortfall, not simply a lower balance.


A need is a requirement in the person's situation; a want is something desired without the same immediate necessity. Context matters. A bag can be necessary for carrying supplies, while a particular brand may be optional. It is more useful to identify the job an item must do than to label every version of the item a need. Ari needs usable storage and travel; the case says the hoodie is not needed to join club activities.


Notice three kinds of influence


A contextual influence comes from circumstances and relationships: travel options, family habits, cultural practices, community expectations or advice. A psychological influence involves how a person feels, thinks or habitually acts: excitement, anxiety about missing out, buying when stressed or assuming a higher price means higher quality. A marketing influence is part of how an offer is presented, such as a countdown or a small weekly price.


These can overlap. Ari's wish to belong is a feeling, the group photo is a social situation, and the deadline is part of the selling message. The deadline may be accurate, but it does not make extra money appear. Ask two separate questions: “Is the deadline real?” and “Does this purchase fit the commitments?” A truthful advertisement can still emphasize the part of a decision that makes buying feel attractive.


Respect values and examine the claim


A value is something a person considers important. Someone may value shared celebrations, independence, generosity or avoiding debt. Families and communities can hold different views, and individuals within them can disagree. Do not infer a person's beliefs from their background. Use the priorities actually supplied.


A belief such as “using credit always means you can afford something” can be tested: borrowing moves a payment into the future and may add costs. A different belief, “borrowing is always a personal failure,” also overlooks context, such as a planned education expense with a feasible repayment plan. In this lesson there is no borrowing offer or future income available to solve Ari's gap. Inventing one would avoid the decision the records actually support.


Decision path: commitments → money left → benefit sought → pressure or assumption → feasible choice and consequence. A feasible choice fits the supplied money and deadlines. The explanation should show which benefit is kept and which is postponed.


In-course FCAC note, read September 28, 2026: needs and wants depend on a person's circumstances. Identify the function Ari must protect before judging the item. Read “Evaluate your needs and wants” — Financial Consumer Agency of Canada (new tab) ↗.


Show a first-step hint
Hint: Write “Ari has $60, but only ___ is uncommitted” before discussing whether the hoodie is appealing.


Watch or read · FINLIT 101
Factors Influencing Money Decisions
Ari has seen a friend’s message, a family preference and a deadline banner. Watch or read how peers, advertising and values can influence a purchase. Identify an influence without treating it as proof that the purchase is affordable.
Read the video transcript
Visuals: on-screen labels include friends and peers and incentives, followed by a presenter. The labels are examples of influences, not evidence that a purchase is affordable.
Think about the last item of clothing you bought. For me, it was my pants. So let's look at what factors affected that decision. Was it how you felt when you imagined yourself wearing it? Was it your friends? And what you thought they would think? Was it because you've typically worn this style in the past? Maybe your parents, siblings, or other family members had an influence on your choice. Maybe you were trying to stay current. We've all done it. Did you see a commercial? Maybe an ad or celebrity endorsement that helped convince you? Was it because of a sale or a discount code that you had? Or was it because of your own sense of values, style, and knowing what you really want? In addition to all these factors, it's important to ask yourself when making any purchase, can I afford this before spending the money? Think of there are other things you need you rather spend your money on. Listen, whether it's intentional or unintentional, all of these factors can influence the choices and decisions that you make about spending money. So here's a tip. When you make decisions about spending money, take a moment to think about which factors could be affecting your decision. After all, sometimes we make good decisions like my pants.

Follow a complete example
Explain Ari's choice without judging Ari
Connect the video to this task. Watch how the example separates social influence from the calculation. Belonging matters to Ari, but the hoodie is not required for club participation.


I first reserve $42 + $12 = $54. That leaves $6. The hoodie costs $48, so buying it from the remaining money would require another $42. Ari does not have that extra money in the case.


The club notice matters as much as the numbers. It says regular participation does not require the hoodie. Ari can keep the belonging benefit of attending club activities while giving up the matching clothing. The group photo and countdown explain why waiting feels uncomfortable; neither changes the available $6.


Completed decision note: “I recommend Ari skip this order and protect the $54 for transit and the bag repair. Only $6 is uncommitted, so the $48 hoodie would leave a $42 gap. Ari values belonging, but the notice says the club remains open without the hoodie. The group photo and closing deadline create pressure to buy now. Ari could attend in existing clothing and plan for a later optional purchase when money is available.”


“Only careless people buy club clothing” is not supported. The problem is this budget and timing. With different resources, buying the same hoodie could be a reasonable choice.

Build a flexible budget

  2. Meet the situation and read the documents

  4. Watch or read Tracking Your Spending; try the short case check

Core vocabulary
A plan showing income and how money will be used.
When money enters and leaves an account.
Money already in the account at the start of the period.
The amount by which available money is less than a required payment or target.
Start here
Will the money be there on the day it is needed?


Sam's planned monthly spending is lower than monthly income. That sounds reassuring, until several bills arrive before the second payment. A budget needs both totals and dates.


You will read a money calendar, find its lowest balance and revise a plan using confirmed options. Your final product is a dated plan for Nico that covers the stated commitments without spending money before it arrives. All budgets are fictional and all amounts are Canadian dollars. A calculator is available; the challenge is deciding what belongs in the calculation.


How to complete this lesson: Read Sam's October money calendar. Learn Two checks for a workable budget, then follow the complete revision. In Handle an unexpected repair, change the plan and check its balances. Answer six questions, then complete Nico's November plan, compare the model and sign off. You may pause after Sam's revision; saved practice and final work remain separate.


Meet the situation and read the documents


Sam's October money calendar


Sam, a fictional adult learner, starts October with $80 already in the account. Net income arrives as $450 on October 1 and $450 on October 15. Income is available before any outgoing payment on the same date. The $80 is an opening balance, not another monthly wage. No overdraft, credit or other income is available in this case.


Planned payments

Housing and food amounts are exercise assumptions, not suggested living-cost estimates. Sam wants to finish the month with at least the original $80 account buffer. Transfers to savings move money out of this spending account but do not destroy it; keep them in the cash-flow calculation because that money is no longer available here.


Check the calendar: Which money can Sam use on October 8?
Learn the method
Two checks for a workable budget


A budget is a plan for receiving, using and setting aside money. A cash-flow calendar puts those movements in date order. Start with the opening balance, add money when it arrives and subtract payments when they leave. The number after each movement is a running balance.


First check the whole period: income minus expenses and planned saving. A positive result is a surplus; a negative result is a shortfall. A surplus does not mean that every day is covered. If the second payment arrives after a bill, that later income cannot pay the earlier bill without some arrangement that actually makes money available.


Second check timing: calculate the running balance through the month. The lowest balance is the smallest amount reached after a movement. In this case any negative amount signals that the plan uses money unavailable in the account. It is a planning warning, not a fee calculation. No overdraft terms have been supplied.


Calendar method: opening balance + income received − payments made = balance at this point. Repeat from the new balance, not from zero. A simple sequence of dated balances makes a timing problem visible even when the monthly total looks fine.


Separate a feasible change from a wish


Some amounts are fixed by the case; others can change. Food and transit are required here. Removing them produces a lower total while leaving Sam unable to carry out the stated plan. A confirmed payment arrangement can change a date without changing total cost. A request that has not been accepted cannot be treated as an agreement.


Overextending means committing more money than the plan can support, including repayments that leave too little for other obligations. A small individual payment can contribute to overextension when several commitments fall together. Check their combined effects rather than judging one price in isolation.


A buffer is money left accessible for variation. It has a job even while unspent. However, a buffer target can sometimes need review: preserving it at all costs is not more important than a real essential need. State the trade-off rather than pretending there is no constraint.


Financial Consumer Agency of Canada (FCAC) reading note, September 28, 2026: its budgeting guidance connects income, spending and saving, and recommends reviewing the plan as circumstances change. Here, the dated records let you perform that review inside the lesson. Optional “Making a budget”.

Hint: Draw a line after October 10. Compare payments before that line with the opening $80 plus the first $450. Do not include October 15 yet.

Now I follow the dates. After the first income, Sam has $530. Room payment leaves $110; food leaves $20; phone takes the plan to −$25; transit takes it to −$105. The second income comes too late to prevent those shortfalls. I have found the problem before guessing at a solution.

Core vocabulary
An amount needed at the beginning of an agreement or purchase.
An amount paid repeatedly over the stated period.
Money held temporarily that is returned only when the stated return conditions are met.
All costs included within the comparison's stated period and assumptions.
Start here
Compare the whole arrangement


A small monthly price can make two offers look similar. The total, commitment, ownership and costs after purchase can still differ. You will help Dani compare two laptop purchase agreements, then make an independent recommendation about a calculator rental or purchase.


Your final product is a comparison note that distinguishes total cost from cash needed now, explains what the user receives and identifies one fact still worth checking. All offers are invented and all prices include the charges specified in the case. No purchase or live shopping is required.


How to complete this lesson: Read Dani's laptop offers and locate the payment terms. Learn Put offers on the same basis, then follow the complete comparison. In Add a repair possibility, test how one event changes the totals. Answer six questions and complete Riley's sixteen-week calculator choice. Review the model, revise and sign off. Pause after the laptop comparison if needed; every field saves.


Meet the situation and read the documents


Dani's laptop offers


Dani needs a laptop for a two-year program starting next month. Both offers supply the same model, which the fictional program has confirmed meets its software requirements. Dani has $120 available now and can commit up to $40 each month for 24 months after other obligations. Dani has no other purchase fund or borrowing option in this case.


North Computer Shop — purchase offer A


Pay $120 at pickup and $34 each month for 24 months. All scheduled charges and taxes are included. Ownership transfers after the final payment. The price includes a one-year warranty for manufacturing defects, not accidental damage. Accidental repair costs are not supplied. Cancelling does not erase the unpaid purchase balance. There is no extra fee for paying the balance early.


Central Computer Shop — purchase offer B


Pay $0 at pickup and $41 each month for 24 months. All scheduled charges and taxes are included. Same ownership and early-payment terms as A. Same one-year defect warranty, plus 24 months of accidental-damage cover: one eligible repair, with a $50 claim fee. Loss and theft are excluded. No repair occurs in the base comparison.


Check the offers: Which calculation gives A's scheduled total?
Learn the method
Put offers on the same basis


A purchase agreement sets out how a buyer pays for an item and what conditions apply. An instalment is one payment in a series. The term is the period covered by the agreement. A lease or rental pays for use under stated conditions and does not automatically give ownership. Read the ownership rule rather than assuming that the smallest monthly price buys the item.


Choose the same comparison period. Here both offers last 24 months. Add the upfront amount, all scheduled payments and any other mandatory charges. Do not add a fee twice if the offer already includes it. This gives a scheduled total under stated assumptions; a possible repair should be shown separately until an event is specified.


Cost map: amount at pickup + number of payments × payment amount + additional mandatory charges = scheduled total. Alongside it, keep a second line: money needed on the first date and on each later date. A lower total can still be inaccessible if the upfront payment is too large.


Compare benefits and remaining exposure


A warranty promises a remedy for conditions described in its terms. It is not a promise that every future problem will be free. A cover plan can have exclusions, limits and a claim fee. B includes one eligible accidental repair, but theft remains excluded and an accepted claim still costs $50. Writing “B includes free repairs” would erase important terms.


A decision should connect the feature to a plausible need. Both computers already meet the program's software requirements, so a claim that the more expensive plan runs the software better is unsupported. The useful difference is the cover, together with its price and limits.


Keep ownership costs visible


Large purchases can create later costs: maintenance, insurance where needed, replacement parts, interest, storage or operating costs. A vehicle, for example, can require insurance and ongoing maintenance in addition to its purchase price. Amounts depend on the actual vehicle, use and agreement, so do not invent a universal estimate. Mark missing costs and find an appropriate quote before a real commitment.


In this case the task supplies enough to compare scheduled payments. It does not supply a probability of accidental damage or A's repair prices. You can identify exposure without pretending to calculate an expected repair bill.


Optional reference note, September 28, 2026: The personal-loan comparison method from the Financial Consumer Agency of Canada (FCAC) checks payment count and total repayment, alongside fees. Here that arithmetic helps compare the supplied agreements; it does not establish a real loan's legal terms. Read “Comparing loan options”.


Show a first-step hint
Hint: Circle each offer's “at pickup,” “each month” and “24 months” phrases. Put those three figures into the same formula.


Follow a complete example
Compare Dani's base plan


Offer A totals $120 + 24 × $34 = $936. Offer B totals 24 × $41 = $984. B costs $48 more in scheduled payments. That difference buys a defined cover feature, not a different computer.


Now I check Dani's resources. A needs the full $120 available at pickup and then $34 monthly, leaving $6 of the $40 monthly allowance. B needs no upfront payment but requires $41 each month, $1 above the stated limit. Having no upfront payment does not solve that repeated shortfall.


Completed comparison: “Offer A fits Dani's supplied upfront and monthly limits and has a $936 scheduled total. B costs $984 and includes one eligible accidental repair with a $50 claim fee, but its $41 monthly payment exceeds Dani's $40 limit. I recommend A within this case, while checking repair prices before a real purchase and considering how to set aside the remaining $6 monthly. A's warranty does not cover accidental damage; the cheaper scheduled total does not eliminate repair risk.”


The alternative “B is best because it costs nothing today” considers only the first date. The alternative “A will definitely cost less under every possible event” confuses a base comparison with a guarantee about unknown repairs.


Next: Add a repair possibility. Try “A total including this repair ($)” before opening its comparison model.
Practise with support
Add a repair possibility


Keep both offer terms, but examine a specified event: one accidental screen break in month 10. A's shop provides a confirmed $160 repair quote. B confirms that this event is eligible and its only charge is the $50 claim fee. Assume no other repair and no change to scheduled payments. This is a comparison scenario, not a prediction that the break will happen.


Enter A total including this repair ($), B total including this claim ($) and What changes, and what does not? (2–3 sentences). Use Check these totals, then compare the model.


Show a first-step hint
Hint: Start with the scheduled total, not just the monthly price. Add the new event cost once.


Feedback: A $1,096; B $1,034. An answer of $160 or $50 names only the event cost. $984 for B omits its claim fee. $1,144 adds A's repair price to B instead of using B's supplied claim terms. Other answers show the matching formula and invite revision.

A real decision would need a feasible payment plan and a way to handle any repair charge when due.”

Open Credit: A 6-Letter Word for Debt ↗
Core vocabulary
The amount borrowed or still owed before the interest for the period is added.
The charge for borrowing money under the agreement's rate and method.
An asset pledged as security for a debt.
A person who shares responsibility for a debt under the agreement.
Start here
A smaller payment can create a larger commitment


Two offers let Alex borrow $600. One advertises a smaller monthly payment but lasts twice as long and has a separate fee. You will identify what is borrowed, what is repaid and which facts an application would need.


Your final product is a borrowing decision for a different fictional adult, including a non-borrowing alternative. You will not apply for credit, supply identification or enter real financial details.


How to complete this lesson: Read Alex's two offer summaries. Learn Separate the money borrowed from the promise to repay, then follow offer A's complete calculation. Practise comparing B and an income change. Answer six questions and complete Bea's coat decision. Compare, revise and sign off. Pause after the product explanations if useful; entries save automatically.


Meet the situation and read the documents


Alex's two offer summaries


Alex is a fictional adult considering borrowing $600 for equipment needed next month. After all other commitments, Alex has $60 each month available for repayment and $20 separately available now for a setup fee. Both offers provide exactly $600; no optional insurance is included. All required payments are stated, and neither offer permits additional borrowing through the same agreement.


Offer A — fixed instalment loan


Receive $600. Repay $55 monthly for twelve months, starting one month after receiving the money. No setup fee or other charge if paid as scheduled. The payment total includes the loan principal and borrowing charges. Missed-payment consequences and early-payment terms are not supplied; they need checking before a real agreement.


Offer B — longer instalment loan


Receive $600. Pay a separate $15 setup fee from existing cash when the loan begins. Repay $31 monthly for twenty-four months, starting one month later. The payments include principal and borrowing charges; the separate setup fee is not included in the $31. No other charge if paid as scheduled. Missed-payment and early-payment terms remain unspecified.


Application-information card


A lender may examine identity, income, existing obligations and credit history before approving an application. A quote is not approval. Some products require collateral or another responsible borrower. You are reading a fictional offer, not deciding legal eligibility or completing an application.


Check the offer: What does B's $31 describe?
Learn the method
Separate the money borrowed from the promise to repay


Credit is an arrangement that permits borrowing. Debt is the amount owed after borrowing occurs. The principal is the borrowed amount before interest and other charges. Interest is a charge for using borrowed money, while a fee is another specified charge. Total repayment includes returning the principal; cost of borrowing is the amount paid above the principal, including relevant fees in the comparison.


An instalment loan provides an amount repaid through a stated series of payments. A line of credit permits borrowing up to a limit under its terms; repaid amounts may become available again, and the outstanding amount can change with new borrowing. A credit limit is not a gift or income. Paying only interest on an outstanding line-of-credit balance does not reduce the principal.


Offer-reading map: amount received → payment amount and frequency → number of payments → fees → total paid → amount above principal → fit with the repayment budget. Keep separately paid fees separate until adding the total, so they are not omitted or counted twice.


Recognize purposes and responsibilities


Different products serve different purposes. A vehicle loan finances a vehicle and may use that vehicle as collateral, an asset securing repayment. A mortgage is a loan used for a property purchase, with property security and further terms. A student loan supports education under its program's rules; it is different from a bank's student line of credit. A credit-card cash advance takes borrowed cash against credit, with its own fees and interest terms. Buy now, pay later spreads or defers a purchase payment and is still credit, even when presented as a checkout option.


A secured loan has specified collateral; an unsecured loan does not use a pledged asset in that way. Unsecured does not mean optional repayment. A co-borrower shares responsibility for the debt under the agreement. Asking another person to join an application is not simply asking for a reference; the responsibility must be understood.


An app can make a product convenient and can emphasize an attractive first payment. Ease of tapping “accept” is not evidence of affordability. Read the repayment schedule before treating the approval screen as a recommendation.


Test the commitment, not just approval


A lender's willingness to offer credit does not prove that repayment will leave enough for a particular person's goals and obligations. Compare the payment with available money and consider a lower-income period. If key charges or consequences are absent, name exactly what must be clarified. Do not invent a missing late fee, and do not silently treat it as zero.


Dated Financial Consumer Agency of Canada (FCAC) reference notes, read September 28, 2026: its line-of-credit explanation distinguishes a borrowing limit from money actually borrowed. Its buy-now-pay-later page identifies these arrangements as credit and directs attention to payment schedules and fees. Use these definitions to recognize the product before comparing it. Lines of credit · Buy now, pay later plans.


Show a first-step hint
Hint: Multiply the regular payment by its count first. Then add fees paid outside those payments and subtract the amount actually borrowed to find the extra cost.


Watch or read · FINLIT 101
Why Borrow Money?
The excerpt names reasons people borrow and emphasizes affordability. Alex’s two quotations let you test that idea with actual terms. Look for the difference between a smaller payment and a smaller total cost.
Read the video transcript
Visuals: a presenter speaks to the camera. No loan offer in the clip replaces the terms in the fictional document below.
It can actually be a very smart move for financially confident people. And there are different ways to borrow money. You can borrow from a friend or family member if you're comfortable with that. Many people also borrow from a bank, lines of credit, a credit card, a car loan, or a mortgage for a house. There's also some loans available from the government like student loans. Borrowing money can help you achieve financial and life goals. But it's important to borrow wisely, manage your debt well and limit your borrowing to what you can afford. You know your own financial situation best. So set your own debt limits. Don't let others set them for you.
FINLIT 101 · Why Borrow Money? · selected excerpt, used with permission.
Offer B has a smaller monthly payment than Offer A. What can Alex conclude from that fact alone?
This short practice check saves with your lesson work. You can change your answer after reading the feedback.
Follow a complete example
Read offer A all the way through
Connect the video to this task. Use the FINLIT affordability question twice: can Alex manage each payment, and is the total extra cost justified by the benefit?


Alex receives $600. Twelve payments of $55 total $660. No separate fee is listed for scheduled repayment, so the borrowing cost in this comparison is $60, calculated as $660 − $600. Calling $660 “interest” would include money merely being returned.


The $55 payment fits the supplied $60 monthly allowance, leaving $5. That is a narrow margin, and the allowance is a planning assumption. It does not show how a reduction in income would be handled.


Complete offer note: “A advances $600 and requires twelve $55 payments, or $660 total. The extra borrowing cost is $60 under on-time repayment. The payment fits Alex's current $60 allowance with $5 remaining each month. Before a real agreement, Alex would need the missing early-payment and missed-payment terms and a plan for a lower-income month. The quote itself does not establish approval.”


“$55 is cheap, so borrow” gives no duration or purpose. The complete note supplies a total and a limit before a recommendation.


Next: Compare B, then change the available money. Try “B total paid, including setup ($)” before opening its comparison model.
Practise with support
Compare B, then change the available money

Optional investigation · Compare two borrowing products
Alex’s required quotation comparison stays above. This separate investigation adapts questions 1–2 of FINLIT’s Why Borrow Money Assignment 6.1: what does borrowing cost, and what does a line of credit allow? Use the supplied FCAC example; do not apply for credit or request a quote.
Read the same amount over the same period

FCAC illustrative example · checked September 28, 2026
$300 borrowed for 14 days
Payday loan
$42 cost, using a flat fee of $14 per $100 borrowed.
Line of credit
$5.92 cost, using a $5 administration fee and 8% annual interest.
These are illustration assumptions, not current offers to Alex. The cost excludes the $300 principal that must also be repaid.
Follow one calculation
Payday fee: 3 × $14 = $42. Principal plus fee: $300 + $42 = $342. The $14 figure is a fee per $100, not a directly comparable annual rate.
A line of credit permits borrowing within an approved limit and charges interest on the amount used. Fees can also apply. Lenders assess factors such as income, debts and credit history; the lower example cost does not establish that a person qualifies. Payday repayment is tied to the pay schedule; a line of credit has minimum payments, and paying only interest leaves principal owing.
Now compare
Use the two displayed costs. Find the cost difference, then distinguish price from access.
What can this table establish?
Compare your question with a model
“Does the person qualify for a line of credit, and can they repay principal as well as charges without missing essentials?” Either access or repayment is a useful question. “Which is cheapest in this table?” is already answered by the supplied numbers.

Calculate interest with the right time unit

Optional reference · Financial Consumer Agency of Canada (FCAC) Module 4: Dealing with Debt
All facts needed for the activities are supplied in the lesson. Use the named original for further reading or to check current details.
Open FCAC Module 4: Dealing with Debt ↗
Core vocabulary
A rate expressed for a one-year period.
Interest calculated on the stated original principal for the specified time.
The part of a year used when matching time to an annual rate.
Money paid back, including the amounts required by the agreement.
Start here
Twelve percent of what, and for how long?


An interest rate needs a principal amount and a time period before it can tell you a cost. A 12% annual rate does not mean paying 12% of the principal every month. You will calculate a deliberately simple loan, then explain where that model stops being useful.


Your final product is a calculation note for a new fictional offer: show interest, principal plus interest, a missing fee and what can be concluded about a repayment limit. A calculator is provided. No real borrowing, rate lookup or personal financial information is needed.


How to complete this lesson: Read Mina's simple-interest agreement and check its time unit. Learn Match the rate to the time, follow the three-month example and practise changing the duration and rate. Answer six questions, then complete Imani's four-month offer. Compare, revise and sign off. You can pause after the worked calculation; all fields save.


Meet the situation and read the documents


Mina's simple-interest agreement


Mina is a fictional adult borrowing $600 for exactly three months. The agreement expressly uses 12% simple interest per year, with months counted as twelfths of a year. No interim payment is made; the full principal stays outstanding until the end. Interest is not added to principal during the period. Principal and interest are paid together at the end of month three. There is no setup fee or other charge in this example.


This is a mathematical teaching agreement, not an offer from a lender. Real products can calculate interest daily, add fees or use changing balances. Use this model only with the stated assumptions.


Terms on the agreement


    

  • Principal, amount borrowed: $600.
    • 

  • Annual rate: 12%, or 0.12 as a decimal.
    • 

  • Duration: three months, or 3/12 of a year.
    • 

  • Interest rule: principal × annual decimal rate × years.
    • 

  • Repayment at the end: principal + interest.
    • 



Check the time unit: Which duration belongs with the annual rate in this formula?
Learn the method
Match the rate to the time


Simple interest is calculated on the stated principal without adding earned or charged interest to that principal during the model period. Let P mean principal, r mean annual rate written as a decimal, and t mean time in years. Then I = P × r × t. I is the interest charge, not the whole repayment.


A percent means “per hundred.” Twelve percent becomes 12/100=0.12. Multiplying $600 by 12 rather than 0.12 would charge twelve times the principal for one year instead of twelve hundredths. Check whether the size of the answer makes sense: at 12% annually, one full year's simple interest on $600 is $72. Three months is only a quarter of that year, so the charge should be a quarter of $72.


The rate and time must use the same unit. With an annual rate, divide the number of months by 12. Three months is 0.25 year; six is 0.5 year. Do not apply the whole annual amount to every month. A useful alternative representation is annual interest ÷12 × number of months, which gives the same result under this agreement's month rule.


Keep three amounts distinct


Principal is the amount borrowed. Interest is the charge calculated by the formula. Principal plus interest is the repayment before any additional fee. With a separate fee, add that fee once to the total paid. Do not call the whole repayment “interest,” and do not assume a missing fee is zero.


Write units beside each step. “600×0.12×3/12=18” becomes more meaningful as “$18 interest over three months.” A sentence about what the number means is part of the answer, not decoration around it.


Change one assumption at a time


For a fixed principal and simple annual rate, doubling the time doubles interest. Doubling the rate or principal also doubles interest when the other two stay constant. These relationships help catch errors, but they do not establish the behaviour of every loan.


If payments reduce the principal, later interest may apply to a smaller balance. If interest is added to a balance and later interest is charged on that enlarged amount, the process involves compounding. The following lesson uses a reducing-balance repayment schedule. It would be wrong to apply this unchanged-principal formula to that whole schedule without accounting for payments.


Model boundary: this agreement uses months/12, not an actual-days convention. A real offer must state its own calculation and fee terms. Optional FCAC background on loan rates and charges, read September 28, 2026. No external page is needed to solve the fictional agreement.


Show a first-step hint
Hint: Calculate a full year's interest first, then take the fraction of a year. This can be easier to reason through than entering every symbol at once.


Follow a complete example
Calculate Mina's three-month cost


The agreement supplies P=$600, r=0.12 and t=3/12. First, $600×0.12=$72 for a full year at the stated simple rate. Three months is one-quarter of a year, so $72×0.25=$18 interest. Repayment is $600+$18=$618.


Completed calculation note: “The $600 remains outstanding for three months. At 12% simple annual interest, I=$600×0.12×3/12=$18. With no fees, Mina repays $618 at the end of the three months. The $18 is the borrowing charge; $600 is the return of principal.”


An answer of $216 comes from $600×0.12×3. It treats three months as three years. An answer of $72 uses a whole year. Neither matches the agreement's duration, even though the multiplication itself was carried out correctly.


Now you will change the duration rather than the person or calculation rule. Keep the unchanged assumptions visible when comparing results.


Next: Change the duration, then the rate. Try “Six-month interest ($)” before opening its comparison model.
Practise with support
Change the duration, then the rate


Practice 1: Mina instead keeps the same $600 for six months at the same 12% simple annual rate. There are still no interim payments or fees. Enter Six-month interest ($) and Six-month repayment ($). Use Check the duration change.


Feedback: $36 interest and $636 repayment. $18 repeats the three-month result. $72 uses twelve months. $432 treats six months as six years. Other answers receive the full-year amount $72 and the 6/12 time fraction, then a retry prompt.


Practice 2: Keep six months and $600, but change the annual rate to 9%. Enter Interest at 9% for six months ($) and Explain the comparison (2–3 sentences identifying what changed and what stayed constant). Use Check the rate change, then compare the model.


Feedback: $27 interest. $54 is one year's interest; $36 retains the old rate; $270 reflects a decimal-place error. Other answers receive P600, r0.09, t6/12 and a prompt to retry.

The change isolates the rate, so I can attribute the lower interest to that rate difference in this model.”

The fee is paid at repayment for this exercise, not deducted from the advance.

Lending and debt · Lesson 3
Read a loan payment schedule
How to complete this lesson
  1. Start here
  2. Meet the situation and read the documents
  3. Learn the method
  4. Follow a complete example

Optional reference · Mortgage Calculator — Financial Consumer Agency of Canada (FCAC)
All facts needed for the activities are supplied in the lesson. Use the named original for further reading or to check current details.
Open Mortgage Calculator — FCAC ↗
Core vocabulary
Repaying a debt over time through scheduled payments.
The total amount paid at a scheduled time, which may include interest and principal.
The portion of a payment that reduces the amount borrowed.
The debt left after the period's interest and payment are applied.
Start here
Where does a loan payment go?


A payment can contain both an interest charge and repayment of the amount borrowed. You will follow those two parts through a schedule, then use a calculator to compare repayment lengths. A smaller monthly payment can help a monthly budget while increasing the total cost.


Your final product is a comparison of two fictional loans for the same purchase. You will identify the monthly payment, total borrowing cost and remaining balance after the first payment, then explain a choice using a supplied budget. All rates and terms are teaching examples, not available offers.


How to complete this lesson: Read Alex's repayment schedule. Learn what each column means, follow the first two payments, then change the repayment length in Try 24 months. Answer six checks. Complete Ren's equipment loan comparison, review the model and sign off. Pause after the calculator comparison if needed; your entries save. Practice and final work are separate.


One rule for the core lesson: divide the stated annual rate by 12 to get the monthly rate. For Alex, 12% ÷ 12 = 1% per month. Each month: opening balance × monthly rate = interest; payment − interest = principal repaid; opening balance − principal repaid = closing balance. Round money to cents. Ren uses the same method with 9% ÷ 12.
Checks help you learn; they are not grades. An incorrect answer gets a hint first. Revise and check again, or deliberately open a worked comparison when you need more support. Repeated clicks on an unchanged answer do not count as a new try.
Meet the situation and read the documents


Alex's repayment schedule


Alex, a fictional adult, borrows $1,000. The agreement charges a fixed nominal annual rate of 12%, divided by 12 for a monthly rate of 1%. Interest is charged on the opening balance each month. A payment is made at the end of every month. No further money is borrowed, no payments are missed and no fees apply. The loan is scheduled to finish in 12 months.


An amortization schedule is a row-by-row record of how regular payments reduce a debt. “Opening” means before this month's interest and payment; “closing” means after them. Money is rounded to cents at each interest posting. The last payment is adjusted to clear the remaining cents.






Month
Opening balance

Payment

Closing balance

Schedule summary: 11 payments of $88.85 and a final payment of $88.84; total paid $1,066.19; total interest $66.19. Open All 12 payments to inspect the complete schedule. The visible rows and summary supply everything needed for the teaching.


Read the document: Which figure says how much of the first payment reduces the original debt?
Learn the method
Follow one row from left to right


Start with the opening balance: the unpaid principal before that month's charge. Multiply it by the monthly rate to find interest. Subtract interest from the payment to find principal repaid. Finally, subtract principal repaid from the opening balance to find the closing balance. That closing balance becomes next month's opening balance.


The same process can be read as a flow:


Opening debt → calculate interest → split the payment → subtract its principal part → carry the balance forward.


For month one, 12% per year divided by 12 gives 1% per month, so $1,000 × 0.01 = $10. The $88.85 payment first covers that $10. The remaining $78.85 reduces principal. Subtracting the whole $88.85 from $1,000 would ignore the interest charge and understate the debt.


Explain the changing split


The payment stays almost constant, but the split changes. In month two, interest is charged on $921.15 rather than $1,000. The smaller balance produces $9.21 interest after rounding, so $79.64 of the same $88.85 payment can reduce principal. A constant payment does not mean a constant interest charge.


The amortization period is the planned time to repay the loan. Spreading the same debt over more months usually lowers each payment under the same rate and calculation rules. It also leaves some principal unpaid for longer, creating more interest charges. Both effects matter: a payment that cannot be sustained is not made suitable just by having a low lifetime cost.


Use the tool as a model you can explain


The calculator repeats the row calculation. It does not know whether a purchase is needed, whether income will continue, or whether a real lender will approve an application. Read its principal, annual rate, months and fee inputs before trusting its answer. This lesson uses equal monthly payments, a fixed rate and end-of-month payments. Real agreements may use different timing or calculation conventions.


A fee paid separately adds to total cost. It does not become loan principal in this model. If a real fee is added to the loan, it can also attract interest; that would require a different principal input.


Optional reference: FCAC's Personal loans explains comparing loan terms and charges. Its page supports the comparison questions; Alex's agreement and the supplied schedule determine these figures. You do not need to open it to complete the task.


Show a first-step hint
First-step hint: Find the opening balance and monthly rate before looking at the payment. This prevents you from treating the payment itself as the amount on which interest is charged.


Follow a complete example
Explain Alex's first two payments


The first row begins with $1,000. Interest is $10, leaving $88.85 − $10 = $78.85 to repay principal. The debt falls to $1,000 − $78.85 = $921.15. The second row starts with that exact amount. Its interest is $921.15 × 0.01 = $9.2115, rounded to $9.21. Principal repaid is $88.85 − $9.21 = $79.64; the closing balance is $841.51.


Completed explanation: “Alex pays $88.85 in each of the first two months. The first payment reduces principal by $78.85 and the second by $79.64 because the second interest charge is smaller. The full schedule totals $1,066.19, which is $66.19 above the $1,000 borrowed. I used the schedule's adjusted final payment rather than multiplying $88.85 by 12 and ignoring the one-cent adjustment.”


“Alex owes $911.15 after month one” is unsupported: it subtracts the entire $88.85 payment from the $1,000 balance. Of that payment, $10 pays interest, so only $78.85 reduces the principal. Show the split once, then subtract only the principal portion from the debt.
