Employee rights and responsibilities · Lesson 4
Recognize discrimination and seek help
How to complete this lesson
  1. Start here
  2. Meet the situation and read the documents
  3. Learn the method
  4. Follow a complete example
  5. Practise with support
  6. Check your understanding
  7. Apply independently
  8. Review and complete
At a check, try an answer, read the hint and revise. A different incorrect answer brings method support and an option to show the worked reasoning. Written responses use the comparison and self-checks; they are not automatically graded.
Optional reference · Alberta Human Rights Commission
All facts needed for the activities are supplied in the lesson. Use the named original for further reading or to check current details.
Open Alberta Human Rights Commission ↗
Core vocabulary
Unfair adverse treatment connected to a protected ground in an area covered by human-rights law.
A characteristic protected by the applicable human-rights legislation.
An adjustment considered to address a protected need within the applicable legal duties and limits.
A conclusion drawn from facts that must be distinguished from what was directly observed.
Start here
Being treated badly at work can leave someone uncertain about what to call it or whom to ask. A useful first step is to separate what happened, why a protected characteristic may be connected, and what still needs to be understood. You do not need to decide a legal case before asking for information or support.


You will examine a documented disability-related concern, practise updating a record when an employer provides new information, and then prepare a support plan for a different scheduling and religious-accommodation concern. Use the supplied fiction; no personal experience or identity disclosure is requested.


Your route is Meet the situation and read the documents → Learn the method → Follow a complete example → Practise with support → Check your understanding → Apply independently → Review and complete. Pause whenever needed, including between the case and the example. All learning can be completed in this course. No interview, confrontation, complaint submission or external account is required. Guided writing and six questions are practice; the independent concern record and support plan form your final evidence.


Vocabulary. A protected ground is a characteristic covered by human rights law. An adverse impact is a negative effect, such as loss of a work opportunity. A connection is evidence that a protected characteristic was a factor in that effect. Accommodation is a change that addresses a need linked to a protected ground so a person can participate. An allegation is a concern someone reports; it is not itself a legal finding. An inquiry asks for information; a complaint begins a formal process with its own requirements.


Optional disclosure: Official pages for a current concern. Dated in-course records below support every required task. Direct links are optional for checking current information. These practice fields do not contact the Commission or your employer.


Meet the situation and read the documents


Jules is 18 and works at fictional Clearview Tickets, an Alberta provincially regulated employer. Jules has a hearing disability and normally uses written confirmations of work instructions. Jules is seeking scheduled shifts at the customer counter, where work includes reading booking information, speaking or writing with customers, and processing tickets. The concern concerns access to those shifts.


Document A — Role and training record


Counter-shift criteria, issued September 1, 2026: complete booking training, demonstrate accurate booking entry in the assessment, and be available for the offered shift. Employees can use the approved written instruction checklist.


Training record, September 4: Jules completed the training and met the booking-entry assessment standard. The record shows availability for the two counter shifts advertised for September 14 and 16. No missed qualification is identified in this record. This does not reveal every operational decision the employer may have made.


Document B — Dated communication record






Date
Exact supplied record





September 5
Jules emailed supervisor Pat: “I would like the September 14 and 16 counter shifts. Because of my hearing disability, please provide changes to the instructions in writing as well as spoken instructions. I can use the approved checklist.”




September 6
Pat replied by email: “I am not assigning counter shifts to someone with your hearing disability. You can stay on filing.” No individual assessment or accommodation discussion is included in that reply.




September 8
The published schedule assigned Jules to filing and assigned the two counter shifts to other staff. The reasons for the other staff's assignments are not supplied.





Jules saved the role criteria, training record, email thread and schedule. No threat of violence or immediate physical danger is reported. Jules wants advice and a fair review; Jules has not made a formal complaint.


Document C — Supplied workplace support route




An employee may raise a concern with HR coordinator Ash, including a concern involving the employee's immediate supervisor. Ash can receive a written summary and arrange a private discussion. The employee may ask to bring a support person. Requests about work-related access needs can be made in writing. This route is an available option, not a requirement to confront Pat alone.




Document D — In-course human rights records


Alberta Human Rights Commission, “Discrimination,” “Protected grounds,” and “Rights & Responsibilities”; checked September 28, 2026. Employment is a protected area. A discrimination inquiry examines a protected characteristic, a negative impact and whether the characteristic contributed to that impact. Examples of protected grounds include disability, religious beliefs, race, colour, ancestry, place of origin, gender, gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation, marital status and family status. The Act's age ground concerns people 18 or older. A concern outside a protected ground may still need another workplace response.


Commission, “Duty to accommodate at work”; checked September 28, 2026. Employers must consider needs connected to protected grounds and take reasonable accommodation steps up to undue hardship. Workers explain relevant needs and cooperate in the process. Assessment is individual; a preferred solution is not automatically the only reasonable one. Disability-related documentation may be needed, but a specific diagnosis does not have to be disclosed to the employer. Undue hardship requires more than ordinary inconvenience.


Commission, “Making a complaint,” “Accessibility,” and “Contact us”; checked September 28, 2026. The Commission provides human-rights information and can explain complaint requirements; it does not give legal advice. Its stated complaint limit is one year after the discriminatory act or treatment, so timely information matters. Support may include accessible formats, interpretation, a support person or adjusted communication arrangements. Availability is discussed according to the person's needs. A formal complaint has its own process; an inquiry does not automatically file one.


Read the documents


Which statement gives evidence of a possible connection between Jules's disability and the lost counter shifts? Choose, 
Learn the method
Use three connected questions


Start with the employment event rather than a label. What opportunity, condition or treatment changed? Then ask which protected ground may be involved and what evidence connects it to the negative effect. The source's three-part test helps focus the record, but this lesson does not replace the full assessment of the facts, explanations and applicable law.






Question
Jules's evidence
What the evidence does not decide





Is a protected characteristic involved?
Hearing disability is stated in Jules's request.
Every medical detail or diagnosis.




What is the negative effect?
Jules requested two counter shifts and was assigned filing instead.
The complete reasons for every other worker's assignment.




What suggests a connection?
Pat's email expressly links the decision to disability.
The final legal outcome after a complete review.





Not every disappointment establishes discrimination. If two qualified applicants seek one shift, one will not get it; that fact alone does not show a protected-ground connection. At the same time, a rule that sounds identical for everyone can create a barrier for someone with a protected need. “Everyone must receive instructions only by hearing them once” could disadvantage a worker who needs accessible communication. Ask what the rule does in practice.


Do not require proof of a person's private motive


A worker often cannot know what a manager privately intended. Document the words, decisions and effects instead. A stated positive intention does not erase a barrier, and feeling upset does not by itself establish the legal connection. Jules has a specific email worth preserving; there is no need to add guesses about Pat's character.


Use three labels while writing: fact, possible interpretation, information needed. “Pat sent the September 6 email” is a fact within the supplied record. “Disability appears to have been a factor” is a supported concern. “I want the employer's individual assessment and explanation of the decision” identifies needed information. Writing “possible” does not mean dismissing the concern; it shows where a proper review is still required.


Understand accommodation as a process


Accommodation aims to address a barrier connected to a protected need. The worker should explain the relevant work need and participate in exploring reasonable options. The employer should consider it individually and take reasonable steps up to undue hardship. In Jules's case, the request is written confirmation of changed instructions. It is not a request to waive accurate booking work.


The job's actual tasks and available controls matter. An unsupported assumption that a disability makes someone unsuitable is different from examining whether the person can do the work with reasonable accommodation. A request also does not automatically entitle someone to any chosen shift or their preferred solution. The question is whether the opportunity and accommodation need were considered fairly under the applicable duties.


Protect privacy while explaining the need. A support record can state “written confirmations needed for work instructions” without including unnecessary medical history. Other employees' private diagnoses or religious practices are not yours to demand or circulate. Relevant scheduling criteria and accommodation steps can be discussed without collecting a coworker's medical file.


Choose a safe, suitable support route


An internal route such as Ash may help arrange review. If the supervisor is involved in the concern, an alternative recipient can be useful. A worker may ask about an accessible communication method or support person before a meeting. The Commission can provide information about human rights and complaint requirements. The source describes approaching the other party as something to consider; this lesson does not require a worker to confront them first or alone.


Different needs may need different supports. The Commission addresses protected-ground concerns; Employment Standards addresses minimum employment conditions such as wages and hours; Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) addresses workplace health and safety. An immediate threat requires moving to safety and an appropriate emergency response rather than waiting for an administrative complaint process. Our fictional records do not describe such a threat.


Keep dates because formal processes have time limits. The Commission's one-year limit is a reason to seek timely information, not a reason to wait until the last day. An internal discussion should not be assumed to pause that limit. For a real situation, verify the current process and get help calculating deadlines if uncertain; this lesson does not ask you to calculate or submit a real claim.


Optional first-step hint: “Begin your guided response with one exact event from the timeline, its effect and the words connecting it to the protected ground. The question you write can ask for information a fair review would need.”


Follow a complete example
I begin with September 5 because it establishes the request and the work-related need before the decision. The September 6 email supplies a direct connection, so I do not need to invent a remark about disability that was never in the record. The September 8 schedule establishes the effect.


I include Jules's completed assessment because it is relevant to the published criteria. I still leave room for the employer to explain its assessment and the other relevant circumstances. That is different from ignoring the explicit email: the concern deserves a specific response.


Complete concern record and support plan:




Jules requested the September 14 and 16 counter shifts on September 5 and asked for written confirmation of changed instructions because of a hearing disability. The supplied training record says Jules completed the booking training and met the entry standard. Pat's September 6 email states that Jules will not receive counter shifts because of the hearing disability. The September 8 schedule assigns Jules to filing. This is a possible disability-discrimination and accommodation concern: there is a protected characteristic, an adverse work-opportunity effect and explicit wording connecting them. The complete individual assessment and any other relevant explanation are still needed; this record does not decide the legal outcome.


Jules can keep the original criteria, training record, emails and schedule together and make a dated summary. An available safe next step is a written request to HR coordinator Ash for a private review of the counter-shift decision and the written-instruction need, with a support person or accessible communication if helpful. Jules can also seek information from the Alberta Human Rights Commission about the protected-ground concern and current requirements without first proving the case. A question is not a filed complaint. The dated source says the formal complaint limit is one year after the discriminatory treatment, so the internal review should not become indefinite waiting.




“Jules is automatically entitled to both shifts and a guaranteed legal victory” goes beyond the evidence. “There is no issue unless someone admits bad intentions” also misreads the method: the recorded words and effects already support seeking a review.


Next: Practise with support. Try “What is confirmed, and what remains unresolved?” before opening its comparison model.
Practise with support
Keep Documents A–D. Add this new entry:


Document E — September 10 response from Ash. “I have received Jules's concern. I will review the training record, the September 6 email and the allocation criteria. I would like to discuss the written-instruction need with Jules. No decision about the two shifts has yet been made.” Jules can reply in writing or ask for an accessible meeting with a support person under the supplied workplace route.


Write an update in three fields:


    

  1. What is confirmed, and what remains unresolved? Distinguish receipt/review from a changed decision or completed accommodation.
    2. 

  2. Draft Jules's response to Ash. Identify the relevant work need and two records/questions to include. Use a short respectful message; do not supply a real medical diagnosis.
    3. 

  3. Record the follow-up and support choice. Choose written communication or an accessible meeting, state why it fits this case and keep the option of Commission information visible.
    4. 



Show a first-step hint
 “Ash has promised a review, not yet its result. Ask what will be reviewed and when Jules can expect an update; do not invent a promised date.”

Next: A different concern: a religious observance and a schedule. Read the new situation and its supplied records before filling your independent response. Use the method you practised with the evidence in this new case.
Apply independently
A different concern: a religious observance and a schedule


Noor is 19 and an ordinary employee at fictional Riverbend Market, a provincially regulated Alberta business. Prepare a concern record and support plan. Do not decide a legal complaint. Use these records only; no personal religious information is requested.


Document F — Request, October 5, 2026. Noor emails scheduler Vic: “I need to attend a religious observance on Saturday, October 17, from 10:00 a.m. to noon. I am requesting accommodation for this religious need. I can work that day from 1:00–5:00 p.m. or discuss another reasonable arrangement. Please let me know what information you need.” Noor's usual Saturday shift is 10:00 a.m.–2:00 p.m.


Document G — Reply and schedule. Vic replies October 6: “We are short-staffed, so the 10:00–2:00 shift stays.” No accommodation options or supporting staffing details are discussed in the reply. The schedule posted October 9 retains Noor's 10:00–2:00 shift. Two coworkers' October 17 shifts have changed, but Noor does not know why, when they requested changes or what duties they cover. No comment attacking Noor's religion is reported. Noor remains employed and has not been disciplined.


Document H — Available route and privacy. Riverbend has a people-services coordinator, Sam, who accepts written accommodation-review requests and can arrange a discussion with a support person. Noor may keep copies of Noor's own request, reply and schedule; private coworker records are not supplied. Noor wants the religious need considered and prefers a written first contact. No immediate physical threat is reported. No review beyond Vic's reply has occurred.


Write one coherent product using four fields:


    

  • Dated facts and effect — summarize the request, response and resulting conflict, without inventing discipline or remarks.
    • 

  • Possible protected-ground connection and missing information — identify the ground, explain the concern and name at least two relevant questions. Distinguish what is known from what the coworker comparison cannot establish.
    • 

  • Draft the review request — write a short message to Sam describing the need, the request already made and a reasonable question about options. Do not demand private coworker details or claim only one accommodation can work.
    • 

  • Support, records and timing plan — choose a safe accessible route, list relevant records and explain why timely information about the Commission's process matters. You are planning, not submitting anything.
    • 



Success means recognizing a possible protected-need barrier, using accurate dates and effects, asking for individual consideration and retaining uncertainty about the complete staffing evidence and outcome.

Your current response
Compare your response with a model




On October 5, Noor requested accommodation for a religious observance from 10:00 a.m. to noon on October 17 and offered 1:00–5:00 p.m. or another reasonable arrangement. Vic's October 6 reply cited short staffing, and the October 9 schedule retained 10:00 a.m.–2:00 p.m., which overlaps the stated observance. Religious beliefs are a protected ground; the remaining schedule creates a possible barrier linked to that need. There is no supplied religious insult or disciplinary action. We need to understand the actual staffing/essential-duty needs and what options were considered. The coworkers' changes do not prove unequal treatment because their reasons, timing and duties are unknown; their private information should not be demanded.


Sam, please review my accommodation request for October 17. My October 5 message explained a religious need from 10:00 a.m. to noon and offered 1:00–5:00 p.m. or another reasonable arrangement. Vic's reply cited short staffing, and the posted shift still overlaps the observance. Could we discuss which duties need coverage and whether a later shift, swap or another arrangement could address both needs? Please explain what relevant information you need from me and when I can expect a response. I prefer written communication initially and may ask for a support person if a meeting is useful.


Noor can retain the original request, reply and schedule with a dated summary and any response. Sam is an available internal review route; Noor can also seek Alberta Human Rights Commission information about religious accommodation and complaint requirements. Accessible communication or a support person may be requested according to need. The source's one-year complaint limit makes timely information important; Noor should not assume internal discussion pauses it. The final outcome cannot be determined from these limited records. No live request or complaint is part of the lesson.




Other reasonable options can be proposed, but no answer should guarantee a particular shift or treat “short-staffed” as a complete proven undue-hardship finding.

Use feedback to revise a career route

Core vocabulary
A specific action or result noticed in the record.
An explanation of what an observation may suggest.
An ability or habit that needs further development.
A possible career direction to investigate, not a final verdict from one experience.
Start here
Turn a comment into a next step


Feedback is useful when it helps you identify what worked, what needs practice and what evidence to gather next. “You were great” is encouraging, but it does not tell you which skill to keep developing. One difficult moment also does not decide an entire career.


You will help Rowan revise an employability claim and choose a realistic next test. Your final product is a short reflection and plan based on a new feedback note. Everything happens in the supplied simulation; you do not need a real supervisor, placement or personal work history.


How to complete this lesson: Read Rowan's feedback and current plan. Learn Move from observation to a testable plan, then follow the printer-feedback example. Practise a communication claim and compare working arrangements. Answer six questions, then complete A second lead's observation. Compare your revised plan with the model, check the criteria and complete the lesson. Pause after practice if useful; all entries save.


Meet the situation and read the documents


Rowan's feedback and current plan


Rowan has completed fictional welcome-desk tasks. Morgan's comments refer to specific moments, not to every ability Rowan has. On the recorded shift, Morgan provided approved access and a demonstration before Rowan updated any reservation entries.


Morgan's feedback note — September 14






Observation
Evidence Morgan reports
Suggested improvement





Clear visitor directions
Visitors followed Rowan's sign-in explanation without needing it repeated.
Try explaining a different procedure and check whether it is understood.




Accurate record work after training
Eight checked entries matched the supplied forms.
Keep checking against the original form when something is unclear.




Late report of a blocker
Printer stopped at 10:05; Rowan reported it at 10:20. The approved backup still finished before 11:00.
Report when the blocker is first noticed, including the affected deadline.





Rowan's current career-plan note


“I am interested in helping people understand a process and keeping information organized. I am considering welcome-desk or program-support work. I want to protect school study time: at most eight hours each week for work plus travel during the school term. I do not yet know the training needed for more advanced program coordination.”


Fictional work-arrangement cards for comparison


    

  • Ongoing part-time desk role: four work hours on Saturday plus one hour total travel each week; no stated end date; employer supplies local-system training. Benefits are not specified.
    • 

  • Temporary records project: six work hours plus three hours total travel weekly for ten weeks, then the contract ends; training is supplied. Benefits are not specified.
    • 

  • Seasonal summer role: twelve work hours plus two hours travel weekly in July and August only. Rowan has sixteen hours weekly available then, but this is not a school-term opening.
    • 

  • Self-employed project option: an estimated six hours of client work plus three hours of quoting, administration and travel weekly. Client bookings and income are not guaranteed. Rowan would organize the business tasks as well as the service.
    • 



Check the evidence: Which comment supplies an observation that can support a specific strength claim?
Learn the method
Recognize what kind of experience the record describes


Work-related learning can take different forms. Volunteering contributes time to an activity; community service supports a community need. Job shadowing observes someone doing a role, while a career fair offers information and conversations about several directions. A workplace visit can build familiarity with a setting; an entrepreneurship project can practise organizing a service or product. The specific arrangement determines what the learner actually observes or does. Being present at an event does not prove performing its skilled tasks.


Rowan's supplied record describes actions in a fictional community setting. Your response can analyze those actions and the feedback. It cannot turn the simulation into a real placement. When reflecting on your own growth in this course, use something you actually did here—such as checking a timetable or revising an unsupported claim—and name that learning context.


Move from observation to a testable plan


An observation describes something noticed: eight accurate entries or a fifteen-minute delay before reporting. An interpretation explains what it may suggest: attention to detail or a communication habit worth improving. A career hypothesis is a possibility to investigate, such as “A role combining explanation and record work may suit these emerging skills.” It is not a final verdict about a person's future.


Build the interpretation from the evidence, not from the emotional force of the comment. “I am terrible under pressure” is broader than a late report. “I need to report a blocker earlier” names a behaviour that can be practised and checked. Likewise, “I am a professional records expert” exceeds eight entries completed with training.


Make growth observable


A growth action states what the person will do differently. A next test creates another opportunity to observe it. “Improve communication” is too vague to check. “Draft a two-sentence blocker update at the first sign of a delay, including the deadline” is visible. The test also needs a criterion: does the update identify the problem, consequence and request before repeated troubleshooting?


Inside this course, a next test can be another supplied scenario or a written rehearsal. A real placement might provide other evidence later, but it is not required to finish this simulation. Label the scope honestly when saving the reflection in a portfolio.


Fit the work arrangement to the wider plan


Employment arrangements affect time, income predictability and responsibilities. Full-time generally describes a substantial regular weekly work schedule, while part-time involves fewer hours; exact thresholds and benefits depend on the context and agreement. Temporary describes work with an expected endpoint. Seasonal work occurs during a particular part of the year. Self-employment involves organizing work or a business and finding customers, with costs and responsibilities beyond the service itself. Having multiple jobs combines commitments; each small schedule does not create a separate week of available time.


Do not infer benefits or guaranteed hours from a label. Read the supplied offer. Rowan's part-time card totals five weekly hours and fits the eight-hour school-term limit. The temporary role totals nine and does not. The fourteen-hour seasonal role fits the sixteen-hour summer limit, but does not provide current school-term work. The self-employed estimate totals nine, with uncertain bookings; flexible scheduling does not eliminate those hours.


Reflection path: observation → limited skill claim → growth action → next test and criterion → revised career/education direction that fits time and resources.


alis (Alberta’s career information site) reference record, retrieved September 28, 2026: occupational exploration uses questions about duties, conditions, training and prospects to compare possibilities. Rowan's missing training question belongs in the revised plan rather than being filled by a guess. Optional “Explore Your Occupational Options,” Ask probing questions.


Show a first-step hint
Hint: Begin “In this task, the record shows…” and end “Next I would test…”. That keeps the inference connected to evidence.


Follow a complete example
Use the late-report feedback


I separate the outcome from the process. The cards were ready for the activity; that is a successful outcome. Morgan still needed the information earlier. The record gives exact times: 10:05 to 10:20 is fifteen minutes. I should not rewrite that as either “never reported” or “reported immediately.”


Completed reflection: “The approved card backup was accurate and ready before 11:00, but Rowan waited fifteen minutes to report the printer problem. This suggests Rowan can complete the task with support while needing a more immediate reporting habit. In the next written shift simulation, Rowan will draft a two-sentence update as soon as a blocker appears: what stopped, what deadline is affected and what approval is needed. The test is whether the update appears before repeated troubleshooting and contains all three details. Program-support work remains worth investigating, with communication under changing conditions as a growth focus; this single incident does not rule the pathway in or out.”


The next test is a specific learning action. It does not require claiming an actual workplace experience. A plan that says “be confident” might describe a hoped-for feeling but gives no behaviour to practise or evidence to review.


Next: Keep the useful evidence and test it again. Try “Supported directions claim” before opening its comparison model.
Practise with support
Keep the useful evidence and test it again


Use Morgan's clear visitor directions observation, not the printer incident. First select the supported claim: Rowan explained one local procedure clearly / Rowan can train everyone in any system / Rowan never needs clarification. Use Check the claim. The first follows the observed result; the other two extend beyond it.


Fill Observation and limited strength, Next explanation test and criterion, and Work arrangement that fits the school term. For the arrangement, use the supplied cards and show work plus travel hours.


Show a first-step hint
Hint: Choose a new explanation task that can be simulated here. You can use the reservation-access rule from the previous lesson without speaking to another person.

Compare phone contracts and subscriptions
How to complete this lesson
  1. Start here
  2. Meet the situation and read the documents
  3. Learn the method
  4. Watch or read Smartphones and Plans; try the short case check
  5. Follow a complete example
  6. Practise with support

Optional reference · The Wireless Code, simplified — CRTC
All facts needed for the activities are supplied in the lesson. Use the named original for further reading or to check current details.
Open The Wireless Code, simplified — CRTC ↗
Core vocabulary
A temporary price that applies only for its stated period and conditions.
An agreement lasting for a specified period under its terms.
An agreement continuing by monthly periods under its stated cancellation terms.
An amount that the agreement says may be payable when ending it under specified conditions.
Start here
What happens after the promotional price ends?


Marin sees a phone offer advertised at $20 a month. The written offer also has a device payment and a later service price. You will read the whole schedule and compare it with using an existing phone.


Your final product is a recommendation for another fictional customer, with a full-year comparison and a shorter-use scenario. You will distinguish what the agreement actually says from what a headline suggests. No real signup, credit check or personal account is needed.


How to complete this lesson: Read Marin's phone offers and check the first bill. Learn Read the service, device and exit terms, then follow the twelve-month comparison. Try Leave after nine months, answer six questions, and complete Sacha's two service offers. Compare your reasoning, revise and use the four sign-offs. Pause after the practice if needed; your entries save.


Meet the situation and read the documents


Marin's phone offers


Marin needs at least 4 GB of data each month and calling/texting. The existing phone works, is compatible with both fictional networks and meets Marin's needs. Both offers have confirmed coverage for Marin's current location and include 8 GB, calling and texting. No extra usage occurs in the comparison. Marin can spend at most $45 each month after other commitments.


Offer A — new phone and service, twelve-month written agreement


Headline: “Service from $20/month.” Service is $20 monthly for months 1–3, then $38 monthly for months 4–12. A new device adds $15 each month for twelve months: $180 total, with no interest. No setup fee. All stated prices include taxes. Service prices are fixed to this schedule for the twelve-month agreement. If service ends early, the unpaid device balance becomes due immediately; no other cancellation charge is included in this fictional agreement. At the end of twelve months the device is paid off. Service continues at $38 monthly unless cancelled or changed under the stated process. No resale value is assumed.


Offer B — use the existing phone, month-to-month service


Service is $43 monthly; no device payment or setup fee. All stated prices include taxes. Cancel before the next monthly billing period without a cancellation fee; there is no partial-month refund in this fictional comparison. For the twelve-month calculation, assume this price remains unchanged. The notice does not promise that every future year will have the same price.


Check the first bill: Under A, what is the monthly bill in months 1–3?
Learn the method
Read the service, device and exit terms


A subscription is a recurring arrangement for access to a service. Its payment repeats until the agreement ends or changes. A fixed-term agreement has a specified commitment period; month-to-month describes a shorter recurring period. Neither phrase tells you every cancellation rule. Read the actual notice, payment dates and any separate device obligation.


A promotional price is a temporary price. Count the months it applies, then count the remaining months separately. Adding a device payment can change the bill even while the service price stays the same. Three labels are therefore useful: service, device and combined bill. The combined bill is the one that must fit the monthly allowance.


Payment timeline: A months 1–3 = service 20 + device 15; months 4–12 = service 38 + device 15; after month 12 = stated ongoing service, device paid off. B has one service payment and no new device in this case. This is a comparison of ways to meet a need, not a claim that buying a new phone and keeping an old one provide identical ownership benefits.


Count the whole period, then test the hardest month


A twelve-month total answers “What will the supplied plan cost over a year?” It does not answer “Can I meet every bill?” An average can hide higher later months. Check the largest required bill and the amount available then. Paying a low first bill is not evidence that the later schedule is affordable.


An exit cost is money due when the agreement ends. Some balances remain payable even when service stops. Here, ending A does not erase the unpaid device amount. Separate payments already made from the remaining balance; do not count the same device payment twice.


Use the right consumer reference


CRTC reference record — read September 28, 2026: the Wireless Code requires clear wireless contract information, including prices, service limits, commitment period, relevant cancellation terms and one-time costs. It applies to wireless service; it is not a rulebook for every streaming or gym subscription. Optional official page: sections A and B.


For an unfamiliar real agreement, use its permanent written copy to verify these terms. In this lesson all needed terms are supplied. No external page can fill a deliberately missing fictional price; flag the gap instead.


Show a first-step hint
Hint: Make two rows for A's service price, one for three months and one for nine months. Add the twelve device payments afterwards.


Watch or read · FINLIT 101
Smartphones and Plans
Marin’s two offers include features, promotional prices and device payments. Watch or read the three questions in this excerpt: what features are needed, how the phone will be used and what can be spent. Then apply all three to the offers.
Read the video transcript
Visuals: a presenter speaks to the camera. The HTML contract table below supplies the specific terms and calculations for this lesson.
Finding the right mobile data plan is tricky. Each different provider offers a number of different packages. You need to know what you want out of your plan and just how much you want to spend. Think about how you use your phone.
FINLIT 101 · Smartphones and Plans · selected excerpt, used with permission.
Which comparison answers Marin’s decision?
This short practice check saves with your lesson work. You can change your answer after reading the feedback.
Follow a complete example
Compare Marin's first year
Connect the video to this task. Keep Marin’s needs and spending limit beside the calculation. The complete example tests both the twelve-month total and the monthly payment after the promotion.


A's service costs 3 × $20 + 9 × $38 = $60 + $342 = $402. Its device costs 12 × $15 = $180. The first-year total is $582. B costs 12 × $43 = $516. B is $66 lower, while using a phone Marin already has.


A's first three bills are $35, within the $45 allowance. Its next nine bills are $53, $8 above that allowance. B's $43 bill fits, leaving $2 monthly. The first-year average of A is $48.50, but the $53 later bill is the more direct timing check.


Completed recommendation: “I recommend B for Marin's stated needs. Both plans supply the required data and coverage, and the existing phone is adequate. B costs $516 over twelve months under the given price assumption, $66 less than A. Its $43 bill fits the $45 monthly allowance. A includes a new phone, but its $53 bills after month three exceed the allowance; the $20 headline omits that later price and the device payment.”


“A is only $20, so it saves $23 monthly” compares one part of one offer with the whole of another. Always state what is included in the figure.


Next: Leave after nine months. Try “A: nine months paid plus remaining device balance ($)” before opening its comparison model.

Leave after nine months
Connect the video to this task. Use the changed end date in practice to check remaining device obligations. Ending service does not automatically erase an amount still owed.


Marin now expects to end service immediately after the ninth full month, before a tenth service bill. Keep the stated prices and exit terms. No refund or resale payment is available. For A, three of the twelve $15 device payments remain unpaid.


Enter A: nine months paid plus remaining device balance ($), B: nine months paid ($) and Explain the exit difference (2–3 sentences). Use Check this calculation and then the model.


Show a first-step hint
Hint: A has three promotional service months and six later service months before departure. The device still costs $180 in total.


Feedback: A $468: 3×20 + 6×38 + 9×15 + 3×15. B $387: 9×43. An A answer $423 omits the $45 device balance. $582 charges service for months not used. $603 or a second full $180 device charge double-counts paid device instalments. Other answers receive the timeline and retry prompt.

Apply independently
Sacha's two service offers


Sacha has a suitable existing phone and needs 6 GB monthly for study. Both fictional offers provide 8 GB and calling/texting, with confirmed coverage in the current location. No device purchase or extra usage is involved. Sacha can spend $50 at signup and $42 in any later month. All charges include taxes.


Offer C: twelve-month written service agreement: $28 monthly for six months, then $40 monthly for six months; $18 setup paid with the first bill. Economic and financial decisions · Lesson 6
What a major purchase really costs

Optional reference · Making a budget
All facts needed for the activities are supplied in the lesson. Use the named original for further reading or to check current details.
Open Making a budget ↗
Core vocabulary
The purchase and continuing costs of keeping and using an item.
An initial expense needed to begin using a purchase or service.
A calculated amount based on stated information and assumptions.
Something relevant that is not known or not guaranteed.
Start here
The advertised price is the beginning of the plan


A room can be advertised at $480 a month while requiring much more money on move-in day. A bicycle can cost $340 while also needing a lock, service and storage. You will separate starting costs, repeated costs, refundable money and amounts still unknown.


Your final product is a four-month transport-cost note with a recommendation and a condition to check before committing. All people, offers and prices are fictional. No personal budget or real purchase is required.


How to complete this lesson: Read Tess's move-in folder, check what is due, and learn Sort costs by what happens to the money. Follow the complete move-in calculation. Practise with a confirmed utility quote and a cheaper setup option. Answer six questions, then complete Lee's four-month transport choice, compare the model and sign off. You can pause between the housing example and transport task; entries save automatically.


Meet the situation and read the documents


Tess's move-in folder


Tess is a fictional adult planning a first move. Tess has $1,250 available by September 1. All listed starting amounts are due by that date. No loan, overdraft or additional money is available unless a later practice update explicitly supplies it.


Room offer — September 1 start


Room contribution: $480 for September, then $480 monthly. Deposit: $480, held separately and refundable at the end if the stated return conditions are met. It cannot be used to pay the next month's room contribution. Utilities are additional; the provider's quote has not arrived. This invented agreement is a cost-reading example, not a statement of Alberta tenancy law.


Starting checklist with quotes


    

  • September transit pass: $75, repeated monthly.
    • 

  • Basic setup items: $160 once, including all stated charges.
    • 

  • September food allocation: $190, repeated monthly under the exercise assumptions.
    • 

  • Utility cost: unknown, separate from the $480 room contribution.
    • 



Tess expects $900 net income each month after moving. This is a supplied planning assumption, not a guarantee about employment. Other living expenses are outside this simplified exercise and would need investigation in a real plan.


Check the deposit: How should the $480 deposit appear in the move-in calculation?
Learn the method
Sort costs by what happens to the money


An upfront cost is due at the beginning. A recurring cost repeats, such as a monthly transit pass. A refundable deposit ties up money now with a possible later return under specified conditions. These categories can overlap: the first monthly payment is both an upfront cash requirement and part of an ongoing cost. Count it once in the period being analysed.


An ownership or use cost is something needed to keep using the purchase or arrangement: maintenance, storage, utilities, insurance or interest, depending on the situation. A vehicle's advertised price, for example, does not include every future insurance, maintenance and operating expense. The relevant amounts require quotes and a time period; guessing that they are zero hides rather than resolves the uncertainty.


Use two views. Cash needed by the start date includes every payment due then, including a deposit. Cost over the use period separates money expected back from money used up, and states return assumptions. A deposit can affect affordability even when it is not a permanent expense.


Give an unknown its own line


An unknown is a missing figure, not a zero. A known minimum is the total of amounts already established. If the known minimum exceeds available money, you can identify a problem without knowing every extra cost. If it fits, you still cannot call the plan fully affordable until material unknowns are resolved or a justified allowance is supplied.


A quote should state what it includes, how long it applies and when payment is due. “Utilities around something small” is not a quote. “$65 for this month's supplied utility package, due September 1” is usable in a dated exercise.


Change the plan deliberately


A shortfall can be addressed by reducing an optional cost, choosing a different arrangement, delaying the start or adding confirmed resources. Each change has consequences. A cheaper setup might be suitable; skipping necessary food is not an equivalent saving. Promised extra hours that have not been scheduled cannot be counted as confirmed money.


Cost map: start-date payments → accessible money remaining → repeated monthly commitments → irregular/unknown costs → decision and condition. This keeps “Can I start?” separate from “Can I keep doing it?”


Optional Financial Consumer Agency of Canada (FCAC) note, read September 28, 2026: distinguish an unexpected expense from an occasional expense that can be planned. A known monthly storage bill belongs in the plan before an emergency occurs. “Setting up an emergency fund”.


Show a first-step hint
Hint: Mark each quote “now,” “repeats,” “may return” or “unknown.” More than one label may apply; the label is not another payment.


Follow a complete example
Find Tess's known move-in requirement


By September 1, Tess must have $480 room + $480 deposit + $75 transit + $160 setup + $190 food = $1,385, before utilities. Available money is $1,250, so the known amounts already exceed it by $135. The refundable deposit is still needed on the start date.


I also look beyond move-in. Known repeated costs are $480 + $75 + $190 = $745 monthly, plus utilities and any other relevant costs outside this exercise. The $480 deposit and $160 setup are not repeated each month. Comparing $900 income with $745 gives $155 before those remaining costs, not $155 guaranteed spare spending.


Completed note: “Tess needs at least $1,385 by September 1, $135 more than the $1,250 available, and utilities are still unknown. The move cannot be treated as funded on the supplied figures. I would obtain the utility quote and examine a lower setup cost or different start arrangement before committing. Known recurring costs are $745 per month; the $155 difference from assumed income must still cover utilities and other relevant costs.”


“The room is only $480, so Tess has $770 spare” ignores the rest of the move-in folder. “Utilities cost zero because no number is written” turns missing information into an invented fact.


Next: Use two confirmed updates. Try “Revised cash needed by September 1 ($)” before opening its comparison model.
Practise with support
Use two confirmed updates


Tess receives a $65 utility quote, due September 1 and repeated monthly for this exercise. A checked second-hand setup package supplies the same needed items for $90 instead of $160. No other amount changes. An additional $130 will be paid into the account August 30 for already completed work; treat this as confirmed received money available before move-in.


Enter Revised cash needed by September 1 ($), Confirmed cash available by September 1 ($), Known monthly recurring total ($) and What can Tess conclude now? Use Check the updated amounts and compare the model.


Show a first-step hint
Hint: Replace $160 with $90; do not add both packages. Add utilities to starting and recurring calculations once in each distinct view.


Feedback: starting requirement $1,380; available $1,380; recurring $810. $1,450 retains the old setup price. $1,315 omits utilities from the revised starting amount. $1,250 omits the confirmed payment. $1,290 recurring wrongly repeats the deposit. For other values, show the relevant sum and invite revision.

Your current response

Available money is $1,250 + $130 = $1,380, so the listed move-in payments are exactly covered with no accessible money left. Recurring costs are $480 + $75 + $190 + $65 = $810, leaving $90 from the assumed $900 monthly income before other costs. The starting plan is tightly funded, not comfortable. Tess should account for missing real-life expenses and a buffer before making a real commitment.”


Revise your note if it calls “exactly covered” the same as “no remaining risk.” The exercise can establish a conditional calculation without guaranteeing a real move is affordable.

Apply independently
Lee's four-month transport choice


Lee has $550 for travel over four months, with no additional transport money during that time. A bicycle would allow flexible trips along a suitable route supplied in the case. A bus pass also covers all required trips, but its schedule is less flexible. Lee already owns a suitable helmet and does not need to buy one for this case. All listed prices include charges.


Used-bike offer: purchase $340; required secure lock $45; confirmed initial service $65. These are due before riding. A shop has checked fit and basic function; the service addresses the identified maintenance needs. Secure storage costs $18 at the start of each of the four months. No resale money is assumed. Future repairs are not quoted and not included in the base total.


Bus option: $75 at the start of each month for four months. It meets the stated required trips. No other transport fee is included in this exercise.


Write a four-month comparison. Fields: Bike cash needed before the first ride, excluding storage ($), Four-month bike cost including storage ($), Four-month bus cost ($) and My transport recommendation (4–6 sentences). Include money remaining from $550 for each option, one benefit relevant to Lee, and one unknown or condition that matters. If recommending the bike, recognize the small remaining repair allowance.

Your current response

I recommend the bus for this budget because it meets all required trips and leaves more room for an unexpected cost, although the schedule is less flexible. A bike choice would provide more flexible trips, but future repairs are unknown and only $28 remains in the four-month transport fund.”


A bike recommendation may be defensible if it acknowledges the flexibility benefit, the $522 base cost and the limited repair allowance. Do not invent a free storage space, guaranteed resale value or repair warranty. Compare and revise your own note.

Lending and debt · Lesson 6
Test a fixed or variable rate
How to complete this lesson
  1. Start here
  2. Meet the situation and read the documents
  3. Learn the method
  4. Follow a complete example
  5. Practise with support
  6. Check your understanding
  7. Apply independently
  8. Review and complete
At a check, try an answer, read the hint and revise. A different incorrect answer brings method support and an option to show the worked reasoning. Written responses use the comparison and self-checks; they are not automatically graded.
Optional reference · Financial Consumer Agency of Canada (FCAC) personal loans
All facts needed for the activities are supplied in the lesson. Use the named original for further reading or to check current details.
Open FCAC personal loans ↗
Core vocabulary
A rate that stays the same during the agreement's specified period.
A rate that can change according to the agreement's terms.
A specified point when the rate changes in the supplied scenario.
A check of whether a plan remains workable under a stated less favourable condition.
Start here
A starting rate is only the beginning


Two loans can start with different payments and finish with different costs. You will compare a fixed-rate agreement with a variable-rate agreement under two supplied rate paths. A scenario lets you test a possibility; it does not predict future rates.


Your final product is a recommendation using a new pair of fictional loans, their calculated outputs and a monthly limit. Explain both cost and uncertainty. No outside rate search or loan application is required.


How to complete this lesson: Read Ari's two quotations and their calculation rules. Learn Read what changes when the rate changes, follow the first comparison, then test a higher second-year rate. Answer six checks. Complete Jules's three-year comparison, compare your reasoning and sign off. Pause after the stress scenario if helpful; your work saves.


Meet the situation and read the documents


Ari's two quotations


Ari, a fictional adult, needs to compare financing for the same $5,000 purchase over 24 months. Both agreements have no setup fee, insurance charge or other fee under on-time repayment. Interest uses nominal annual rate/12 each month; payments occur at month-end. No additional advances occur. Ari has $223 a month available for this loan, after other planned costs.
Names used in this comparison: F means Ari's fixed-rate offer; V means Ari's variable-rate offer. The 5%-then-7% scenario shows one possible rate change for the variable offer. These letters only help you find the matching quotation; they are not ratings.


Fixed offer F: 6% annually for all 24 months. Regular payment $221.60; final payment $221.69; total payments $5,318.49; interest $318.49.


Variable offer V: begins at 5%. If its rate changes at month 13, the payment is recalculated to repay the remaining balance over the remaining 12 months. This agreement changes the payment, not the original finish date. Its first 12 payments are $219.36.


Supplied 5%-then-7% scenario: 5% for months 1–12, then 7% for months 13–24. The recalculated regular payment is $221.71; the final payment is $221.70. Total payments are $5,292.83 and interest is $292.83. This is one possible path, not a quotation promising next year's rate.


Read the terms: Under V, what happens at month 13 if the rate changes?
Learn the method
Read what changes when the rate changes


A fixed rate remains the same for the specified contract period. A variable rate can change according to its agreement. These terms describe the interest rate; you must also read what happens to the payment or repayment period. In Ari's variable agreement, a change triggers a new payment calculated over the months still remaining.


Other agreements may hold a payment temporarily constant, which changes how much goes to principal as interest changes. Do not assume that “variable” always means the same payment behaviour. The written rule in the case is essential information, not fine print to skip.


A lower starting rate can be attractive, but comparing only month one leaves out future payments. Compare the entire supplied scenario and test a less favourable one. A higher future rate may reduce the original saving or reverse it. A fixed rate offers rate certainty during its stated period; it does not eliminate income changes, missed-payment consequences or every other risk.


Hold the comparison steady


Use the same principal, repayment length, payment frequency and fee assumptions when isolating a rate choice. Otherwise, a lower payment might be caused by a longer period or smaller loan rather than the rate. Our comparison holds those features constant.


The calculator first pays down the balance at the starting rate. At month 13 it uses the remaining balance, not the original $5,000, for the recalculation. This matters because twelve payments have already reduced principal. We supply complete output records so you can analyse the decision without deriving the payment formula.


Test a budget and a cost separately


Subtract the required payment from the available monthly amount to find the payment margin. A positive margin means the stated payment fits that stated limit. A small margin provides little room if another cost changes. It does not prove the whole financial situation is secure.


Then compare total payments and interest. A loan may have a smaller total under one rate path but a later payment that fails the budget under another. Keep those findings separate so your recommendation can explain the tradeoff clearly.


Optional source note: FCAC distinguishes fixed rates, variable rates and different payment arrangements. Its Choosing a mortgage rate section is an example of why rate type and payment behaviour must both be read. Ari's case is a fictional instalment agreement, not a mortgage or a forecast of lender practice. No outside page is needed.


Show a first-step hint
Hint: Make two columns: “fits each monthly limit?” and “costs less under this path?” Answer each before choosing.


Follow a complete example
Compare the fixed offer with the 5%-then-7% scenario


F's regular payment leaves $223 − $221.60 = $1.40 monthly margin. Its $221.69 final payment also fits. The 5%-then-7% scenario begins with $3.64 margin and later leaves $223 − $221.71 = $1.29. Both fit the supplied budget in this scenario, but neither leaves much room.


Interest in the 5%-then-7% scenario is $292.83 compared with F's $318.49. The difference is $25.66. That comparison includes the whole supplied path and the final adjusted payments.


Completed comparison: “With a 5%-then-7% path, V costs $25.66 less interest than F, and its payments fit Ari's $223 limit. However, the 7% later rate is a scenario, not guaranteed. F fixes its rate for the full 24 months and also fits, with a small margin. I would test a higher later rate before deciding whether the possible saving is worth the uncertainty.”


“V will definitely save $25.66” removes the condition that made the calculation true. “Fixed means cheaper” is also unsupported: the supplied 5%-then-7% scenario costs less. The correct explanation preserves both the observed numbers and their limits.

Keep every original input except V's rate in months 13–24. Use 10% instead of 7%. The first twelve payments remain $219.36. The recalculated regular payment becomes $225.27, final payment $225.23, total payments $5,335.52, interest $335.52.

The payment exceeds the limit by $225.27 − $223 = $2.27. Interest exceeds F by $335.52 − $318.49 = $17.03. If you enter $25.66, you have reused the old scenario's cost difference. Lending and debt · Lesson 7
Read a mortgage beyond its monthly payment
How to complete this lesson
  1. Start here
  2. Meet the situation and read the documents
  3. Learn the method
  4. Follow a complete example
  5. Practise with support
  6. Check your understanding
  7. Apply independently
  8. Review and complete
At a check, try an answer, read the hint and revise. A different incorrect answer brings method support and an option to show the worked reasoning. Written responses use the comparison and self-checks; they are not automatically graded.
Optional reference · Financial Consumer Agency of Canada (FCAC) mortgage terms
All facts needed for the activities are supplied in the lesson. Use the named original for further reading or to check current details.
Open FCAC mortgage terms ↗
Core vocabulary
A loan secured on property.
The buyer's own contribution toward the purchase price.
The period during which the mortgage agreement's particular conditions apply before renewal or repayment.
A stated allowance for extra repayment without the charge that would otherwise apply.
Start here
Five years can be part of a twenty-five-year plan


A mortgage quotation can name both a five-year term and a twenty-five-year amortization. Those numbers answer different questions. You will read them alongside the down payment, remaining balance and rules for extra payments.


Your final product is a comparison note for two fictional mortgage quotations. Explain the payment, balance at the end of the term and a planned extra payment. This is a document-reading exercise, not a recommendation to buy a home or a mortgage approval.


How to complete this lesson: Read Lee and Noor's quotation, learn Separate the contract from the repayment plan, and follow the five-year calculation. Practise changing amortization. Answer six checks. Compare Morgan's two quotations, revise your note and sign off. The full text and schedules are provided; live lender contact is not required. Pause after the first comparison if useful.


Meet the situation and read the documents


Lee and Noor's quotation


Lee and Noor are fictional adults considering a teaching-example property price of $160,000. They have $40,000 for a down payment, leaving $120,000 mortgage principal. Other purchase and ownership costs have a separate allocation and are excluded from this loan-only illustration; their exclusion does not mean homes have no taxes, insurance, utilities, repairs or legal costs.


Quotation M: fixed 6% nominal annual interest compounded semi-annually, monthly payments, five-year term and 25-year amortization. Regular payment: $767.77. During the first 60 months, scheduled payments total $46,066.20, of which $33,870.12 is interest. The balance after payment 60 is $107,803.92. No extra payment or fee is included in these outputs.


Extra-payment condition: up to 10% of original principal per contract year may be paid in one additional lump sum without a prepayment charge. Unused allowance does not carry forward. A larger extra payment may incur a charge whose calculation must be requested. These are invented terms for this quotation, not a rule for every mortgage.


A mortgage is borrowing secured on property. Failing to meet its terms can put that property at risk. Down payment means the buyer's contribution to the purchase price; it is not the same as a regular loan payment.


Read the quotation: What ends after five years here?
Learn the method
Separate the contract from the repayment plan


The term is how long the current mortgage agreement applies. Its rate and other conditions are established for that period. At the end, any unpaid balance must be addressed: for example, by repayment or an appropriate new agreement. Do not assume renewal has the same rate.


The amortization is the planned time over which scheduled payments would repay the loan under the model's assumptions. It can be much longer than one term. A five-year term within a 25-year amortization therefore does not promise the same rate for 25 years. A long-run calculator illustration holding a rate constant must say that it is conditional.


Read a quotation as three connected records: money borrowed today → payments during this contract → debt still owing when the contract ends. The remaining balance explains why someone may still need financing after years of payments.


Know what the payment leaves out


A quoted principal-and-interest payment is not necessarily the entire cost of housing. Taxes, insurance, utilities, maintenance and transaction costs may be separate. This exercise supplies a loan-payment limit only after those other costs have been considered; you cannot reuse it as a real affordability approval.


An application may require evidence of income, down payment, existing debts and credit history. The lender assesses its current criteria and the property. Knowing the payment is only part of that assessment. Do not upload personal records or infer eligibility from this fictional calculation.


Read flexibility as carefully as the rate


A prepayment is money paid toward principal beyond scheduled payments. A prepayment privilege is the amount and timing the contract permits without a specified charge. Some agreements are more flexible than others. A percentage needs a base: M uses original principal, so its 10% allowance is based on $120,000, not the current balance or property price.


Extra principal paid earlier can reduce later interest under unchanged terms, but the amount, timing and any charge matter. This lesson compares permission only; its schedules contain no extra payments. Do not use an unchanged schedule to claim the precise saving from a proposed prepayment.


Optional official reading record: FCAC's mortgage guidance distinguishes contract term, amortization and prepayment conditions. Read September 28, 2026. It supports these reading questions; the complete fictional quotation supplies the numbers and conditions used here.


Show a first-step hint
Hint: Circle the words “term,” “amortization” and “original principal” before calculating. Each determines which number answers a different question.


Follow a complete example
Explain the balance after five years


The initial loan is $160,000 − $40,000 = $120,000. Sixty regular payments total 60 × $767.77 = $46,066.20. However, not all of that pays down principal: $33,870.12 is interest. Principal repaid is $46,066.20 − $33,870.12 = $12,196.08. Subtracting that from $120,000 leaves $107,803.92, matching the schedule.


M's annual extra-payment allowance is 10% × $120,000 = $12,000. It does not mean $12,000 is available in Lee and Noor's budget; it is a contract permission.


Complete explanation: “M fixes its rate for five years, while payments are calculated over a 25-year repayment plan. After the first five years, $107,803.92 remains because only $12,196.08 of the $46,066.20 paid reduced principal. The contract allows a lump sum up to $12,000 in each contract year without the stated prepayment charge. Future rates and any actual extra-payment saving require a new calculation.”


“The balance must be $73,933.80 because they paid $46,066.20” incorrectly treats interest as principal repayment. The schedule makes the split visible.

Saving, investing, and financial plans · Lesson 6
Revise a plan when life changes
How to complete this lesson
  1. Start here
  2. Meet the situation and read the documents
  3. Learn the method
  4. Follow a complete example
  5. Practise with support
  6. Check your understanding
  7. Apply independently
  8. Review and complete
At a check, try an answer, read the hint and revise. A different incorrect answer brings method support and an option to show the worked reasoning. Written responses use the comparison and self-checks; they are not automatically graded.
Optional reference · Financial Consumer Agency of Canada (FCAC) saving and investment goals
All facts needed for the activities are supplied in the lesson. Use the named original for further reading or to check current details.
Open FCAC saving and investment goals ↗
Core vocabulary
A condition a plan relies on.
A difference between what was planned and what actually happened in the case.
A change or date that signals the plan should be checked.
A recalculated future result using the updated balance and stated conditions.
Start here
Keep the record; change the next action


A plan can be reasonable when written and still need revision after an unexpected cost. You will separate what has already happened from what can change next. The task is to recalculate from the actual balance, explain the adjustment and set a new review point.


Your final product is a revision note for a fictional saving plan after a necessary expense. It will show the current balance, remaining gap and feasible future contributions. No personal loss, income or account information is required.


How to complete this lesson: Read Ari's original plan and transaction record, learn Update from the present balance, and follow a revised contribution. Practise a flexible deadline and optionally test a monthly budget shock. Answer six checks. Complete Devon's changed plan, compare, revise and sign off. All entries save; the original record remains visible.


Meet the situation and read the documents


Ari's original plan and transaction record


Ari is fictional and wants $350 by the end of month 6 for a purchase. The plan began with $200, then scheduled $25 at each of six month-ends. No interest or fee applies. The deadline was initially treated as fixed.


What actually happened:






Event
Change
Balance





Start
Opening $200
$200




End of month 1
Deposit $25
$225




End of month 2
Deposit $25
$250




Immediately after month 2
Necessary repair, withdrawal $80
$170





New budget information: Ari can normally save $30 in each remaining month after other costs. A confirmed temporary change can instead free up to $45 monthly for months 3–6, without missing essential costs or required payments. There is no other money available. The repair has already been paid and is not refundable in the case.


Read the record: Which balance should the revised plan start from immediately after the repair?
Learn the method
Update from the present balance


A revision changes a future action in response to evidence. It does not rewrite earlier transactions. Start with the actual balance, subtract it from the target and count the deposits still available before the deadline. This creates a new gap and a new required contribution.


For Ari, two months have passed. Only four month-end deposits remain before month six. Using six deposits in the revised calculation would pretend time already elapsed is still available. Similarly, restarting at the old $200 balance would erase both saving progress and the repair cost.


Change a constraint openly


There are several possible levers: contribution, target amount, deadline or a confirmed resource. Each has consequences. A higher contribution must fit the revised budget. A lower target must still meet the need. A later date must actually be flexible. A resource must be confirmed rather than hoped for.


Sometimes no combination satisfies every original condition. Naming the conflict is better planning than hiding it. A revision note should say which condition changes and why. It should also distinguish a temporary adjustment from an ongoing one so that next month's plan does not accidentally repeat a one-time cost.


Review goals as circumstances change


Education, work, relocation, family responsibilities and retirement can change a person's purposes, time horizons and ability to take risk. A plan made for one life stage may need different priorities later. Reviewing does not mean changing every goal whenever a headline appears; it means checking relevant evidence against the decision's assumptions.


For investments, a market value change can affect a plan without being a deposit or withdrawal. A $500 holding worth $450 has depreciated by $50; that record does not reveal whether it will recover. Keep contributions, withdrawals, fees and market changes distinct. A short-term bill should not rely on an assumed rebound.


A useful revision note follows actual event → present balance → remaining need and time → feasible change → review trigger. This is the second representation of the method; each part will appear in your final response.


Optional reference: FCAC's budget guidance recommends comparing a plan with actual income and spending and updating it as circumstances change. Read September 28, 2026. All required records and alternatives in this lesson are supplied.


Want to explore growth on earlier growth? The optional FINLIT compounding investigation uses a separate 40-year model. Ari’s and Devon’s saving plans here still assume no interest.
Follow a complete example
Keep Ari's month-six deadline
Use Ari’s record. The repair reduced the balance; confirmed future deposits rebuild it. No interest term belongs in this calculation.


After the repair, the balance is $170. The target gap is $350 − $170 = $180. With four deposits remaining, $180 ÷ 4 = $45 monthly is required.


The normal $30 amount would add only $120, ending at $290 and leaving $60 short. The supplied temporary budget change permits $45, so the revised plan can still meet the deadline. This conclusion relies on that confirmation; it does not assume every person can simply save more.


Complete revision: “The $80 repair leaves $170 after month two. To reach $350 at month six, Ari needs another $180 across four deposits, or $45 monthly. I would use the confirmed temporary adjustment for months 3–6 and check after month 3 that the first revised deposit happened and the $45 remains available. If it no longer fits, I would revisit a flexible date or target rather than erase the repair from the record.”


“Continue $25 and everything is fine” ignores the changed balance. “Start the original six-month plan again” changes the deadline without saying so. A complete revision preserves both the history and the condition being changed.


Next: Keep $30 monthly and move the date. Try “Deposits still needed” before opening its comparison model.
Practise with support
Keep $30 monthly and move the date
Use the same method in practice. Count the deposits required at $30 monthly, then choose the first whole month that meets the revised target.


Use a changed version: Ari cannot make the temporary $45 adjustment, but the purchase deadline can now move. The balance after month two is still $170, the target is still $350, and $30 monthly is available from month three onward. No interest or additional resource is supplied.


Enter Deposits still needed and New completion month. Write My revised instruction, two sentences stating what changes and what stays. Use Check the revised date.


Six $30 deposits provide the remaining $180. They occur in months 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8, so the new date is month 8. Feedback on month 6: six deposits are needed after month two, not from the beginning. Feedback on four deposits: four at $30 leave the plan $60 short. Feedback on six deposits of $45: that exceeds this changed version's available amount.

Optional budget-shock experiment


A separate fictional monthly budget has income $600, essentials $400, flexible spending $80, required debt payment $50 and saving $70. It initially balances. A one-time $60 repair creates a gap. Load this example into Test a budget change only if you want the additional experiment.


The case confirms that up to $60 of this month's flexible spending can be postponed without affecting essentials. Choose reduce flexible spending and enter $60 reduction. The revised flexible amount becomes $20, and the budget balances while keeping debt and saving allocations. Choose a review note such as “return to the ordinary budget next month if the repair does not recur.” Reducing saving is another possible adjustment, but its goal and recovery date must be reconsidered. New borrowing cannot be treated as free income; no loan approval or terms are supplied here.


The optional experiment is separate from Ari's balances. Do not move its $600 income into Ari's savings plan. Compare and revise your required practice instruction.
