Protecting personal information · Lesson 4
Compare the promise, the price and the terms
How to complete this lesson
  1. Start here
  2. Meet the situation and read the documents
  3. Learn the method
  4. Follow a complete example
  5. Practise with support
  6. Check your understanding
  7. Apply independently
  8. Review and complete
At a check, try an answer, read the hint and revise. A different incorrect answer brings method support and an option to show the worked reasoning. Written responses use the comparison and self-checks; they are not automatically graded.
Optional reference · Alberta consumer protection
All facts needed for the activities are supplied in the lesson. Use the named original for further reading or to check current details.
Open Alberta consumer protection ↗
Core vocabulary
A claim made about a product, service, price or agreement.
A charge the buyer must pay to obtain the advertised offer under the supplied terms.
A disagreement with the seller about the transaction, product or agreement.
An action that may address a problem under the relevant rules; it is not automatically guaranteed.
Start here
A low advertised price can change when a shopper reaches checkout. A subscription can also sound flexible in an advertisement while a later term describes a costly commitment. A useful consumer response identifies the exact contradiction, preserves the documents and asks the right organization for the kind of help it can provide.


You will compare a tablet advertisement with a fully supplied checkout, write a supported response to a changed offer, and then prepare a new subscription-dispute file. Your final product will explain the disputed terms, include a clear message to the business, and choose suitable escalation routes without promising a refund.


Follow Meet the situation and read the documents → Learn the method → Follow a complete example → Practise with support → Check your understanding → Apply independently → Review and complete. Pause after the price comparison if useful. All writing stays in the course; do not buy anything, contact a business or submit a complaint. The guided work and six questions are practice. The independent file and four sign-offs complete the lesson. Fields save automatically.


Vocabulary. An advertised price is the price presented to attract a purchaser. A mandatory fee is a charge the purchaser cannot decline while buying that offer. An optional addition can be declined. Drip pricing involves advertising an unattainable price because mandatory fixed fees are added later; the specific federal rule described here treats government-imposed charges on purchasers, such as sales tax, differently. A consumer dispute is a disagreement about a transaction or its terms. A remedy is a requested solution; requesting it does not establish that the business must provide it in every case.


Optional disclosure: Consumer-source records and live references. Everything needed is supplied below. Official live links are optional for checking a current real situation.


Meet the situation and read the documents


Mina is a fictional adult in Alberta considering a tablet from Clearview Devices, a fictional business selling online from Alberta. Mina has reached checkout but has not agreed to purchase or paid. The tablet model and quantity are the same in each document. No accessory, delivery upgrade or other optional item was selected.


Document A — Saved advertisement, October 12, 2026, 10:00 a.m.




Clearview Devices — Cedar tablet, one tablet. $120 before sales tax. Mandatory store fees included. Standard pickup included. Offer available today while stock remains.




Document B — Checkout, October 12, 2026, 10:05 a.m.






Checkout line
Amount
Supplied condition





One Cedar tablet
$120.00
Same model as the advertisement.




Setup fee
$25.00
Automatically added; no decline control.




Processing fee
$5.00
Automatically added for every payment method.




Subtotal before tax
$150.00
No other item or fee.




Sales tax
$7.50
Supplied tax line for this fictional checkout.




Total
$157.50
Nothing has been paid.





The tax amount is supplied so the receipt is complete. This lesson asks you to analyze the store fees, not infer or research a tax rate.


Document C — Saved business reply, October 12, 2026, 10:15 a.m.




Both the $25 setup fee and the $5 processing fee are required for every purchaser of this tablet. Neither can be removed. Neither is a government charge. The $120 advertisement refers to the tablet line only. You can decide whether to continue at checkout.




Document D — Dated in-course consumer records


Competition Bureau, “Drip pricing”; checked September 28, 2026. The Bureau explains that an advertised price made unattainable by mandatory fixed fees is contrary to the Competition Act, apart from government-imposed charges on purchasers such as sales tax. Variable fees can also raise concerns. A report about deceptive marketing can be made through the Bureau's official site. An individual learner cannot determine a legal outcome from a short case.


Government of Alberta, “Unfair business practices”; checked September 28, 2026. Alberta's Consumer Protection Act addresses unfair practices, including misleading representations and pricing. Its protections can apply before, during or after a transaction, even when a purchase has not been completed. Keep the offer, terms, receipts and communications that show the concern. These fictional parties and the offer are in Alberta; this course does not generalize Alberta jurisdiction to every online purchase.


Government of Alberta, “File a consumer complaint against a business”; checked September 28, 2026. Start by trying to resolve a concern with the business and retain the record. Alberta's Consumer Investigations Unit assesses possible violations within its authority. The described complaint route begins with the Consumer Contact Centre and a complaint ID before the portal stage. The unit does not recover a consumer's financial losses, mediate the dispute or renegotiate the contract. A complaint is not a guaranteed refund procedure.


Financial Consumer Agency of Canada, “How credit cards work,” “Credit card purchases”; checked September 28, 2026. Compare the statement with receipts. For a mistake, contact the merchant; if the problem is not corrected, contact the financial institution for assistance. Explain the facts accurately. Disagreement with recognized purchase terms is different from saying a transaction was never made or approved.


Read the documents


Which fact most directly supports Mina's concern about the advertised price? Choose and select Check document reading.
Learn the method
Compare the same offer at each stage


Begin with the product, quantity and choices. A difference caused by selecting a larger model or optional delivery does not establish the same issue as a required charge added to an unchanged offer. Mina's documents hold those details constant: one Cedar tablet, standard pickup and no optional additions.


Then compare prices on the same basis. The advertisement says $120 before tax; checkout says $150 before tax. Subtracting those amounts isolates the store-fee difference. Comparing $120 directly with the tax-inclusive $157.50 would mix the fee concern with a separate supplied tax line.


Write the arithmetic with labels. A dollar difference is useful evidence only when the reader understands what the two amounts represent. Do not replace the comparison with “the business is stealing”; that is an accusation about conduct or intent that these documents do not establish.


Read what a condition actually does


A condition matters when it changes a consumer's practical choice. A charge called “service,” “processing” or “setup” is still mandatory in this case because the customer cannot decline it. A small font or a final opportunity to abandon checkout does not make the advertised $120 purchase available.


Subscriptions require the same close reading. “Monthly payment” describes when money is charged; it does not by itself prove that the commitment lasts only one month. Compare statements about duration, renewal, cancellation and fees across the advertisement and the accepted terms. If they conflict, identify both statements. Do not hide an inconvenient term, and do not assume its presence automatically resolves a misleading-advertisement concern.


Build a concern that someone can investigate


Use promise → conflicting document → effect → requested response. Name the date and document, quote only the short wording necessary, and state the amount or condition affected. Then ask for a specific response, such as an accurate written quote, correction of a disputed charge, or confirmation of cancellation terms. A focused request makes it easier to understand the disagreement.


Keep copies already available. A later corrected advertisement is useful new evidence but does not replace the earlier version in the chronology. A record should distinguish “requested a correction,” “business acknowledged the request” and “correction confirmed.” These are different stages.


Match the route to the job






Need
Suitable route in these cases
Limit to state





Clarification, correction or a requested refund/cancellation
The business through the contact in the saved order or independently reached official service
A request is not a promised outcome.




Possible Alberta consumer-law violation
Alberta Consumer Contact Centre and, where appropriate, Consumer Investigations Unit process
The unit assesses enforcement matters; it does not recover losses or mediate a personal dispute.




Possible deceptive advertising, including drip pricing
Competition Bureau's independently reached official reporting route
Reporting the marketing concern does not itself correct a card statement or cancel a subscription.




Unresolved recognized credit-card purchase problem
Card issuer/financial institution through the existing card or genuine app
Provide the terms, receipt and merchant correspondence; do not invent an unauthorized transaction or guaranteed reversal.





The routes can serve different purposes for the same documents. There is no need to submit a report to every organization for every disagreement. Explain what assistance is being sought and whether a purchase or payment has even occurred.


Optional first-step hint: “Underline ‘before sales tax’ in both price records. Compare the two subtotals first, then name which fees account for the difference.”


Follow a complete example
I check that Mina selected the same tablet and no extras. I then read the advertisement's promise: mandatory store fees are included in $120 before tax. The business reply confirms that both added fees are required and are not government charges. That removes two possible explanations—optional choices and tax—for the $30 difference.


My calculation is $25.00 + $5.00 = $30.00 in required store fees. Equivalently, $150.00 − $120.00 = $30.00 above the advertised pre-tax price. The supplied checkout total is consistent: $150.00 + $7.50 = $157.50. I do not subtract the full total from the advertised amount and call all of the difference a prohibited fee.


Complete concern and action note:




On October 12, 2026, Mina saved the $120-before-tax Cedar-tablet advertisement stating that mandatory store fees were included. The same tablet with no optional additions reached a $150-before-tax subtotal because checkout required a $25 setup fee and $5 processing fee. Your 10:15 a.m. reply confirms both are unavoidable store charges. The required store-fee difference is $30. Please explain and correct the discrepancy, and provide an accurate written price including all mandatory store fees before Mina decides whether to buy. No purchase or payment has occurred.


Retain the advertisement, checkout and reply with their times. The supplied facts raise a drip-pricing concern under the Bureau's record and an Alberta misleading-pricing concern; this note does not declare a final legal finding. If the concern remains unresolved, Mina can use Alberta's consumer-information/complaint route and report the marketing concern to the Competition Bureau through their independently reached official pages. No card charge exists to dispute. Neither report itself promises compensation.




An unsupported alternative would say “the bank must refund $157.50.” Mina has paid nothing, and the sources do not establish an automatic refund. A useful response follows the actual stage of the transaction.

There are no other required fees. The tablet is still available. Mina has still not purchased it. We have not offered a $120 price.

Apply independently
Omar's subscription file


Omar is a fictional 19-year-old Alberta resident. SoundShelf is a fictional Alberta online audio-library business. The issue concerns a recognized subscription and conflicting cancellation representations. No password theft, card theft or unfamiliar merchant is reported.


Document E — Advertisement saved October 1, 2026. “SoundShelf: $9 each month. Cancel anytime. No exit fee.” The same plan appears in the following records.


Document F — Checkout and accepted terms, October 1. The payment summary shows $9 due that day and future billing on the first day of each month. Below the summary, the terms say: “This plan has a twelve-month commitment. Ending before the commitment ends requires a $45 early-exit fee.” Omar accepted the checkout; the record does not say whether Omar noticed that sentence. The receipt shows the initial $9 payment and the same business name. No tax or other fee is part of this exercise.


Document G — Cancellation correspondence. On October 20, Omar wrote through the business contact on the saved receipt: “Please cancel before the November 1 renewal. Your advertisement said cancel anytime with no exit fee. Please confirm cancellation with no further charge.” On October 22, the business replied: “We will end the plan on November 1. We will charge the November $9 payment and a $45 early-exit fee under the commitment term. We will not waive either.” There is no further explanation of why another monthly payment is due after the October 20 request.


Document H — Statement and follow-up. The genuine card statement shows a November 1 SoundShelf charge of $54. On November 2, Omar sent the business the advertisement, October 20 request and statement and asked it to correct the $54 charge and confirm no future billing. On November 4, the business replied: “We stand by the October 22 reply. The subscription is closed; there will be no future monthly charges.” No refund is shown. The issuer is available through the existing physical card or genuine app. No issuer dispute has yet been opened. Every date is a supplied fictional case fact, even though the source records were checked earlier.


Prepare one subscription concern and escalation file in four fields. Short paragraphs or labelled bullets are suitable; include the exact dates and amounts needed to make the disagreement understandable.

    •

The October 1 advertisement promises $9 each month, cancellation at any time and no exit fee. The accepted checkout terms instead describe a twelve-month commitment and $45 early-exit fee. Protecting personal information · Lesson 5
Coordinate a recovery plan
How to complete this lesson
  1. Start here
  2. Meet the situation and read the documents
  3. Learn the method
  4. Follow a complete example
  5. Practise with support
  6. Check your understanding
  7. Apply independently
  8. Review and complete
At a check, try an answer, read the hint and revise. A different incorrect answer brings method support and an option to show the worked reasoning. Written responses use the comparison and self-checks; they are not automatically graded.
Optional reference · Report a Scam or Identity Theft — Canada Revenue Agency (CRA)
All facts needed for the activities are supplied in the lesson. Use the named original for further reading or to check current details.
Open Report a Scam or Identity Theft — CRA ↗
Core vocabulary
An ordered response to an incident that addresses security, evidence and appropriate reporting.
The organization controlling the account or service involved.
A notice asking potential creditors to take additional identity-verification steps.
A record separating planned actions, actions taken and confirmed results.
Start here
After fraud, a person may need several kinds of help. A bank can address a payment route; an email provider can address account access; police and fraud-reporting services have reporting roles. Sending one report does not automatically complete the other jobs. A calm plan assigns each action to the organization that can carry it out and records what has actually happened.


You will coordinate a response to a ticket-payment and password incident, update the plan when providers reply, and then build a distinct plan for identity information and an independently observed tax-account change. The final product is a prioritized response plan with specific recipients, safe routes, evidence and follow-up conditions.


Follow Meet the situation and read the documents → Learn the method → Follow a complete example → Practise with support → Check your understanding → Apply independently → Review and complete. Work in small parts and pause after the response table if useful. Everything happens in the fictional record. Do not open a real financial account, disclose a Social Insurance Number (SIN), contact an agency or ask another person to supervise. Guided work and six questions are practice; the new independent plan and sign-offs complete this lesson. Your writing saves automatically.


Vocabulary. Recovery is the process of responding to an incident and restoring security or addressing losses; it does not promise that money will be returned. An affected provider controls a relevant account or service. Identity fraud involves misuse of identity information; exposure and confirmed misuse should be distinguished. A credit report records credit information; a fraud alert asks potential creditors to take additional identity-verification steps. A recovery scam offers to recover losses as a way to demand more money, access or secrets. A status log separates planned actions, actions taken and confirmed results.


Optional disclosure: Official recovery records and routes. The in-course records below support all required decisions. Live pages are optional for current real use.


Meet the situation and read the documents


Ari is a fictional adult who tried to purchase a concert ticket. The incident has two confirmed exposures: a personally approved payment induced by deception, and a password entered on a false delivery page. Read the complete starting record before choosing agencies.


Document A — Incident log, October 18, 2026






Time / category
Supplied facts





2:00 p.m., payment
Ari personally approved a $160 electronic transfer from Ari's bank to a supposed ticket seller. The transfer shows as deposited in the genuine bank app. No ticket was supplied. The actual recipient/account details are omitted from this course.




2:10 p.m., information entry
A false “ticket delivery registration” page asked for email login details. Ari entered the email login/password, name and mailing address. That same password is used for a music account. The email is the music account's recovery address.




Not entered / not observed
No SIN, date of birth, identity-document image, banking password, payment-card details or one-time code was entered. No app was installed and no remote access granted. No new credit account, unfamiliar bank transaction or CRA-account change is reported.




2:20 p.m., current status
Ari can still access the bank, email and music services through previously known routes. A separate updated personal device is available. No provider has yet been contacted and no security change has been recorded.




Evidence already available
Seller conversation, original transfer record, message requesting the delivery login and a screenshot without the entered password. No need to reopen the false page.





Document B — Available independent routes and controls


    

  • Ari's genuine bank app, opened directly on the separate device, contains the bank's fraud-contact route. The bank can review the transfer and advise on the payment/account response. The record does not promise the deposited transfer can be recovered.
    • 

  • Ari has the known email app and a saved official music-service bookmark. These fictional providers allow a unique new password, recovery-detail review, review/sign-out of other sessions and MFA. Their guide says a password change does not automatically end all other sessions. Official recovery support is available if access is lost. These interface details are case assumptions, not universal service instructions.
    • 

  • The official local police website and CAFC's official “What to do if you're a victim of fraud” page can be reached independently. The latter links to Report Cybercrime and Fraud, the official online reporting route. A course response is not sent to either service.
    • 



Document C — New message from an unverified stranger, 2:25 p.m.




I recover stolen ticket money. I know your loss was $160. Pay my $40 administration fee and send your email verification code, and I guarantee the money will be returned today. Do not speak to the bank because that will delay us.




The sender is not independently verified. No actual address, link, telephone number or code is supplied. Knowing the amount does not explain how the sender obtained it or establish authority.


Document D — In-course agency and response records


CAFC, “What to do if you're a victim of fraud,” and “Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre Impersonation”; checked September 28, 2026. Keep relevant records, promptly contact the institution that transferred money, and report fraud to local police and the official fraud/cybercrime reporting route. Recovery offers can demand fees or more information. Independently reach official services; a convincing name, document or detail from the incident is not sufficient verification. Reporting does not guarantee recovery.


Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, “Protecting yourself from identity theft online”; checked September 28, 2026. Identify the information and accounts affected, secure compromised/reused credentials and connected accounts, contact affected providers and monitor relevant activity. Choose identity-protection measures from the actual exposure or misuse, not an invented list of every possible stolen document.


CRA, “Report a scam or identity theft”; checked September 28, 2026. Suspected CRA-account compromise or unauthorized changes to CRA information, including bank or address details, warrant contacting CRA through its official reporting/support route. An unfamiliar call is not itself proof of an account change. A person can independently open the official CRA page to identify the relevant secure or telephone option. CRA account support is distinct from a CAFC report.


Service Canada, “SIN fraud and data breaches”; checked September 28, 2026; page modified May 13, 2026. Suspected SIN misuse or exposure calls for monitoring credit information and relevant accounts. The page points to both Canadian credit bureaus, Equifax and TransUnion, and explains fraud alerts and responses when fraud is identified. It says a person does not need to notify the SIN Program about suspected misuse or a breach. Issuing a new SIN is not a routine cure: the old number and its records do not simply disappear. Contact affected institutions or government programs for the misuse involving them.


Read the documents


Which action best fits Ari's confirmed financial event? Choose and select Check document reading.
Learn the method
Start with an exposure map


List what actually left the person's control: money, a password, card details, a SIN, an identity document or device access. Then connect each item to its provider. This is more useful than a universal instruction to “call everyone.” Ari's payment belongs in a bank response; the reused credential belongs in email and music-account responses.


Separate facts from possible consequences. Ari's name and address could assist future impersonation, so continued caution matters. Those facts do not establish a new credit account or tax-account intrusion. Conversely, if a case supplies a SIN exposure and an independently observed unauthorized tax-account change, identity and CRA responses have concrete reasons. Match the measure to the evidence.


Prioritize time-sensitive controls, then coordinate


Do not postpone urgent provider contact while perfecting an evidence file. Ari already has the essential payment record and message. The bank needs prompt notice of the deceptive transfer, and exposed accounts need prompt protection through independent trusted routes. Write an order and a reason; some actions could occur close together rather than waiting days for one organization to finish.


For the connected credentials, securing the recovery email before the music account is defensible because access to that email can help reset the music account. Follow the supplied session and recovery controls as well as changing passwords. A person who has lost access may need the provider's official recovery process instead. The course cannot certify that a real account is secure.


Give each organization one clear job






Confirmed issue
Suitable recipient and route
Evidence / requested help





Deceptive transfer or exposed financial account
Financial institution through an existing statement/card or genuine app
Payment details and truthful account of approval/exposure; ask about protection, investigation and possible recovery.




Entered/reused credentials
Affected account providers through known apps or independently reached official support
Affected account names and access status; secure credentials, sessions and recovery methods.




Fraud incident or identity misuse
Local police via independently reached official local route; CAFC-linked Report Cybercrime and Fraud
Dated incident, amounts/categories, evidence and provider references; reporting is separate from account controls.




Unauthorized CRA-account information change
CRA through the official Canada.ca report-scam/identity-theft page
Identify the observed change and request the relevant account protection/identity assistance.




SIN exposure or credit identity concerns
Both credit bureaus through links on Service Canada's official SIN page, plus affected creditors/programs when relevant
Review reports, ask about appropriate alerts or dispute unfamiliar credit activity; an alert is not a universal account lock.





The table supplies routes rather than memorized phone numbers. A route is independent when it comes from a trusted source already held or an official page reached without the suspicious message's link. A caller who says “use this number to verify me” is still controlling the proposed route. An official-looking logo or knowledge of an incident does not change that.


Keep a living status log


Use three columns: action planned → action taken and reference → result or next check. “Reported to bank” does not mean “money refunded.” “Changed password” does not mean every active session ended. “Subscription closed” does not mean a disputed charge was reversed. Specific status language prevents false reassurance and shows which task remains.


Record times, amounts, contact labels, categories disclosed, responses and case references. Do not put a password, SIN, full account number or one-time code into the course. Existing evidence can be kept safely; do not revisit an unsafe page or continue a scam conversation to gather more. Real institutions may have secure evidence processes; reach them independently before sharing sensitive originals.


Reject a second loss without blame


An offer of guaranteed recovery can be attractive after a loss. That is why a recovery scam may repeat the amount, impersonate an agency and insist on a fee, code or secrecy. Ari's stranger asks for both money and an email code while discouraging the bank. Stop that interaction and preserve the existing message. The person's first mistake does not create an obligation to keep paying or to prove they deserve help.


Optional first-step hint: “Draw two branches from Ari's record: $160 → bank; reused email/music password → connected providers. Add reporting and follow-up after those controls.”


Follow a complete example
I begin with the financial fact: Ari approved the transfer under deceptive circumstances. I do not call it an unapproved transaction, and I do not assume a deposited transfer can simply be cancelled. I direct prompt notice to the bank through its genuine app, using the separate device.


Next I connect the email and music accounts. Both use the entered password, and the email is a recovery path for music. The provider guide tells me to handle sessions separately. The stranger's knowledge of $160 does not verify the offer; the proposed $40 payment and email code would create further exposure.


Complete coordinated plan:




At 2:00 p.m. on October 18, 2026, Ari approved a $160 transfer for a ticket that was not supplied; the genuine bank app shows it deposited. Promptly use that app's independently known fraud-contact route from the separate updated device. Explain the deception, approval and deposited status; ask about payment/account protection, investigation and any available recovery. Preserve the existing transfer record and record the bank's reference and instructions. No refund or cancellation is established.


Stop using the false delivery page and do not answer the recovery stranger, pay $40 or send a code. Promptly secure the email account, then music, through the known app/bookmark. Use different strong passwords, review recovery details and other sessions, sign out other sessions using the supplied controls, and enable supported MFA. If access or recovery details cannot be secured, use official provider recovery support. Record completed steps and remaining issues.


Keep the seller conversation, transfer record, login request and recovery message without putting passwords or full financial details in this plan. Report the fraud to local police through the independently reached official local route and to the CAFC-linked Report Cybercrime and Fraud service; retain any references. Continue checking the affected bank and accounts for changes and follow provider advice. The supplied exposure is money, an email/music credential, name and mailing address. Do not invent SIN theft, a new credit account or a CRA change, or assume a credit alert is automatically necessary solely because the name/address were disclosed. Reassess if new evidence appears. Reporting supports the response but does not itself secure the accounts or guarantee the $160 returns.




The unsupported shortcut is “CAFC will recover everything; wait for its answer.” It leaves the bank and exposed credentials unattended and invents a result. Coordination means several specific jobs, each with a relevant recipient.


Next: Practise with support. Try “Update completed and pending work” before opening its comparison model.
Practise with support
Keep the original exposure facts. At 3:10 p.m. on October 18, these new fictional status records are supplied:


    

  • Bank acknowledgement T-18: the deceptive-transfer report has been opened. Review is pending. No recovery is confirmed. The bank asks Ari to retain the transfer evidence and follow its further instructions through the genuine app.
    • 

  • Email security log E-18: a unique new password has been set, recovery details reviewed, other sessions signed out and supported MFA enabled. No unfamiliar recovery detail was found. This records completed email controls, not proof that no information was previously copied.
    • 

  • Music status: its reused password and sessions have not yet been addressed; access still works through the saved official bookmark.
    • 

  • The recovery stranger repeats the $40/code demand and now writes “case T-18 proves I work with your bank.” The bank acknowledgement contains no referral to this person. How the stranger obtained that label is unknown.
    • 



Use these three fields:


    

  1. Update completed and pending work — distinguish the bank report, email controls and unresolved music-account task.
    2. 

  2. Write the next priority and safe route — give the next account action and explain the continuing bank follow-up without inventing a result.
    3. 

  3. Respond to the new verification claim in the plan — explain why the case label is insufficient and state a safe response/evidence action.
    4. 



Show a first-step hint: “A reference label describes a report; it does not authenticate everyone who repeats it.” Select Compare your response with a model to see: “Have you left the bank result pending, recognized completed email controls, prioritized the still-reused music password, and rejected the code/fee request? A new label in the stranger's message does not replace independent verification.” Open Compare your response with a model when useful.

Compare your response with a model
Your current response


Bank report T-18 is open, with review pending and no confirmed recovery. Email controls E-18 are recorded as completed; this does not establish that nothing was copied earlier. Music remains exposed through the reused password and any existing sessions. Next, use the saved official music bookmark on the separate device to set a different strong password, review recovery details, sign out other sessions and enable supported MFA. Retain the bank acknowledgement and follow further instructions through the genuine app while continuing to monitor the affected accounts.


Do not pay the stranger or send a code. Knowledge of T-18 does not establish a bank role, and the bank record contains no referral. Save the already received message as an additional impersonation/recovery-scam concern. If checking any claimed bank instruction, return independently to the genuine app's contact route. Record later actual provider/reporting results without inventing a refund.


Select Return to my response to return to the first field. Keep the plan precise enough that another reader could identify the unfinished work.
Next: Check your understanding. Choose an answer and check it. Use the hint to revise; a repeated unchanged check is not another attempt.
Check your understanding
Why does Ari's bank need an accurate description that Ari approved the transfer under deception?
Which status entry is supported after guided document T-18?
A stranger knows Ari's loss and bank reference and demands a code plus fee. What should the plan conclude?
Only a public name is known to a suspicious sender; no sensitive identity exposure or credit misuse is established. Which response is best supported?
According to the supplied current Service Canada SIN record, what follows from suspected SIN exposure?
An independently opened CRA account shows a bank-detail change the person did not request. Which recipient is specifically needed in addition to general fraud reporting?
Next: Nico's identity and account-response file. Read the new situation and its supplied records before filling your independent response. Use the method you practised with the evidence in this new case.
Apply independently
Nico's identity and account-response file


Nico is a fictional 19-year-old. This new case has no ticket transfer and no entered account password. Prepare a coordinated identity-response plan from the supplied records.


Document E — Job-form exposure, October 21, 2026, 9:00 a.m. Nico submitted a supposed employer's onboarding form before any interview or verified job offer. It requested and received Nico's full name, date of birth, mailing address, SIN and bank direct-deposit routing/account details. The actual numbers are omitted. Nico did not enter any bank/email/CRA password, card number, PIN or one-time code, upload an identity-document image, install an app or grant remote access. No money was sent. Nico later independently reached the named employer through its known public office and learned it had no such application or offer. The saved form summary and messages are available without reopening the false form.


Document F — Independently observed records, October 21, 10:00 a.m. Nico opened the genuine bank app and the official CRA account using a separate updated personal device and previously established sign-in routes. The bank showed no unfamiliar transaction at that time. The CRA account showed direct-deposit information changed that morning to an account Nico does not recognize and did not request. The actual account digits are omitted. How the change was made is unknown. Nico can still access the account. No CRA support report or bank notification has yet occurred. No credit reports have yet been reviewed; no new credit account is confirmed.


Document G — Recovery message, 10:10 a.m. An unverified sender claims to be a national fraud-recovery officer and requests a $65 “identity reset” fee plus a CRA one-time sign-in code. The sender promises to erase all identity records and tells Nico not to contact CRA. No referral to this person appears in any independently reached official record. Nico has not paid or sent a code.


Document H — Routes and evidence available. Nico has the genuine bank app's security/support contact, the official CRA report-scam/identity-theft page, the official Service Canada SIN fraud/data-breach page with its links to Equifax and TransUnion, the official local police site, and CAFC's official victim-response page linking to Report Cybercrime and Fraud. These are independently reached official resources, represented by the dated source records in this lesson. No live visit is needed. The evidence set includes the job messages, form summary with sensitive numbers safely excluded from this exercise, independent employer verification, the observed CRA-change record, bank observation time and recovery message. There is no result from an investigation yet.


Use four fields. Label the actions so the recipient, purpose, route and pending result are easy to see. Do not write any real identity or account number.


    

  • Map confirmed exposure, misuse and unknowns — distinguish what the form received, what was independently observed and what remains unconfirmed.
    • 

  • Build the prioritized response plan — choose the first account/institution actions with reasons, independent routes, and appropriate identity/credit steps. Explain the role of the current SIN guidance without requiring routine SIN replacement.
    • 

  • Prepare the reporting and evidence log — name the separate police/fraud-reporting roles, list the useful dated records and show how later references/results will be recorded.
    • 

  • Set boundaries and follow-up triggers — respond to the recovery message, explain what to monitor and what new evidence would change the plan; state what cannot yet be promised.
    • 



Use CRA’s reporting guidance for Nico’s observed change
FINLIT’s Avoiding Frauds and Scams Assignment 8.3, question 1 asks what to do after CRA-related fraud. Nico’s file gives that question a specific reason: an unauthorized direct-deposit change is visible in the genuine CRA account.
CRA: Report a scam or identity theft ↗ — read “Report the incident to the CRA,” then “Inform other authorities.” Checked September 28, 2026; the page displayed March 20, 2026 as its update date.
Relevant guidance: CRA asks people to contact it about unauthorized account changes. Its official reporting page provides online and telephone routes for requesting protection. It also identifies other organizations to notify for compromised information and asks people to notify the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre after reporting account changes.
Use it in your plan: connect Nico’s observed change to CRA account protection; connect the disclosed bank details to the bank; connect identity misuse concerns to credit-record checks and reporting. A general fraud report does not itself correct CRA or bank records. No diverted payment is confirmed in Nico’s file.
Which line belongs in Nico’s response plan?

The false job form received Nico's name, date of birth, mailing address, SIN and bank direct-deposit details. No password, card data, PIN, code, ID image, app installation, remote access or payment is supplied. At 10:00 a.m., the genuine CRA account showed an unauthorized direct-deposit change; its mechanism and any diverted payment are unknown. The bank showed no unfamiliar transaction at that observation time. Credit reports have not been checked, so no new credit account is established. These are stronger identity-misuse concerns than name exposure alone.


Stop interacting with the false employer and recovery sender. Promptly contact CRA through the independently reached Canada.ca report-scam/identity-theft route because an actual unauthorized CRA change is visible. Describe the observation and seek its account-protection, identity and correction instructions; do not assume a CAFC report performs those controls. Promptly notify the bank through its genuine app's security/support route about the exposed direct-deposit details and identity information, even though no unfamiliar transaction was visible at 10:00. Ask what monitoring and account protections fit that exposure, and follow its instructions rather than claiming the bank password or card was stolen.


Use the official Service Canada SIN page's links to both Equifax and TransUnion to review credit information and ask about fraud alerts appropriate to this SIN exposure and observed identity misuse. Investigate and dispute any unfamiliar credit activity through the relevant bureau and creditor if it appears. A fraud alert is an additional verification measure, not a guarantee that every account is locked. Follow the current SIN page: suspected misuse does not require notifying the SIN Program or routinely getting a new SIN. Contact the affected program—CRA here—for the misuse involving it. Do not infer that a new SIN would erase the old records.


Report the suspected fraud/identity misuse to local police through the independently reached official local route and to the CAFC-linked Report Cybercrime and Fraud service. Retain report references and give consistent facts. A privacy-safe log begins: “October 21: 9:00 false onboarding form received name, birth date, address, SIN and direct-deposit details; no passwords/codes/payment. Employer independently denied application/offer. 10:00 genuine CRA account showed unrequested bank-detail change; bank app showed no unfamiliar transaction at that time. 10:10 unverified recovery sender demanded $65 and CRA code; neither supplied.” Retain the already available messages, safe form summary, employer verification and account observations; append actual provider actions, references and results without putting the numbers or code into the course.


Do not pay $65, send a code or follow the stranger's contact route. A claimed agency title and an “identity reset” promise do not establish authority. Continue monitoring the bank, CRA information and credit records through trusted routes and follow official provider instructions. An unfamiliar credit account would add contact with that creditor and bureau; an unfamiliar bank transaction would require prompt bank reporting; an uncorrected CRA change would require CRA follow-up. No refund, clean identity record, recovered payment or completed investigation is established. The plan can prioritize CRA and bank actions close together; a different order is acceptable if it explains both urgent exposures and does not postpone them for a general report.
